questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspepsia and unintentional weight loss over 3 months. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. CT scan shows thickening of the gastric mucosa without distant spread. Upper GI endoscopy reveals nodular gastric folds. Biopsy demonstrates proliferation of small, clonal B lymphocytes expressing CD20 within the gastric mucosa. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
options: Chronic antigenic stimulation by persistent infection
Viral oncogene–mediated inhibition of tumor suppressor genes
Immune evasion through downregulation of MHC molecules
Activation of somatic hypermutation in germinal centers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic antigenic stimulation by persistent infection

This patient has gastric MALT lymphoma, a low-grade B-cell lymphoma strongly associated with Helicobacter pylori infection. The pathogenesis involves chronic antigenic stimulation, where persistent infection leads to continuous activation and proliferation of B cells in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT). Over time, this can result in monoclonal expansion and lymphoma formation.

Importantly, early-stage disease may regress with eradication of H. pylori, highlighting the immune-driven mechanism.

Why not other options?

B. Viral oncogene–mediated p53 inhibition → Seen in HPV-related cancers (e.g., cervical carcinoma)

C. Immune evasion (↓ MHC expression) → Mechanism used by tumors to escape immunity, not primary cause

D. Somatic hypermutation activation → Normal germinal center process; not the initiating mechanism
questions.learning: Chronic antigenic stimulation by persistent infection This patient has gastric MALT lymphoma, a low-grade B-cell lymphoma strongly associated with Helicobacter pylori infection.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought to the emergency department with respiratory distress. On evaluation, imaging reveals a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect as shown in the X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms and X-ray findings indicate a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), specifically a Bochdalek hernia. This is the most common type of CDH, accounting for 90% of cases, and typically presents through a posterolateral defect, occurring predominantly on the left side (80–90%). Morgagni hernia (Option B) is a retrosternal defect occurring through the foramen of Morgagni and accounts for only 2–6% of cases. Hiatal hernia (Option C) occurs specifically at the esophageal hiatus and does not present with the massive herniation of abdominal organs seen here. Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia (Option D) is not the diagnosis in this newborn scenario because there is no history of significant trauma. Pathologically, CDH leads to lung compression and pulmonary hypoplasia, causing respiratory distress, cyanosis, and a scaphoid abdomen. Immediate management requires neonatal stabilization with intubation and gastric decompression before surgical repair is performed, usually after 48 hours

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: True about therapeutic index of a drug is:
options: Denotes safety and efficacy after experiments on humans
Denotes safety and efficacy in the population
Denotes safety and efficacy in an individual
Ratio of median lethal dose in 50% of population to median effective dose in 50% of population
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Denotes safety and efficacy in the population

The therapeutic index of a drug denotes the safety and efficacy of the drug in the population (option B), not the individual (option C).

The therapeutic index is calculated with the following equations:

LD50/ED50 or TD50/ED50

where LD50 is the median lethal dose, TD50 is the mean toxic dose, and ED50 is the median effective dose

The therapeutic index (TI) describes a relationship between the doses of a drug that causes lethal or toxic effects with the dose that causes therapeutic effects. It is also called the therapeutic ratio. The therapeutic index is used to assess the safety of the drug administered.

Median lethal dose (LD50) and median toxic dose (TD50)

• LD50 is the dose of the drug at which 50% of the experimental animals die
• In human trials, TD50 can be considered. It is the dose of the drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population (Option D)
• The larger the LD50 or TD50, the safer the drug

Median effective dose (ED50) is the quantity of a drug that can produce the desired therapeutic effects in 50% of the population.

Therapeutic window refers to a range of concentrations at which the likelihood of efficacy is high and the probability of adverse effects is low.

Note: Option D is incorrect as it does not make the necessary distinction that the therapeutic index is the ratio of the median lethal dose in 50% of animals (as the human population cannot be used for lethal studies) to the median effective dose in 50% of the population. LD50 is measured in animals, not in humans. Option B is a better choice.
questions.learning: Denotes safety and efficacy in the population — The therapeutic index of a drug denotes the safety and efficacy of the drug in the population (option B), not the individual (option C).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presents with hematuria, edema, and hypertension. Laboratory investigations reveal low serum C3 levels with coarse granular C3 deposits on immunofluorescence. Renal biopsy shows diffuse glomerular hypercellularity on light microscopy, while electron microscopy demonstrates characteristic subepithelial “hump-shaped” electron-dense deposits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a post-infectious immune complex– mediated nephritic syndrome that typically occurs 1– 3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3– 6 weeks after skin infection (impetigo). It presents with hematuria, edema, hypertension, and low serum C3 due to complement activation.

• The classic pathological triad of PSGN is:

• Light microscopy (LM): Diffuse endocapillary proliferative glomerulonephritis with hypercellularity.
• Immunofluorescence (IF): Coarse granular (“starry sky/lumpy-bumpy”) deposits of IgG and C3 along the GBM and mesangium.
• Electron microscopy (EM): Subepithelial electron-dense “hump”-shaped deposits (hallmark finding).

Why not the other options?

• A. Goodpasture syndrome: Linear IgG deposition on IF; anti-GBM antibodies; pulmonary hemorrhage is common.
• B. Membranous nephropathy: Diffuse GBM thickening with subepithelial deposits and spike-and-dome appearance; presents with nephrotic syndrome.
• D. Minimal change disease: Normal LM, negative IF, diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on EM; presents with nephrotic syndrome.
questions.learning: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a post-infectious immune complex– mediated nephritic syndrome that typically occurs 1– 3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3– 6 weeks after skin infection (impetigo).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During minimally invasive inguinal hernia surgery, in order to obtain the “critical view of MPO (Myopectineal orifice)”, the space of Retzius must be dissected. At what distance must the dissection be carried out from the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 cm

The “Critical View of the Myopectineal Orifice (MPO)” is an essential step during laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair (TEP/TAPP) to ensure complete mesh coverage of all potential hernia sites and minimize recurrence. Adequate dissection of the space of Retzius should extend at least 2 cm beyond the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament.

• Dissection of the space of Retzius should be carried ≥2 cm medial to the pubic tubercle and Cooper’s ligament.
• This ensures:

• Complete exposure of the myopectineal orifice
• Adequate medial mesh overlap
• Reduced risk of mesh migration and hernia recurrence

Why not the other options?

• A. 0.5 cm: Inadequate medial dissection.
• B. 1 cm: Insufficient to achieve the critical view.
• D. 4 cm: More extensive than routinely required and not part of the standard definition of the critical view.
questions.learning: 2 cm The “Critical View of the Myopectineal Orifice (MPO)” is an essential step during laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair (TEP/TAPP) to ensure complete mesh coverage of all potential hernia sites and minimize recurrence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A car driver was brought into the A&E following a RTA with complaints of breathlessness. On examination his vitals are PR-112/min, BP-100/70, SpO2-90% and there is extensive bruising on his chest.Chest Xray is as below. What is the management of this patient?
options: Internal operative fixation of the fractures segments
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IPPV

The diagnosis here is flail chest with respiratory failure and the management with respiratory failure is IPPV.

Flail Chest :

* A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage.

* This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places.

* The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well.

Clinical Features:

On inspiration the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air therefore moves into the lungs.On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration).

Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement and the associated lung contusion are all causes of the hypoxia and respiratory failure.

The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Treatment

* Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided

* Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) or epidural analgesia and physiotherapy.

* IPPV (Intermitent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for cases developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with diarrhea, cognitive impairment, and a characteristic rash. Which vitamin deficiency most likely explains these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with the "3 Ds" of pellagra: Diarrhea, Dermatitis (distinctive rash), and Dementia (memory impairment). Pellagra is the clinical result of Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency (Option B). The rash in pellagra is typically symmetrical and appears on sun-exposed areas, classically forming a "necklace" pattern around the neck known as Casal's necklace. Niacin is essential for the production of NAD and NADP, which are vital coenzymes for energy metabolism. Thiamine deficiency (Option A) leads to Beriberi or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Cyanocobalamin (B12) deficiency (Option C) causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological degeneration. Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) deficiency (Option D) leads to scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Pellagra can be caused by a diet based primarily on corn, which is low in available niacin and its precursor tryptophan. Thus, Niacin is the responsible vitamin
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with the "3 Ds" of pellagra: Diarrhea, Dermatitis (distinctive rash), and Dementia (memory impairment). Pellagra is the clinical result of Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency (Option B).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most probable diagnosis based on the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6th nerve palsy

The given image depicts restricted lateral movement of the left eye when the person is in left lateral gaze. This is suggestive of left lateral rectus muscle paralysis due to isolated 6th cranial nerve palsy.

Isolated abducens(6th cranial) nerve palsy presents with esotropia / convergent squint in primary position with limitation of abduction on the side of the lesion.
This is due to unopposed action of the medial rectus muscle in the affected eye. There is also a compensatory head turn towards the side of the lesion to reduce the symptom of diplopia. The adduction is normal in 6th nerve palsy.

The various causes of 6th nerve palsy includes:

• Raised intracranial pressure
• Nasopharyngeal tumors
• Gradenigo syndrome as seen in mastoiditis or acute petrositis
• Basal skull fracture

Option A: 3rd Cranial nerve palsy presents with

• ptosis due to weakness of levator palpebrae superioris muscle(LPS)
• Abduction and depression in the primary position(down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus(6th nerve supply) and superior oblique muscles(4th nerve supply)
• Dilated pupil and defective accommodation due to parasympathetic palsy(involvement of Edinger Westphal parasympathetic supply)
• Limited adduction, elevation due to ipsilateral paralysis of medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus .

Option D: Bell’s palsy is an acute onset, idiopathic lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve which involves the ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.
It presents with an inability to close the eye and any attempts to close the eye results in the eye turning upwards and outwards which is known as the Bell’s phenomenon. Other features of Bell's palsy include drooling of saliva, deviation of angle of the mouth and facial asymmetry. Additionally there may be noise intolerance and a loss of taste sensation.
The following image shows a patient with Bell’s palsy:

Option D: Horner syndrome, also called oculosympathetic paresis, is produced by a lesion anywhere along the sympathetic pathway supplying the head, neck and eyes. It is characterized by the classical triad of ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis(reduced ipsilateral sweating). Other features include mild enophthalmos, hypochromic heterochromia and anisocoria that is accentuated in dim light.

Tests for confirmation of Horner's syndrome -

• Cocaine drops (2-4%)
Horner pupil does not dilate
Normal pupil dilates
• Apraclonidine drops (0.5-1%)
Horner pupil dilates - due to upregulation of α1 receptors in the dilator pupillae.
Normal pupil does not dilate

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging reveals an abnormal finding marked by an arrow. Based on this radiological feature, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The axial Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) scan shows renal tissue crossing the midline anterior to the aorta and vertebral column, connecting the lower poles of both kidneys. This "isthmus" of tissue is the definitive diagnostic feature of a Horseshoe Kidney (Option B). Appendicitis (Option A) would show a thickened, blind-ending tubular structure in the right iliac fossa, not renal tissue crossing the aorta. Wilms Tumor (Option C) is a large, distorted renal mass primarily seen in children, not a symmetrical fusion anomaly. An abdominal aortic aneurysm (Option D) would show an enlarged, dilated aorta often with mural thrombus, which is unrelated to renal fusion. Although often asymptomatic, horseshoe kidneys can cause abdominal pain if there is associated hydronephrosis or stone formation. Therefore, the anatomical bridge of renal parenchyma across the great vessels identifies this fused renal state
questions.learning: The axial Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) scan shows renal tissue crossing the midline anterior to the aorta and vertebral column, connecting the lower poles of both kidneys.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, headache, and a focal seizure. EEG reveals temporal lobe spike activity, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows 50 cells with lymphocytic predominance. Based on these findings, which drug is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fever, headache, and focal seizures combined with temporal lobe involvement on EEG is highly suggestive of Herpes Simplex Encephalitis (HSE) . The CSF profile showing lymphocytic pleocytosis further supports a viral etiology. Intravenous Acyclovir is the gold-standard, life-saving initial treatment for HSE. It acts as a nucleoside analog that selectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase. Valacyclovir (Option A) is an oral prodrug used for less severe infections like shingles or genital herpes, but it is not appropriate for the acute management of encephalitis. Ganciclovir (Option C) and Foscarnet (Option D) are primarily used for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Because HSE is a medical emergency with high mortality if untreated, immediate empiric administration of IV Acyclovir is the definitive standard of care while awaiting PCR confirmation
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of fever, headache, and focal seizures combined with temporal lobe involvement on EEG is highly suggestive of Herpes Simplex Encephalitis (HSE) .

questions.text: Cytotoxic and expired drugs are disposed by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incineration

Cytotoxic and expired drugs are collected in a yellow bag and then disposed of by incineration.

Expired cytotoxic drugs are to be returned to the manufacturer and subjected to incineration, encapsulation, or plasma pyrolysis. Other discarded medicines can be disposed by incineration.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised A public health worker is going out into the community once every 15 days for collection of blood smears for malaria surveillance. What type of surveillance is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Active

Active case detection is done every fortnight by examination of blood smears by house visits and it is a type of active surveillance.

Malaria surveillance system:

Active case detection: Blood smears are collected by the Multipurpose Workers/Auxiliary nurse midwife on house visits every fortnight.

Passive case detection: Detection of fever cases that report to ASHAs or peripheral health volunteers.

Surveillance: There are factors which determine occurrence and distribution of diseases and other conditions of ill health. These factors are continuously scrutinised in surveillance. Monitoring is one of the essential components of surveillance concept.

Objectives of surveillance are:

* To provide information about changing health trends

* To provide feedback which can change health policy

* To provide public health disaster warnings

* Objectives:

* By 2024, incidence of malaria to be reduced to less than 1 case per 1000 population.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following instruments is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lim’s forceps

The instrument shown in the image above is Lim's forceps.

Lim's forceps are a type of surgical instrument used in ophthalmic procedures. They are designed for delicate manipulations within the eye during surgery. These forceps typically have fine tips and a delicate grip, allowing surgeons to handle delicate tissues with precision.

Other options:

Option B: McPherson suture tying forceps are commonly used in ophthalmic surgery for grasping and tying sutures. They have a fine, curved tip which allows surgeons to manipulate sutures within the eye or in areas where precision is required, such as in delicate eye surgeries like cataract surgery.

Option C: Corneoscleral forceps are specialized instruments used in eye surgery for handling the cornea and sclera, the outer layers of the eye. These forceps have a unique design that allows surgeons to securely grasp and manipulate these tissues during various procedures, such as corneal transplantation or scleral flap surgery.

Option D: Lens holding forceps are surgical instruments used in ophthalmic procedures involving the removal or manipulation of the lens of the eye. They are designed to securely grasp the lens during procedures such as cataract surgery or intraocular lens implantation, allowing surgeons to manipulate the lens safely and precisely.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A research study is being conducted on patients in rehabilitation where the impact of addiction among young adults was assessed on their subsequent divorce. Among two groups of study subjects, divorced and non-divorced, the history of alcohol or drug use was assessed. What kind of study is being done here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Case control study

The above study design is typical of a case-control study. Here the divorced group acts as a case study group while the non-divorced group acts as a control group.

* A case-control study uses individuals as the unit.

* The study proceeds from effect to cause and is done after the exposure and outcome have occurred.

* This is the first approach to test causal hypotheses and uses controls to support or refute an inference.

* A nested case-control study is a case-control study nested in a cohort study and it is a type of cohort study which moves in the forward direction.

Pearl PF0958: Types of Epidemiological Study Designs

Types of Epidemiological Study Designs

The flow chart below gives a glance into the types of epidemiological study designs and where they are generally used.

Note: Descripitve study is used to formulate aetiological hypothesis of a disease. Whereas analytical study is used to test the hypothesis (i.e to accept or reject the hypothesis).

Pearl PF1701: Case Control Study

In a case-control study, progression is from effect (disease) to cause (exposure) as the outcome or disease has already occurred. It is also called a retrospective study.

Design of case-control study:

* Steps of case control study:

* Selection of cases and controls

* Matching

* Measurement of exposure

* Analysis in the form of exposure rates, risk ratio, and odds ratio

* Advantages of case control study:

* Easy to carry out, rapid and inexpensive

* Requires few subjects, no risk to subjects

* Used to investigate rare diseases

* Different etiological factors can be studied and risk factors can be identified

* No attrition problems, minimal ethical problems

* Disadvantages of case control study:

* Relies on memory or past records giving rise to bias

* Selection of appropriate control groups is difficult

* Incidence cannot be measured

* Does not distinguish between causes and associated factors

* Not suited for evaluation of therapy or prophylaxis

* Representativeness of the cases and controls is often inadequate

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Asbestos exposure may be associated with which of the following malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mesothelioma

Asbestosis is most commonly associated with Mesotheliomas.

Asbestos-related diseases include:

* Localized fibrous plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis

* Pleural effusion

* Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)

* Lung carcinoma

* Mesotheliomas

* Laryngeal, ovarian, and colon carcinomas

Asbestosis:

* Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that occurs after 5-10 years of exposure to asbestos. However, once established, it progresses even in the further removal of the worker from its contact. Asbestosis affects the basal part of the lung causing diffuse peribronchial fibrosis.

* Asbestos is of 2 types i.e Serpentine/Chrysolite variety and Amphibole type

* Amphibole type has the following varieties:

* Crocidolite(blue)

* Amosite(brown)

* Anthophyllite(white)

* Sputum shows asbestos bodies, which are asbestos fibers coated with fibrin.

* They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea and predominantly affect the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.

* X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. HRCT shows subpleural fibrotic lines, irregular opacities, traction bronchiectasis, and honeycombing. Lung parenchymal involvement occurs after years of exposure (at least 10 years).

* The complications that can occur are

* Pulmonary fibrosis

* Carcinoma of the lung

* Malignancy of the Gastrointestinal tract

* Mesothelioma of the pleura

Preventive measures:

* Using a safer type of Asbestos (chrysolite and amosite)

* Substituting other insulants like glass fiber, mineral wool, calcium silicate, plastic foams, etc.

* Dust control

* Periodic examination of workers

* Continuing research

Option B: Acute myeloid leukemia may be caused by benzene exposure.

Option C: Hepatic angiosarcoma can be seen in exposure to vinyl chloride.

Option D: Skin carcinoma may be seen with exposure to arsenic and arsenic compounds.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the condition depicted in the laparoscopic image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Genital tuberculosis

The laproscopic image above depicts multiple miliary nodules on the uterine and peritoneal surfaces. This guides us towards the diagnosis of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB).

Genital Tuberculosis is caused by M. tuberculosis and almost always occurs secondary to primary infection elsewhere in the extragenital states. Most common route of spread is hematogenous and the most common site is bilateral fallopian tubes (the most common part affected is ampulla and most common pathology encountered is endosalpingitis). 20-30 years age group is affected the most. Infertility is the most common symptom.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which oxygen delivery device provides a fixed and consistent FiO₂ of 0.25–0.60, independent of the patient’s respiratory pattern?
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery systems are classified as low-flow or high-flow. The Venturi mask (Option C) is a high-flow system that utilizes the Bernoulli principle to mix a specific flow of oxygen with room air. This creates a fixed, accurate fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) typically ranging from 0.24 to 0.60, which remains constant regardless of the patient's inspiratory flow rate or depth of breathing. Nasal cannulae (Option A) and simple face masks (Option B) are low-flow systems where the actual FiO2 varies significantly based on the patient's respiratory effort and room air entrainment. A non-rebreathing mask (Option D) provides high FiO2 (up to 0.90) but is also a reservoir-dependent system that does not offer the same precise titration as a Venturi mask. Therefore, the Venturi mask is the most reliable system for patients requiring a precise, constant oxygen concentration, such as those with COPD
questions.learning: Oxygen delivery systems are classified as low-flow or high-flow. The Venturi mask (Option C) is a high-flow system that utilizes the Bernoulli principle to mix a specific flow of oxygen with room air.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase

Methotrexate is an antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue that inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Methotrexate and its polyglutamate also inhibit the enzymes involved in de novo purine and thymidylate synthesis.

It is curative in choriocarcinoma and is used to maintain remission in children with acute leukemias. It has prominent immunosuppressant properties that are useful in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and many other autoimmune disorders. When toxicity occurs, it manifests as nausea, loose stool, stomatitis, punctate cutaneous eruption, alopecia and hematologic abnormalities, particularly macrocytosis.

Pearl PF1704: Classification of antineoplastic drugs
questions.learning: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase Methotrexate is an antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue that inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Gonadal growth corresponds with
questions.explanation: According to Scammon's curves of systemic growth, the growth of the gonadal (genital) system remains very slow during childhood but undergoes a massive surge during puberty. This pattern of rapid acceleration in adolescence closely corresponds with the skeletal system's growth spurt during the same period. In contrast, the brain (Option A) and nervous system reach nearly adult size by age 6. Lymphoid growth (Option C) actually peaks around age 10–12 (reaching 200% of adult size) before regressing after puberty. Dental growth (Option D) follows a different developmental timeline related to primary and permanent tooth eruption. Understanding these distinct growth patterns is essential for pediatricians and endocrinologists to assess if a child's development is proceeding normally. The synchronization of skeletal maturation (bone age) and genital development is a hallmark of the pubertal process, making the skeletal system the most appropriate correlate for gonadal growth among the listed options
questions.learning: According to Scammon's curves of systemic growth, the growth of the gonadal (genital) system remains very slow during childhood but undergoes a massive surge during puberty.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the section of the intestine shown in the barium study below
questions.explanation: The barium study image displays a characteristic "feathery" or "plume-like" mucosal pattern, which is diagnostic for the jejunum. This appearance is due to the presence of numerous, prominent circular mucosal folds called plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes). In contrast, the ileum (Option A) has fewer folds, appearing smoother on barium studies. The transverse colon (Option B) and splenic flexure (Option D) would show haustrations (sacculations), which are much larger and more widely spaced than the small intestinal folds. Barium meal follow-through is a valuable radiological tool for evaluating malabsorption syndromes or obstructions. In conditions like Celiac disease, the jejunal folds may become flattened, a process known as "jejunization" of the ileum or loss of the feathery pattern. Consequently, the high density of valvulae conniventes seen in the upper small bowel loops of the provided radiograph definitively identifies the section as the jejunum rather than the distal ileum or large intestine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-nuclear antibodies are required for the diagnosis of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Systemic lupus erythematosus

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are required for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus.

ANAs are autoantibodies that bind to the contents of the cell nucleus. They are present in > 95% of patients with SLE. A positive antinuclear antibody ( ANA ) test with a titer of at least 1:80 is the obligatory entry criterion along with the additive criteria in 7 clinical and 3 immunologic domains. If a total of >10 points achieved, it is indicative of SLE according to 2019 EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

Most sensitive antibody for SLE: ANA

Most specific antibody for SLE: Anti smith > Anti dsDNA
ANA may also be positive in the other options but it is not a criterion for diagnosis of these conditions.

The following antibodies are specific for their respective autoimmune conditions.

• Scleroderma (option A): Anti-topoisomerase I(Scl-70) and anti-centromere antibodies highly specific for Systemic sclerosis.
• Rheumatoid arthritis (option C): RF and anti-CCP antibodies
• Sjogren syndrome (option D): Anti-Ro, Anti-La
questions.learning: Systemic lupus erythematosus Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are required for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus. ANAs are autoantibodies that bind to the contents of the cell nucleus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: How much mg of iron and mcg of folic acid should a pregnant woman be given?
questions.explanation: According to the National Iron Plus Initiative (NIPI) and the Anemia Mukt Bharat guidelines in India, all pregnant women must receive routine iron and folic acid (IFA) supplementation. The standard regimen is one tablet containing of elemental iron and of folic acid, taken daily for at least 180 days, starting from the second trimester. Options A, B, and D provide incorrect dosing frequencies. This supplementation is critical to meet the increased physiological demands of pregnancy, prevent maternal iron-deficiency anemia, and reduce the risk of low birth weight and preterm delivery. For women found to be already anemic (Hb < 11 g/dL), the dose is doubled to two tablets daily. Proper counseling on taking the tablet with water and avoiding tea or coffee is essential to ensure optimal absorption. IFA supplementation is a cornerstone of global public health strategies to reduce maternal mortality and improve neonatal health outcomes
questions.learning: According to the National Iron Plus Initiative (NIPI) and the Anemia Mukt Bharat guidelines in India, all pregnant women must receive routine iron and folic acid (IFA) supplementation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 56-year-old multipara woman presented with grade II/III uterine prolapse with cystocele. She complains of passing urine on coughing and sneezing. What is the type of urinary incontinence seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stress incontinence

The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

Stress incontinence refers to the involuntary leakage of urine when there is increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing, Valsalva maneuver). Absence of detrusor muscle contraction is seen in urodynamic studies.

Causes:

• Age and menopause - due to estrogen deficiency
• Multiparity - due to loss of pelvic muscle tone
• Obesity
• Smoking
• Constipation, chronic cough
• Pelvic organ prolapse
• Pregnancy - due to the effect of progesterone and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder neck.
• Puerperium - due to descent of the bladder neck, loss of urethro-vesical angle, and reduced pelvic muscle tone
• Surgical repair of vesicovaginal fistula

Grading of genuine stress incontinence (GSI) :

• Grade I: Incontinence with only severe stress, such as coughing, sneezing, and jogging.
• Grade II: Incontinence with moderate stress, such as fast walk, going up and down the stairs.
• Grade III: Incontinence with mild stress such as standing.

Investigations are only done prior to surgery to confirm the diagnosis. They include:

• Stress test
• Cotton swab or Q-tip test
• Marshall and Bonney’s test
• Urethroscopy
• Urodynamic studies.

These are not required prior to conservative management.

Conservative management includes Kegel's pelvic exercises, electric nerve stimulation, devices like pessaries, vaginal cones, and artificial sphincters. Medical treatment with estrogen creams, alpha agonists, venlafaxine, and imipramine may be useful.

Other options:

Option A: Overflow incontinence is an old term that refers to the inability to empty the bladder, with involuntary, continuous urinary dribbling. Currently, it refers to another presentation of urge incontinence.

Option B: Urge incontinence is the involuntary escape of urine when there is an imminent need to urinate. It occurs due to detrusor muscle overactivity or detrusor instability. It is seen more commonly in old women with decreased bladder capacity, decreased sensation, and CNS inhibition.

Option D: Neurogenic bladder occurs in patients with neurogenic dysfunction leading to detrusor hyperreflexia. Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and spinal injury give rise to this. They present with urgency or urge incontinence.
questions.learning: Stress incontinence — The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The commonly used muscle relaxant with quickest onset of action and spontaneous recovery is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Suxamethonium

Suxamethonium (Succinylcholine) is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent with the fastest onset and shortest duration of action among commonly used muscle relaxants. It is the drug of choice for rapid sequence induction (RSI) because it produces excellent muscle relaxation within 30–60 seconds and spontaneous recovery occurs within 5–10 minutes due to rapid hydrolysis by plasma pseudocholinesterase.

Why not the other options?

• B. Vecuronium:

• Non-depolarizing muscle relaxant
• Slower onset (2–3 minutes)
• Intermediate duration (30–45 minutes)

• C. Atracurium:

• Intermediate onset (2–3 minutes)
• Intermediate duration
• Eliminated by Hofmann degradation

• D. Rocuronium:

• Fastest onset among non-depolarizing muscle relaxants (60–90 seconds)
• Duration: 30–60 minutes
• Can be rapidly reversed with Sugammadex
questions.learning: Suxamethonium Suxamethonium (Succinylcholine) is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent with the fastest onset and shortest duration of action among commonly used muscle relaxants.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with a history of a road traffic accident. On examination his vitals are stable, but he could not speak. He had no other neurological findings, had normal handwriting skills, and could understand what was being asked of him to which he responds by nodding. Where could be the lesion for this clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Broca's area

Broca’s area is concerned with word formation and is the most likely area to be involved as only speech production is affected here and all other examinating findings are normal.

Broca’s area is in the inferior frontal lobe.

Broca area processes the information received from Wernicke area into a detailed and coordinated pattern for vocalization and then projects the pattern via a speech articulation area in the insula to the motor cortex. This then initiates the appropriate movements of the lips, tongue, and larynx to produce speech.

The probable sequence of events that occurs when a subject names a visual object is shown in the figure and flowchart.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with erythematous plaques covered by silvery scales on the extensor surfaces of both arms, along with punctate nail pitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of erythematous plaques with pathognomonic silvery scales localized to the extensor surfaces (elbows/knees) is highly diagnostic of Psoriasis Vulgaris. Psoriasis is a chronic T-cell mediated autoimmune skin disease characterized by hyperproliferation of keratinocytes. A classic clinical clue provided is punctate nail pitting, which is a highly specific nail finding associated with psoriasis. Lichen planus (Option B) typically presents on flexor surfaces with "purple, pruritic, polygonal papules" and Wickham striae. Eczema (Option C) usually involves the flexural folds (anticubital fossa) and presents with poorly defined, itchy, weeping lesions. Pityriasis rosea (Option D) begins with a "herald patch" followed by a "Christmas tree" distribution of smaller scaly lesions on the trunk. Therefore, the specific combination of extensor plaques, silvery scales, and nail pitting confirms Psoriasis as the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of erythematous plaques with pathognomonic silvery scales localized to the extensor surfaces (elbows/knees) is highly diagnostic of Psoriasis Vulgaris.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a clinical evaluation, a patient reports deriving sexual gratification from inflicting physical injury on their partner, leading to cuts and burns. What term most accurately describes this behavior?
questions.explanation: The behavior described is a paraphilic disorder known as Sexual Sadism (Option C). It involves deriving sexual excitement and pleasure from the infliction of physical or psychological suffering, pain, or humiliation on another person. Masochism (Option D) is the opposite, where an individual derives pleasure from receiving pain or humiliation. Voyeurism (Option A) involves sexual arousal from observing unsuspecting people who are naked or engaging in sexual activity. Fetishism (Option B) involves sexual arousal from non-living objects or specific non-genital body parts. Because the patient's arousal is specifically linked to the active causing of harm (cuts and burns) to a partner, it fits the definitive clinical definition of sadism. This behavior can be part of a consensual relationship or can cross into criminal assault depending on the context and consent
questions.learning: The behavior described is a paraphilic disorder known as Sexual Sadism (Option C). It involves deriving sexual excitement and pleasure from the infliction of physical or psychological suffering, pain, or humiliation on another person.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A family was found dead in a closed room without windows, and smoke coming from a woodfire was present. Which of the following features is likely to be seen on their bodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cherry red hypostasis

In the case of a family found dead in a closed room with smoke from a wood fire, there is likely to be cherry red discoloration on their bodies. This discoloration is due to carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, which can occur from smoke in an enclosed space.

The colour of postmortem staining in CO poisoning is cherry red. Carbon monoxide is a byproduct of incomplete combustion of organic materials, such as wood. When inhaled, CO binds to hemoglobin in the blood with an affinity approximately 240 times greater than that of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, leading to tissue hypoxia.

The cherry red discolouration is a hallmark of CO poisoning. This occurs because COHb imparts a bright red colour, distinct from the darker hue associated with deoxygenated hemoglobin.

Postmortem hypostasis/Postmortem staining/Postmortem lividity/Livor mortis/Suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discolouration of the superficial layers of the skin due to the collection of blood in toneless capillaries.

It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to engorged vessels showing through the skin seen on the dependent parts due to the pooling of blood under the effect of gravity.

This staining starts as mottled patches 1-3 hours following death and develops to a uniform area of staining in 3-6 hours. Full development and fixation of hypostasis occur within 6–12 hours. This finding usually develops within 4 hours and persists until putrefaction. Fixation of hypostasis occurs earlier in the summer. It is delayed in asphyxial deaths and in intracranial lesions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which method is more effective than measuring clotting factors for assessing the intrinsic pathway of coagulation?

PT-Prothrombin time

APTT-Activated partial thromboplastin time

CBC-Complete blood count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. APTT

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is more effective than measuring clotting factors for assessing the intrinsic pathway, i.e. factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

Causes of prolonged APTT:

• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Liver disease
• Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells
• Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants
• A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor)
• Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII (since it is part of the extrinsic pathway)
• APTT is also moderately prolonged in patients taking oral anticoagulant drugs and in the presence of vitamin K deficiency

APTT is also moderately prolonged in patients taking oral anticoagulant drugs and in the presence of vitamin K deficiency (in which factors II, VII, IX, and X will fail to activate). A patient with previously undiagnosed haemophilia or another congenital coagulation disorder can also present with an isolated prolonged APTT.

Other options:

Option A: Prothrombin time evaluates the extrinsic pathway, i.e. factors VII, X, V, II (prothrombin), and fibrinogen. It measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin).

Causes of prolonged PT:

• Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs (vitamin K antagonists)
• Liver disease, particularly obstructive jaundice
• Vitamin K deficiency
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Rarely, a previously undiagnosed factor VII, X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect

Isolated prolonged prothrombin time occurs due to the deficiency of clotting factor VII.

Option C: Fibrinogen levels are used for measuring clotting.

Option D: Complete blood count is used to measure total RBC count, WBC count, and Platelet count.
questions.learning: APTT Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is more effective than measuring clotting factors for assessing the intrinsic pathway, i.e. factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with amenorrhea, headaches, visual disturbances, and milky discharge from the nipples. What is the most appropriate initial investigation to perform?
questions.explanation: The combination of amenorrhea (absent periods) and galactorrhea (milky nipple discharge) is known as the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome. This is most commonly caused by hyperprolactinemia. The presence of headaches and blurred vision (classically bitemporal hemianopia) strongly suggests a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma) that is large enough to compress the optic chiasm. The most appropriate initial test to confirm the diagnosis is measuring the serum prolactin level (Option A). hCG (Option D) should be checked to rule out pregnancy in any woman with amenorrhea, but it would not explain the milky discharge and visual symptoms. LH (Option B) and FSH (Option C) are used to evaluate hypothalamic or ovarian failure but are not the primary diagnostic tests for galactorrhea. If prolactin levels are significantly elevated, an MRI of the sella turcica is then indicated. Thus, prolactin is the prioritized biochemical test
questions.learning: The combination of amenorrhea (absent periods) and galactorrhea (milky nipple discharge) is known as the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome. This is most commonly caused by hyperprolactinemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with hypertriglyceridemia is considered for niacin therapy. She is a known diabetic managed adequately with sugars well under control. Why should niacin be used cautiously in this patient?
options: It can cause scleroderma which makes injecting insulin difficult.
It can increase the metabolism of oral hypoglyemic drugs.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It can cause hyperglycemia.

Niacin should be used cautiously in diabetics as it can cause hyperglycemia.

Niacin induces insulin resistance and also decreases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which may result in severe hyperglycemia. When niacin is prescribed for patients with known or suspected diabetes, blood glucose levels should be monitored at least once a week.
questions.learning: Niacin should be used cautiously in diabetics as it can cause hyperglycemia. Niacin induces insulin resistance and also decreases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which may result in severe hyperglycemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which cells within the liver sinusoids play the primary role in removing bacterial foreign particles from the circulation?
questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are specialized, resident macrophages located within the sinusoidal lining of the liver. They constitute the largest population of tissue-resident macrophages in the body and play a vital role in the innate immune response by filtering the portal blood. Their primary function is the phagocytosis and clearance of bacterial foreign bodies, endotoxins, and cellular debris originating from the gastrointestinal tract. Hepatocytes (Option A) are the functional cells of the liver responsible for metabolism, bile production, and detoxification, but they are not primary phagocytes. Ito cells (Option B), also known as stellate cells, are located in the Space of Disse and are responsible for Vitamin A storage and, when activated, the production of collagen leading to fibrosis. Sinusoidal endothelial cells (Option C) form a fenestrated barrier but do not possess significant phagocytic capacity. The efficient scavenger function of Kupffer cells is essential for preventing systemic sepsis by intercepting pathogens before they reach the systemic circulation through the hepatic veins

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to subcutaneous contraceptive implant?
questions.explanation: Undiagnosed genital bleeding is an absolute contraindication (WHO Category 4) for all hormonal contraceptive methods, including subcutaneous implants. The primary concern is that the bleeding might be caused by an underlying malignancy (like cervical or endometrial cancer) that could be masked or its diagnosis delayed by hormonal use. Hypertension (Option A) and Diabetes (Option B) are not contraindications for progestin-only implants unless they are severe or accompanied by major vascular disease. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) (Option C) is a contraindication for intrauterine devices but not for subcutaneous implants, which do not interact with the pelvic organs directly. Therefore, the etiology of bleeding must be clarified before the implant can be safely used
questions.learning: Undiagnosed genital bleeding is an absolute contraindication (WHO Category 4) for all hormonal contraceptive methods, including subcutaneous implants.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following antidotes are used to treat cyanide toxicity?

1. Amyl nitrite
2. Sodium nitrite
3. Sodium thiosulfate
4. Glyceryl trinitrite
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

Amyl nitrite, sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate are antidotes used to treat cyanide toxicity.

Cyanide acts by inhibiting the activity of enzyme systems like cytochrome oxidase and carbonic anhydrase. It inhibits the final step of oxidative phosphorylation, preventing the synthesis of ATP and its usage as an energy source. Cyanide reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and combines with the ferric iron atom of intracellular cytochrome oxidase, inhibiting oxygen intake for cellular respiration.

Treatment primarily aims at reversing the cyanide-cytochrome combination by providing nitrites which convert haemoglobin to methaemoglobin.

Cyanides combine with methaemoglobin to produce non-toxic cyanmethaemoglobin, which, in the presence of rhodanase and sulphate donors such as thiosulphate, transforms cyanide to thiocyanate, which is eliminated in the urine.

The Cyanide kit contains:

• 21 amyl nitrite pearls
• Two 10 ml vials of 3% sodium nitrite
• Two 50 ml vials of sodium thiosulphate.

Using a handkerchief, a 0.2 ml ampoule of amyl nitrite is broken and held over the patient's nose for 15 to 30 seconds of every minute, until sodium nitrite infusion is started.

IV administration of 0.3 g of sodium nitrite in 10 ml of sterile water is given slowly over a 5-minute interval. Sodium nitrite forms methaemoglobin (Hb-Fe2+), then competes with cytochrome oxidase for the cyanide ion, thus protecting cytochrome oxidase. Folllowing this, 25 g of sodium thiosulphate in 50% solution is given i.v. over a period of 10 minutes. It converts cyanide to non-toxic thiocyanate, which is excreted in urine.

Other antidotes such as Hydroxocobalamin (Vit B12) and Dicobalt EDTA can also be used.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Amyl nitrite, sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate are antidotes used to treat cyanide toxicity. Cyanide acts by inhibiting the activity of enzyme systems like cytochrome oxidase and carbonic anhydrase.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman, P2L2, presents for family planning counseling. She reports that she does not desire any future pregnancies and is seeking a permanent method of contraception. Which of the following is the most appropriate sterilization method for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Modified Pomeroy's method

Modified Pomeroy’s method is the most commonly performed female sterilization procedure, especially in the postpartum period, because it is simple, effective, and associated with a low failure rate.

Principle of Modified Pomeroy’s Method

• A loop of the mid-isthmic fallopian tube is elevated.
• The base of the loop is ligated with an absorbable suture.
• The loop is excised, leaving separated tubal ends after the suture is absorbed, minimizing the chance of recanalization.

Why not the other options?

• B. Partial salpingectomy: A broader term describing removal of part of the tube; Modified Pomeroy is the standard technique used for sterilization.
• C. Salpingostomy: Creates an opening in the tube; used for fertility-preserving management of ectopic pregnancy, not contraception.
• D. Salpingectomy: Complete removal of the fallopian tube. Although bilateral salpingectomy is increasingly performed for ovarian cancer risk reduction, the classical FMGE/NEET PG answer for female sterilization remains Modified Pomeroy’s method.
questions.learning: Modified Pomeroy's method Modified Pomeroy’s method is the most commonly performed female sterilization procedure, especially in the postpartum period, because it is simple, effective, and associated with a low failure rate.

Option B: Microcephaly can be seen in CP due to perinatal insults to the developing brain.

Option C: Ataxia is a common feature of extrapyramidal CP.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of tubercular otitis media?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ear ache

Earache is not a feature of tubercular otitis media. It is a painless condition.

Tuberculosis of the ear is usually secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis. It occasionally spreads hematogenously, from a tubercular focus in the lungs, tonsils, and cervical or mesenteric lymph nodes

It presents as a painless condition with foul-smelling discharge from the ear, that does not respond to standard antibiotic treatment. Patients have severe hearing loss that is out of proportion to symptoms. Although predominantly conductive, sensorineural hearing loss may also occur if the labyrinth is involved.

A thickened tympanic membrane with multiple perforations in pars tensa of the tympanic membrane and pale granulations in the middle ear cleft is seen.

The image below shows the tympanic membrane in tuberculous otitis media:

Histopathology shows submucosal tubercles with Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis. Smears and culture of ear discharge may be positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Evidence of primary pulmonary tuberculosis may also be seen on chest radiography.

Facial nerve palsy is a common complication. Mastoiditis, postauricular fistula, and osteomyelitis are also seen.

Treatment includes aural toilet, treatment of secondary bacterial infections, and a full course of antitubercular therapy followed by reconstructive surgery.
questions.learning: Ear ache Earache is not a feature of tubercular otitis media. Tuberculosis of the ear is usually secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents to the outpatient department with a history of prolonged topical steroid use for a skin disorder. The patient reports an enlarging rash that has become less itchy and less erythematous after steroid application. On examination, well-defined, mildly raised plaques with central clearing and a scaly margin are seen over multiple body sites. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: Tinea incognito is a fungal infection (dermatophytosis) that has had its classic clinical appearance altered by the inappropriate application of topical or systemic corticosteroids. Ordinarily, tinea presents with highly inflammatory, itchy, and well-defined scaly borders. Steroids suppress this local inflammation, making the rash appear "less red and itchy," but they simultaneously impair the local immune response, allowing the fungus to proliferate more extensively into deeper layers of the skin. This often results in a less well-defined, widespread, and "bizarre" looking rash. Tinea corporis (Option B) refers to a standard ringworm infection of the body without steroid modification. Tinea cruris (Option C) is specific to the groin area, and tinea pedis (Option D) is athlete's foot. The patient’s specific history of using steroids followed by an "expanding" but less symptomatic rash is the hallmark of tinea incognito, requiring cessation of steroids and initiation of proper antifungal therapy for resolution
questions.learning: Tinea incognito is a fungal infection (dermatophytosis) that has had its classic clinical appearance altered by the inappropriate application of topical or systemic corticosteroids.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The instrument shown in the image is used to insufflate the abdomen for laparoscopic surgery. What is its name?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Veress needle

The instrument shown in the image is the Veress needle which is used to insufflate the abdomen for laparoscopic surgery.

The image below shows the Veress needle:

There are two methods for establishing abdominal access during laparoscopic surgeries:

• Direct puncture using a Veress needle
• Direct peritoneal access (Hasson's technique)

Direct puncture laparoscopy:

In this procedure, first, the abdominal wall is grasped with towel clips or fingers to elevate it away from the underlying structures. Then, a small incision is made in the umbilicus, and insufflation is performed using a Veress needle. When introducing the Veress needle, two distinct pops can be felt as the needle pierces the abdominal wall fascia first and then the peritoneum. The umbilicus is the preferred location for introducing a Veress needle because the abdominal wall is thinner at this site.

Laparoscopic surgeries can be performed under general anesthesia or local anesthesia; although, general anesthesia is preferred. Carbon dioxide gas is usually used for insufflation, and the maximum pressure is typically in the range of 14-15 mm Hg. However, if the procedure is done under local anesthesia, nitrous oxide is used. Insufflation with nitrous oxide is stopped at a pressure of 10 mmHg or when 2L of gas has been insufflated.

Direct peritoneal access technique (Hasson technique): The surgeon makes a small umbilical incision and gains access to the peritoneal cavity under direct vision by dissecting through the abdominal fascia and peritoneum. It is preferred in patients who have undergone previous abdominal operations where the small bowel may be adherent to the undersurface of the abdominal wound.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a true statement about CT?
options: The higher the pitch, the lower will be the CT quality
Helical CT is faster than non-helical CT
The higher the pitch, the higher will be the radiation dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The higher the pitch, the higher will be the radiation dose

In CT imaging, pitch refers to table movement per gantry rotation relative to beam width.

Imagine CT scan table is like a moving conveyor belt.

• Low pitch → Table moves slowly
• High pitch → Table moves fast

When the table moves slowly:

• X-rays overlap more
• Patient gets more radiation

When the table moves faster (high pitch):

• X-rays overlap less
• Patient gets less radiation

So:

• High pitch = Faster scan = Less overlap = Less radiation dose
• That’s why option D is wrong.

Simple rule to remember:

📌 Higher pitch → lower dose → slightly lower image quality

Thus:

• Higher pitch → faster scan, lower radiation dose, slightly lower image quality
• Lower pitch → slower scan, higher radiation dose, better image quality

Multidetector CT (MDCT) enables rapid acquisition and superior 3D reconstruction compared with conventional CT.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the embryological origin of the labelled structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. First pharyngeal arch

The bony structure depicted in the image is the malleus, which can be identified from its hammer shape. It is derived embryologically from the first pharyngeal arch.

The ear ossicles - malleus, incus, and stapes, as shown in the image below, are the three bones of the middle ear which conduct sound energy from the tympanic membrane to the oval window and the inner ear fluid.

The malleus is the largest of the three and is hammer-shaped. The handle of the malleus is attached to the upper half of the tympanic membrane and the head is attached to the incus.

The incus is the middle bone, as described above. Incus is shaped like an anvil. It has a body, a short process, and a long process. It has a saddle-shaped articular facet on its anterior surface that articulates with the malleus. The long process descends vertically and ends as a rounded lenticular process. It is also derived embryologically from the first pharyngeal arch.

The stapes is the smallest and medial most ossicle, which is stirrup-shaped, with two distinct limbs and a footplate attached to the oval window. It has a head, neck, footplate, and anterior and posterior crura. The annular ligament holds the footplate of the stapes in the oval window. It develops mainly from the second pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who stopped consuming alcohol three days ago and subsequently developed irritability, disorientation, paranoid delusions, agitation, visual hallucinations, and altered consciousness?
questions.explanation: Delirium Tremens (DT) is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically occurring 48 to 96 hours (roughly 3 days) after the last drink. The clinical hallmarks perfectly match this scenario: clouding of consciousness (disorientation), autonomic hyperactivity (agitation, irritability), and prominent visual hallucinations (often described as "pink elephants" or insects). Paranoid delusions are also common. Wernicke's encephalopathy (Option B) is characterized by the triad of ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and confusion due to thiamine deficiency. Korsakoff psychosis (Option C) involves chronic amnesia and confabulation. Alcohol-induced psychosis (Option D) usually involves hallucinations in a clear sensorium, unlike the disorientation seen here. Because the symptoms are hyperacute, occur exactly on day 3 of cessation, and involve impaired consciousness with hallucinations, Delirium Tremens is the definitive diagnosis. It is a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Dynein protein is an example of?
questions.explanation: Dynein is a molecular motor protein that functions as a specialized intracellular transport protein. It "walks" along microtubules to move cargo, such as vesicles and organelles, within the cell. Notably, dynein moves cargo in the retrograde direction (from the periphery toward the cell center or the minus end of the microtubule). Another motor protein, kinesin, handles anterograde transport. Dynein also plays a crucial role in the movement of cilia and flagella (axonemal dynein) and in spindle assembly during mitosis. Option B is incorrect as dynein is cytoplasmic. Options C and D refer to different classes of skeletal or anchoring proteins like integrins or cadherins. Clinically, a defect in axonemal dynein results in Kartagener syndrome (Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia), characterized by a triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. These motor proteins are vital for maintaining cellular organization and facilitating the large-scale movement of materials required for neuronal function and respiratory clearance. AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.learning: Dynein is a molecular motor protein that functions as a specialized intracellular transport protein. It "walks" along microtubules to move cargo, such as vesicles and organelles, within the cell.

questions.text: Identify the anomaly seen on the ultrasound.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anencephaly

Anencephaly shows the classic “frog-eye” appearance, with absence of cranial vault and cerebral hemispheres. Encephalocele presents as a sac; lissencephaly shows smooth brain; holoprosencephaly has midline defects, not frog-face.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A counterforce brace is used in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tennis elbow

A counterforce brace is used in tennis elbow.

Tennis elbow, also known as lateral epicondylitis, is a condition involving the lateral epicondyle caused by repetitive contraction of the extensor muscles during activities that require forceful wrist extension and supination, such as playing tennis or using a screwdriver.

A counterforce brace is a treatment option for tennis elbow (shown in the image below). It works by applying compression to the extensor muscles, specifically the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) region, which helps release the forces exerted on the lateral epicondyle. This compression prevents the transmission of tension up to the lateral epicondyle, providing relief and promoting healing in the affected area.

Management options in tennis elbow:

• Conservative management: Rest and physiotherapy
• Medical intervention: Injection of local anesthetic and steroids
• Surgical methods: Percutaneous release of epicondylar muscles
• Other management methods: Extracorporeal shock wave therapy, arthroscopic release, autologous blood injections, counterforce bracing, rehabilitative exercises, and ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle therapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following substances, when present at the specified concentration, renders drinking water unsafe for human consumption according to established safety standards?
questions.explanation: According to standards set by the WHO and the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the safe limit for Cadmium in drinking water is very low, at 0.003 mg/L. The concentration of 0.3 mg/L provided in Option B is 100 times higher than the permissible limit, making the water highly toxic and unsuitable for consumption. Chronic cadmium exposure leads to severe kidney damage and bone demineralization, famously known as Itai-Itai disease. The other listed levels are safe: Fluoride at 0.8 mg/L is below the 1.0–1.5 mg/L threshold. Chloride at 200 mg/L is well within the 250 mg/L limit. Calcium at 7 mg/L is far below the desirable limit of 75 mg/L. Consequently, only the cadmium level in Option B represents a hazardous deviation from global and national safety standards
questions.learning: According to standards set by the WHO and the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the safe limit for Cadmium in drinking water is very low, at 0.003 mg/L.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the definition of a post-term neonate?
options: Neonate born after 37 weeks of gestation
Neonate born between 37- 40 weeks of gestation
Neonate born after 40 weeks of gestation
Neonate born after 42 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neonate born after 42 weeks of gestation

Post-term infants are those born after 42 completed weeks of gestation, as calculated from the mother’s last menstrual period, regardless of weight at birth.

A term neonate is a neonate born any time after 37 completed weeks gestation and up until 42 completed weeks gestation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic female patient presented as shown in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.

Diabetic patients with local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resemble the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus Oryza.

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness, followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The image below shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis:

Risk factors:

* Diabetes (diabetic ketoacidosis).

* Immunocompromised individuals

Treatment of the infection includes 4 steps:

* Initiation of therapy (amphotericin B) as early as possible. Posaconazole can also be used in the management of this condition.

* Surgical debridement

* Reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors

* Treatment of underlying malignancy if present.

The image below shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis:

Other options:

Option A: Invasive aspergillosis leads to the formation of a black or greyish membranes in the nasal mucosa. The maxillary sinus may contain a fungus ball containing semisolid cheesy-white or blackish material.

Option C: Foreign body nose presents with foul-smelling unilateral discharge.

Option D: Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction by a polypoidal mass.

Pearl PF0822: Classification of fungus based on morphology

Fungi are classified into 4 types based on their morphology:

* Yeast

* Yeast-like

* Molds

* Dimorphic fungi

Yeast:

* Unicellular fungi

* Reproduces by budding

* Oval to round forms

* Example: Cryptococcus, Saccharomyces.

Yeast like:

* Unicellular fungi

* Reproduces by budding or binary fission

* Spherical or oval forms

* Pseudohyphae may be seen.

* Example: Candida, Malassezia furfur.

Molds/filamentous fungi:

* Have hyphae which may be septate or aseptate

* Aseptate or coenocytic hyphae – Rhizopus, mucor, Lichtheimia.

* Septate hyphae – Penicillium, Dermatophytes, Aspergillus, fusarium.

Dimorphic fungi

* Filamentous forms in the culture at 220C – 250C and in the environment.

* Yeast form in the culture at 370C and in tissues.

* Examples – Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Coccidioides immitis, Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Talaromyces marneffei, Sporothrix schenckii.
questions.learning: Mucormycosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis. Diabetic patients with local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resemble the presentation of invasive mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which type of macrophages predominantly contributes to tissue repair and resolution of inflammation in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease complicated by pneumonia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. M2 macrophages

Macrophages can polarize into two main functional types during inflammation:

M1 macrophages (classically activated):

• Induced by IFN-γ and microbial products
• Produce pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6)
• Involved in microbial killing and tissue damage

M2 macrophages (alternatively activated):

• Induced by IL-4 and IL-13
• Promote tissue repair, fibrosis, and resolution of inflammation
• Secrete anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) and growth factors

In conditions like pneumonia complicating COPD, M2 macrophages play the dominant role in repairing damaged lung tissue and resolving inflammation.

questions.text: A patient with CKD with refractory hypertension is brought to the casualty with dizziness. His BP was found to be 200/120 mmHg. His BUN was 50 mg/dl and creatinine was 3 mg/dl. Potassium was 6 mEq/L. Which of the following is an indication of emergency hemodialysis?
options: Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine

Emergency Hemodialysis-

| ------ | ---------- | -----------

| A | Acidosis | Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.1) not responding to treatment

| E | Electrolytes | Severe hyperkalemia (usually >6.5 mEq/L or with ECG changes)

| I | Intoxication | Dialyzable toxins (methanol, lithium, etc.)

| O | Overload | Fluid overload refractory to diuretics

| U | Uremia | Symptoms like encephalopathy, pericarditis

Hypertension alone is managed medically, and K⁺ = 6 mEq/L without ECG changes is not an absolute indication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A young sexually active female presented with a symptomatic UTI. Urinalysis and cultures showed novobiocin-resistant coagulase negative staphylococcus with a count of 10^4 cells/HPF. What is true about this condition?
options: Test must be repeated with a fresh specimen
Diagnose and treat as urinary tract infection
Normal skin commensal grown on culture that needed to proved
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diagnose and treat as urinary tract infection

A young sexually active female presenting with a symptomatic UTI and urinalysis and cultures showing novobiocin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococcus with a count of 10^4 cells/HPF should be diagnosed as a urinary tract infection and should be treated.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a gram-positive, coagulase-negative staphylococcus. It is non-pigmented, novobiocin resistant, and non-hemolytic on blood agar. It is a leading cause of cystitis in women. It is a part of the normal flora of human skin and periurethral area and thus causes cystitis in sexually active women.

Other options

Option A: A colony count of >10^5/mL of a clean catch sample is considered significant bacteriuria with no clinical symptoms of UTI. In men, a count of 100,000 CFU/ml is sufficient to diagnose a UTI, while for women a UTI is diagnosed when the count is 100,000 CFU/ml in two consecutive midstream urine samples.

Option B: As the patient already has symptoms of UTI and the culture is showing a significant count redoing the test is not required.

Option D: Though staphylococcus saprophyticus is a normal commensal of skin since the patient already has symptomatic UTI with a proven culture,it need not be proved again.
