questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male came to OPD with a complaint of midline neck swelling which has been persistent for many years. Recently, it has become painful and inflamed. There has been a clear watery discharge from the wound since last week. On examination, the swelling moves with protrusion of the tongue and also on deglutition. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?
options: Untreated condition may lead to squamous cell carcinoma
They are remnants of thyroid tissue
Acid fast bacilli (AFB) staining should be done to come to a diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They are remnants of thyroid tissue

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst which has been complicated by a sinus fistula. These are the remnants of thyroid tissue.

A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood. It represents the persistence of the thyroglossal tract. It can occur anywhere along the migratory course of the duct:

Beneath foramen cecum → Floor of mouth → Suprahyoid → Region of thyroid cartilage → Subhyoid (most common site)

Clinically, the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. This indicates attachment to the hyoid bone. Swelling is smooth, soft, fluctuant (cystic), non-tender, mobile, and often transilluminate.

The most common complication is infection. Thyroglossal fistula is an acquired condition that either follows infection of the cyst which bursts open or due to inadequate removal of the cyst.

Option A: An untreated thyroglossal duct cyst can rarely lead to malignant transformation, with papillary thyroid carcinoma (85%) being the most common type. It is not associated with squamous cell carcinoma.

Option B: Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst. It involves the excision of the whole thyroglossal tract, involving removal of the body of the hyoid bone, and the suprahyoid tract.

Option D: AFB staining is required when a suspicion of cervical lymph node tuberculosis. They present with the associated systemic signs and symptoms of TB. Swellings are laterally located and don't move with protrusion of the tongue or deglutition.
questions.learning: They are remnants of thyroid tissue — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst which has been complicated by a sinus fistula. These are the remnants of thyroid tissue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is true about laryngeal cancer stage T1bNOMO?
options: Both vocal cords involved and fixed
Both vocal cords involved, and No metastasis
One vocal cord involved and metastasis
One vocal cord involved, and mobile
questions.explanation: According to the TNM staging for glottic laryngeal cancer: T1a : Tumor limited to one vocal cord; normal mobility. T1b : Tumor involves both vocal cords; normal mobility. T2 : Tumor extends to supra- or subglottis, or impaired cord mobility. N0: No regional lymph node metastasis. M0: No distant metastasis. Therefore, the statement "Both vocal cords involved, and No metastasis" accurately describes the T1bN0M0 stage. Option A is incorrect as vocal cord "fixation" would make it a T3 tumor. Option C is incorrect due to the "M0" status. Option D describes a T1a tumor. Stage T1b tumors are early-stage cancers with an excellent prognosis. They are typically treated with either radiotherapy or endoscopic CO2 laser excision. Preserving the quality of the voice while ensuring oncological cure is the primary goal of management at this stage. Accurate knowledge of these staging nuances is critical for planning the appropriate surgical or radiation therapy
questions.learning: According to the TNM staging for glottic laryngeal cancer: T1a : Tumor limited to one vocal cord; normal mobility. T1b : Tumor involves both vocal cords; normal mobility.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and is found to have elevated serum uric acid levels. The physician initiates first-line therapy for this condition. What is the mechanism of action of the drug prescribed?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of joint swelling combined with high serum uric acid levels is diagnostic of gout. While NSAIDs or colchicine are used for the acute flare, the "initial" and most common first-line treatment for the long-term management of hyperuricemia is Allopurinol. The mechanism of action of Allopurinol is that of a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (Option D). It works by blocking the enzyme responsible for converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby lowering the systemic levels of urate. A pyrimidine antimetabolite (Option A) refers to drugs like 5-fluorouracil used in chemotherapy. Colchicine acts as an inhibitor of neutrophil recruitment (Option B) and is used for acute attacks, not primary urate-lowering. Uricosuric drugs (Option C), such as probenecid, increase the renal excretion of uric acid but are generally second-line. Thus, xanthine oxidase inhibition is the definitive standard
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of joint swelling combined with high serum uric acid levels is diagnostic of gout. While NSAIDs or colchicine are used for the acute flare, the "initial" and most common first-line treatment for the long-term management of…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Trismus in parapharyngeal abscess is due to spasm of?
questions.explanation: A parapharyngeal abscess is a deep neck space infection. Trismus, which is the inability to open the mouth fully, is a hallmark sign when the infection involves the anterior (muscular) compartment of the parapharyngeal space. This occurs because the medial pterygoid muscle forms the lateral boundary of this space. Irritation or direct inflammation from the abscess leads to reflex spasm of the medial pterygoid, resulting in severe trismus. The masseter (Option A) and temporalis (Option D) are primary muscles of mastication but are not directly adjacent to the parapharyngeal space in the same way. The lateral pterygoid (Option C) is primarily involved in jaw protrusion and opening. Therefore, specifically because of its anatomical position as the lateral wall of the parapharyngeal space, the medial pterygoid muscle is the structure responsible for the clinical finding of trismus in these patients
questions.learning: A parapharyngeal abscess is a deep neck space infection. Trismus, which is the inability to open the mouth fully, is a hallmark sign when the infection involves the anterior (muscular) compartment of the parapharyngeal space.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following indicators stand consolidated in Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI)? 1. Infant mortality 2. Life expectancy at age one 3. Per capita income 4. Literacy Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

The Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) was developed by Morris D. Morris (1979) to measure the physical well-being of a population, independent of economic indicators. It is calculated using three indicators:

• Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)
• Life Expectancy at Age One
• Basic Literacy Rate

Per capita income is NOT included in PQLI.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 The Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) was developed by Morris D. Morris (1979) to measure the physical well-being of a population, independent of economic indicators.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with exertional dyspnea and pedal oedema. His echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with reduced systolic function. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is false?
options: Pulmonary hypertension may develop in this patient
Ejection fraction will be reduced in this condition
Long-term anticoagulation is not needed for this patient
Beta blockers are indicated in chronic management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Long-term anticoagulation is not needed for this patient

The question describes dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

Key features:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Dilated LV | Chamber enlargement

| Reduced systolic function | Weak contractility

| Reduced EF | Usually <40%

| Symptoms | Dyspnea, fatigue, pedal edema

DCM leads to Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF).

Structural Changes in Dilated Cardiomyopathy - Typical findings:

• Dilated LV cavity
• Thin ventricular walls
• Poor systolic contraction
• Reduced ejection fraction

This leads to forward failure + backward congestion.

Pulmonary Hypertension Develops Because: Left ventricular failure → blood backs up into left atrium → pulmonary veins → pulmonary capillaries

This causes:

• Pulmonary venous congestion
• Increased pulmonary artery pressure
• Secondary pulmonary hypertension

Symptoms include:

• Dyspnea
• Orthopnea
• Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea

Normal EF: 55–70%

In HFrEF (Dilated cardiomyopathy): EF < 40%

Mechanism:

• Weak myocardial contraction
• Increased end-systolic volume
• Reduced stroke volume

Main drugs used in HFrEF:

| Drug | Benefit

| ---- | -------

| ACE inhibitors / ARNI | Reduce mortality

| Beta blockers | Improve survival

| Mineralocorticoid antagonists | Reduce remodeling

| SGLT2 inhibitors | New mortality benefit

| Diuretics | Symptomatic relief

Dilated cardiomyopathy causes:

• Blood stasis in dilated ventricle
• Formation of LV mural thrombus

Risk:

• Stroke
• Systemic embolism

Anticoagulation is indicated if:

| Indication | Example

| ---------- | -------

| Atrial fibrillation | Very common in CHF

| LV thrombus | Seen on echo

| Prior embolic event | Stroke/TIA

| Very severe LV dysfunction | Sometimes prophylactic

Therefore the statement “long-term anticoagulation is not needed” is false.
questions.learning: Long-term anticoagulation is not needed for this patient The question describes dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Key features: | Feature | Explanation | ------- | ----------- | Dilated LV | Chamber enlargement | Reduced systolic function | Weak contractility…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What observation can be made from this hysterosalpingogram?
questions.explanation: The hysterosalpingogram (HSG) shows bilateral dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tubes with no peritoneal spill of contrast bilaterally — classic appearance of bilateral hydrosalpinx. Key Radiological Features visible: 1. Bilateral dilated tubular structures filled with contrast 2. No free peritoneal spillage of contrast beyond tube ends 3. Club-shaped/sausage-shaped dilation of both tubes 4. Uterine cavity appears normal 5. Complete blocked tubes at fimbrial ends retaining contrast Why other options are wrong: (B) Extravasation into venous system is incorrect because venous intravasation appears as linear vascular patterns radiating away from uterus in a vascular distribution — not the bulbous dilated tubular pattern seen here. (C) Normal HSG is incorrect because normal HSG shows free bilateral peritoneal spillage of contrast beyond tube ends into peritoneal cavity — absent in this image confirming pathology. (D) Bilateral cornual block is incorrect because cornual block shows non-filling of tubes from the cornual end itself — here contrast has clearly filled and outlined both tubes completely, ruling out cornual obstruction
questions.learning: The hysterosalpingogram (HSG) shows bilateral dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tubes with no peritoneal spill of contrast bilaterally — classic appearance of bilateral hydrosalpinx.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All are criteria of IUGR except?
options: Absent or reversal of diastolic flow in umbilical artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Uterine A PI < 95%

IUGR refers to failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential due to placental insufficiency or other causes.

Common diagnostic parameters include:

| Parameter | Diagnostic finding

| --------- | ------------------

| Estimated fetal weight (EFW) | < 3rd percentile

| Abdominal circumference (AC) | < 3rd percentile

| Abnormal Doppler | Umbilical artery changes

| Placental insufficiency markers | Abnormal uterine artery PI

Progression of Doppler abnormalities:

| Stage | Doppler Finding

| ----- | ---------------

| Early | Increased PI

| Moderate | Absent end-diastolic flow

| Severe | Reversed end-diastolic flow

Uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) <95th percentile is normal, not abnormal.

For IUGR Doppler: High resistance = abnormal

So:

• Umbilical artery diastolic flow ↓
• Uterine artery PI ↑
questions.learning: Uterine — A PI < 95% IUGR refers to failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential due to placental insufficiency or other causes.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with complaints of a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. The radiograph of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteochondroma

The given radiograph and clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of osteochondroma.

Osteochondromas are benign bone tumors that present commonly in the adolescent age group. They usually present as painless masses in long bones like the femur or humerus. They are seen as well-defined bony protuberances which may be pedunculated or sessile. Pedunculated osteochondromas point away from the joint, towards the diaphysis. The cortex and cancellous bone of osteochondroma blend with that of the host bone. MRI shows a classical cartilaginous cap.

Osteochondromas usually grow with skeletal maturity and stop once growth stops. They rarely undergo malignant transformation.

Treatment is not indicated if the lesion does not produce symptoms. Excision can be done for large lesions with local pressure effects.

Other options:

Option A: Enchondroma is an intramedullary tumor of hyaline cartilage. They are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. They are usually seen in individuals aged 20 to 50 years, in the tubular bones of the hands and feet. Radiographically, it appears as a central lesion with well-defined, rounded, edges and a thin rind of reactive sclerosis.

Option B: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor and presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. On x-ray, they are seen as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphysis. The bony cortex is not breached but can appear expanded. The common sites are the ends of long bones. Microscopically, chondroblastoma consists of a sheet of chondroblasts embedded in the chondroid matrix. The calcification is often present and surrounds individual cells giving the appearance of ‘chicken wire.’

Option D:  Giant cell tumor, also known as osteoclastoma, is a benign bone tumor. However, it exhibits locally aggressive behaviour despite its benign nature. It usually affects young adults with a peak incidence in the age group of 20–45 years. It presents as a painful mass. A plain radiograph reveals an eccentric, expansile, lobulated lytic lesion (soap bubble appearance) in the epiphysis. There is minimal calcification within the tumor. Biopsy reveals osteoclast-like giant cells scattered among round or spindle-shaped mononuclear cells.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
Which of the following are direct gonioscopes?

1. Goldmann
2. Richardson
3. Zeis
4. Koeppe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 4

Richardson and Koeppe are direct gonioscopes.

A gonioscope is used for the measurement of the angle of the anterior chamber. The types of gonioscopes include:

• Indirect gonioprism: Provides a mirror image of the opposite angle. Indirect goniolenses include Goldmann, Zeiss, and Posner.
• Direct gonioprism: Provides a direct view of the angle. Direct goniolenses include the Koeppe, Richardson, Medical Workshop, Barkan, and Swan–Jacob.

Applications:

• To view the angle of the anterior chamber. The structures visualized in order from front to back are:

• Schwalbe’s line
• Trabecular meshwork
• Scleral spur
• Ciliary body band
• Root of iris

• The localization of foreign bodies, abnormal blood vessels or tumors in the angle.
• Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae.
• During goniotomy, a surgical procedure for the treatment of congenital glaucoma.

The below instrument is an indirect gonioscope of four-mirror type, which is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber.
questions.learning: 2, 4 Richardson and Koeppe are direct gonioscopes. A gonioscope is used for the measurement of the angle of the anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Identify the correct statement regarding gastric carcinoma.

1. It is mostly hereditary.
2. E-cadherin adhesion defect is seen in diffuse-type of gastric CA.
3. Wnt signaling pathway defect is seen in intestinal-type gastric CA.
4. Depth of cancer has no role in prognosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3

The correct statements regarding gastric carcinoma are 2 and 3.

Most cases of gastric cancer are sporadic (statement 1).

Lauren's system classifies gastric cancer into Type I - intestinal and Type II - diffuse.

At the molecular level,

• the diffuse-type is characterized by decreased E-cadherin mainly due to loss-of-function mutations in the CDH1 gene (statement 2).
• the intestinal type of cancer is characterized by mutations in the APC gene or β-catenin  causes increased signaling via the Wnt pathway (statement 3).

Symptoms of both types include nausea, dyspepsia, dysphagia, weight loss, anorexia, early satiety, and anemia.

The image below shows the histopathological appearances of intestinal and diffuse types of gastric carcinoma:

Endoscopy and biopsy of the lesion (gold standard) are performed to diagnose gastric carcinoma.

When possible, surgery remains the preferred treatment approach. Local invasion into the duodenum, pancreas, and retroperitoneum is common, where chemo or radiation therapy with palliative care is the treatment.

The TNM staging is most widely used. It uses depth of invasion along with nodal and distant metastases as prognostic indicators (statement 4).
questions.learning: 2, 3 The correct statements regarding gastric carcinoma are 2 and 3. Most cases of gastric cancer are sporadic (statement 1).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with both the "lemon sign" and "spina bifida" on a prenatal ultrasound?
questions.explanation: The "lemon sign" refers to the inward scalloping of the frontal bones on an axial prenatal ultrasound of the fetal skull, giving it a shape resembling a lemon. This sign is a highly sensitive secondary marker for open Neural Tube Defects (NTDs), specifically spina bifida. It occurs because the spinal defect leads to a drop in cerebrospinal fluid pressure, causing the brain to shift caudally (Arnold-Chiari II malformation) and the skull to deform. Anencephaly (Option B) is an NTD where the skull vault and brain are largely absent, so a lemon sign cannot be seen. Down Syndrome (Option C) is associated with markers like increased nuchal translucency or a "double bubble" sign, not the lemon sign. Brachycephaly (Option D) refers to a broad, short skull shape seen in various syndromes or as a normal variant, but not specifically linked to spinal lesions. Therefore, the lemon sign is a classic sonographic indicator for identifying occult or overt spina bifida
questions.learning: The "lemon sign" refers to the inward scalloping of the frontal bones on an axial prenatal ultrasound of the fetal skull, giving it a shape resembling a lemon.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Inquest in a case of custodial death is handled by _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Executive magistrate

An inquest in a case of custodial death is handled by the Executive Magistrate.

Magistrate inquest (Section 196 BNSS) is an inquest conducted by a district magistrate, subdivisional magistrate, and magistrate of the first-class rank or any other magistrate as empowered by the state government, such as collector, deputy collector or Tehsildar (executive magistrate).

It is conducted in cases of:

* Death under police custody

* Death due to police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, borstal schools

* Dowry death

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Exhumation

* Death or disappearance of any person, or rape of a woman who is under the custody of police or any other person authorized by the court.

In the above-mentioned scenarios, a Magistrate can conduct the inquest independently or in addition to the police inquest.
questions.learning: Executive magistrate — An inquest in a case of custodial death is handled by the Executive Magistrate. Magistrate inquest (Section 196 BNSS) is an inquest conducted by a district magistrate, subdivisional magistrate, and magistrate of the first-class rank…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Iron absorption is decreased in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Iron absorption, particularly of non-heme iron from plant sources, is significantly influenced by dietary factors. Tea contains tannins (polyphenols), which bind to iron in the gut to form insoluble complexes, thereby decreasing iron absorption. Patients with iron deficiency anemia are often counseled to avoid drinking tea with meals for this reason. In contrast, Amla (Option A), Sprouts (Option B), and Lemon (Option D) are all rich in Vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is a potent enhancer of iron absorption because it reduces ferric iron to the more soluble ferrous form and creates an acidic environment for uptake. Other inhibitors (not listed) include phytates in grains and calcium in dairy. Understanding these nutritional interactions is essential for providing effective dietary advice to patients with nutritional anemias. Proper counseling can significantly improve the efficacy of oral iron supplementation and help manage a major public health challenge
questions.learning: Iron absorption, particularly of non-heme iron from plant sources, is significantly influenced by dietary factors. Tea contains tannins (polyphenols), which bind to iron in the gut to form insoluble complexes, thereby decreasing iron absorption.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn baby presented with a difficulty in breathing. Auscultation of the chest revealed gurgling sounds and heart sounds shifted to the right. The chest radiograph confirmed a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Which among the following is the most common location for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left posterolateral

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with the features given in the clinical vignette occurs most commonly in a left posterolateral defect.

Bochdalek hernia is the most common congenital diaphragmatic hernia which occurs on the left posterolateral side due to a defect in the pleuroperitoneal membrane. The abdominal contents in the thorax compress the developing lungs causing pulmonary hypoplasia which manifests as respiratory distress in most infants. Chest X-ray shows an indistinct diaphragm with radiolucent para cardiac shadow and absent bowel loops in the abdomen. Opacities can be seen in the thorax if solid organs or omentum also herniate. Surgical repair is indicated in all cases either by a thoracic or abdominal approach.

Given below is an X-ray showing Bochdalek's hernia

Other options:

Option A- Sliding and rolling hernias occur via the oesophagal opening(hiatal hernia). Sliding hernia (more common) occurs when the gastroesophageal junction(GEJ) and a part of the stomach slide up into the thorax via the opening. A rolling hernia occurs when the GEJ stays below the diaphragm, but the stomach goes up, lying parallel to the oesophagus in the thorax. Hiatal hernias occur in adults.

Option C- The space between the sternum and costal cartilage is called the space of Larry or space of Morgagni. A defect in this space causes Morgagni hernia, which is the second most common hernia in children. It occurs on the right anteromedial aspect and is often less symptomatic.

The following is an X-ray showing Morgagni's Hernia :

Option D- A defect in the central tendon causes a central congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
questions.learning: Left posterolateral Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with the features given in the clinical vignette occurs most commonly in a left posterolateral defect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents for a follow-up of her disease and her chest X-ray is as shown below. What does the X-ray show?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Post mastectomy of right side

The chest x-ray shows a post-right-sided mastectomy image. The right hemithorax is more lucent (darker) than the left because the patient had previously undergone a right radical mastectomy in which the breast and the pectoralis muscles were removed. We can also see the multiple metallic clips from the surgery.

Mastectomy -

Indications for mastectomy include -

* Inflammatory breast cancer.

* Multicentric disease with more than two primary tumors in different quadrants of the breast.

* Diffuse suspicious microcalcifications on mammography, where the extent is not visible.

* Patients who received chest radiation previously and cannot receive more radiotherapy.

* Pregnancy where breast irradiation is contraindicated.

* Persistently positive resection margins.

* Tumors very large in relation to breast size.

* Patient preference

The radical mastectomy(Halstead's mastectomy) is no longer indicated due to higher morbidity with no survival benefit. The modified radical(Patey's)  mastectomy is done now instead.

Boundaries of Patey's mastectomy

* Laterally -  anterior margin of the latissimus dorsi

* Medially -  midline of the sternum

* Superiorly -  subclavius muscle

* Inferiorly -  2 to 3 cm inferior to the inframammary fold

Structures removed in Patey's mastectomy are -

* The whole breast

* The skin over the tumor and nipple

* All of the fat, fascia, and lymph nodes in the axilla

The pectoralis minor divided/retracted to access the upper axilla. The axillary vein and nerves to the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi are preserved. The intercostal brachial nerves are usually divided and sensation changes may be present postoperatively.

Conservative breast surgery

Referred to as wide local excision. Involves removing the tumor and a margin of normal breast tissue. The term lumpectomy is reserved for when a large amount of normal breast tissue is not resected and it is called quadrantectomy is when an entire segment of the breast is removed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the liver, the Apo-B gene is completely translated to ApoB-100 and in the intestine, it is translated to ApoB-48. Which of the following mechanism explains this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RNA editing

The production of apolipoprotein (ApoB-48) in the intestine and ApoB-100 in the liver is the result of RNA editing in the intestine.

RNA editing is the process by which the coding sequence of the mRNA is changed before translation by post-transcriptional modification. As a result, the mRNA template differs from the DNA from which it was transcribed. This leads to the formation of a different protein. This occurs by the insertion of additional uracils at the 3’ end of the mRNA and proceeds in the 3’ to 5’ direction.

The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves RNA editing.

RNA editing in apoB synthesis:

* In the liver, the apoB gene is transcribed to mRNA, which is then translated to apoB-100.

* In the intestine, the same apoB gene is transcribed to the same mRNA. But now, the mRNA undergoes editing by an enzyme cytidine deaminase, which converts the CAA codon in the mRNA to UAA (stop codon) at a single specific site. Here, a sense codon is changed to a nonsense codon by post-transcriptional deamination of cytosine to uracil. This edited mRNA translates to apoB-48.

The image below shows the RNA editing in the Apo-B gene.

DNA rearrangement, alternate splicing, and RNA interference also alter the gene expression but are not the basis of apoB-48 tissue-specific production.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Testosterone production is mainly contributed by ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leydig cells

Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells.

Testosterone is synthesized from cholesterol in the Leydig cells and also from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex.

The diagnosis of testosterone deficiency should be made only on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms consistent with androgen deficiency, and consistently subnormal serum testosterone concentrations at 8 to 10 AM on three occasions.

Testosterone has been used to treat primary or secondary hypogonadism in adult men.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following modalities are used for the diagnosis of placenta accreta?

1. Ultrasonography
2. MRI
3. Angiography
4. X-ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2 only

Among the given options, ultrasonography and MRI can be used in the diagnosis of placenta accreta.

The term placenta accreta spectrum (PAS)/morbidly adherent placenta refers to abnormal placental implantation characterized by the abnormally implanted, invasive, or adhered placenta. This is due to the absence of decidua basalis and poor development of the fibrinoid or Nitabuch layer.

Risk factors include prior cesarian delivery, prior uterine surgery, prior curettage, and endometrial ablation, associated placenta previa.

Types of the morbidly adherent placenta:

• Placenta accreta: Villi are attached to the myometrium.
• Placenta increta: Villi invade the myometrium.
• Placenta percreta: Villi penetrate through the myometrium and to or through the serosa.

Ultrasound imaging, color Doppler, and MRI have all been useful in the diagnosis of morbidly adherent placenta during pregnancy.

USG findings that suggest PAS are (1) placental lacunae, (2) thinning of the retroplacental myometrium, (3) disruption of the bladder-uterine serosal interface, (4) bridging vessels from the placenta to the bladder-serosal interface, and (5) a placental bulge that pushes outward and distorts the contour of the uterus.

Color flow Doppler study shows hypervascularity of serosa bladder interface.

MRI reveals uterine bulging and dark intraplacental bands on T2-weighted imaging.

Management:

• Partial placenta accreta: Placental tissue is removed as much as possible. Oxytocin helps in uterine contraction and hemostasis. In cases following cesarean delivery, bleeding areas are oversewed.
• Total placenta accreta:

• Parous women- hysterectomy is done
• If the patient desires to have a child- conservative measures include incising the uterus above the placental attachment, clamping, and cutting the umbilical cord as close to its base as possible. The placenta is left behind, which may get autolyzed eventually. Uterine artery embolization or therapy with methotrexate has also been done for the conservation of the uterus.

• If placenta accreta invades the bladder, placental removal alone is avoided. It requires a hysterectomy and partial cystectomy.

The below image shows the placenta accreta, increta, and percreta.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding splenic artery aneurysm?
options: It is twice as common in men.
It is usually situated in the main arterial trunk.
It is caused due to blunt trauma to the abdomen.
It is generally multiple in number.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is usually situated in the main arterial trunk.

Splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) is the most common visceral artery aneurysm, accounting for approximately 60% of all visceral artery aneurysms. Most aneurysms occur along the main trunk of the splenic artery, particularly in its distal third, before it enters the splenic hilum.

Although many SAAs are asymptomatic, rupture is life-threatening, especially during pregnancy, with high maternal and fetal mortality.

Why not the other options?

• A. It is twice as common in men: Splenic artery aneurysms are actually more common in women, especially multiparous women.
• C. It is caused due to blunt trauma to the abdomen: Blunt trauma typically causes a splenic artery pseudoaneurysm, not a true aneurysm.
• D. It is generally multiple in number: Most splenic artery aneurysms are single (solitary).
questions.learning: It is usually situated in the main arterial trunk. Splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) is the most common visceral artery aneurysm, accounting for approximately 60% of all visceral artery aneurysms.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-year-old woman presents to the outpatient department with a complaint of bloody nipple discharge. Clinical examination reveals that the discharge is arising from a single lactiferous duct. Given this localized finding, what is the most appropriate management or treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: A spontaneous bloody nipple discharge originating from a single duct in a 39-year-old woman is most likely caused by an intraductal papilloma. The standard-of-care surgical management for this presentation is a Microdochectomy. This precise procedure involves the excision of the single, offending lactiferous duct and its surrounding tissue through a periareolar incision. Hadfield’s operation (Option A), or total duct excision, is reserved for multi-duct discharge or more extensive disease. IV antibiotics and incision (Option B) are used for treating an acute breast abscess, not a ductal growth. Microdiscectomy (Option C) is a neurosurgical procedure for the spine. While most intraductal papillomas are benign, they can occasionally contain areas of atypia or early cancer; therefore, histological examination of the excised duct is mandatory. Microdochectomy effectively stops the discharge while preserving the rest of the breast tissue
questions.learning: A spontaneous bloody nipple discharge originating from a single duct in a 39-year-old woman is most likely caused by an intraductal papilloma. The standard-of-care surgical management for this presentation is a Microdochectomy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following infection presents with mucus in stools and abdominal pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Entamoeba

Stools with mucus and abdominal pain are seen in infection due to Entamoeba.

Clinical features of intestinal amebiasis:

• Acute intestinal amebiasis presents as dysentery accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort and flatulence. Stools usually have blood and mucus.
• Chronic amebiasis presents with low-grade symptoms such as occasional diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue.
• A granulomatous lesion called an ameboma may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas of the colon which can resemble an adenocarcinoma of the colon.

Other options:

Option a - Giardia is often asymptomatic, but in some cases can lead to fat malabsorption, dull epigastric pain, and flatulence.

Option c - Campylobacter presents with fever, pain and bloody or watery diarrhea. Stool contains leucocytes and blood.

Option d - Staphylococcal food poisoning is toxin-mediated and presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
questions.learning: Entamoeba Stools with mucus and abdominal pain are seen in infection due to Entamoeba. Clinical features of intestinal amebiasis: • Acute intestinal amebiasis presents as dysentery accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort and flatulence.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The most important source of reducing equivalents for fatty acid synthesis in the liver is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hexose monophosphate shunt pathway

The most important source of reducing equivalents (NADPH) for fatty acid synthesis in the liver is the hexose monophosphate shunt pathway (HMP) pathway.

Since HMP shunt pathway and fatty acid synthesis both occur in the cytosol of the cell, there are no membranes or permeability barriers against the transfer of NADPH. This NADPH is involved as a donor of reducing equivalents in both the reduction of the 3-ketoacyl and of the 2,3-unsaturated acyl derivatives.

Other sources are:

* Extramitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase (minor source)

* Malic enzyme

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with localized pain that had a gradual onset and has progressively worsened. An X-ray reveals the shown abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a "sunburst appearance" and Codman's triangle, which are classic signs of aggressive periostitis seen in osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor and typically affects the metaphysis of long bones in young adults. Ewing sarcoma (Option B) characteristically presents with an "onion-skin" or lamellated periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of long bones. Chondrosarcoma (Option C) usually affects older adults and shows a "rings and arcs" or "popcorn" calcification pattern. Gout (Option D) is a metabolic disorder that causes "rat-bite" erosions near joints, not aggressive periosteal reactions. Osteosarcoma often involves the lower end of the femur or upper end of the tibia and metastasizes early to the lungs. Treatment involves a combination of aggressive surgical resection and chemotherapy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding 10 years after attaining menopause and has no significant past medical history. What is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding in this patient?
questions.explanation: A 65-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated for malignancy. Although endometrial atrophy is the most common cause worldwide, it is not given in the options. In Indian exam context, the most important and commonly emphasized cause of PMB is carcinoma cervix. Cervical cancer is highly prevalent in India and often presents with: 1. Postmenopausal bleeding 2. Postcoital bleeding (most common presentation) 3. Foul-smelling discharge Because of its high incidence and clinical importance, examiners frequently consider it the most likely cause of PMB when atrophy is not listed. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Decubitus ulcer → Rare, associated with prolapse (C) Tubercular endometritis → Uncommon cause (D) Hormone replacement therapy → Recognized cause but less common than malignancy
questions.learning: A 65-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated for malignancy. Although endometrial atrophy is the most common cause worldwide, it is not given in the options.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mutation of the gene of cystic fibrosis occurs with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phenylalanine at 508 position, chloride channel

The mutant gene of cystic fibrosis (CF gene) produces a mutant CFTR protein with the deletion of a phenylalanine residue at 508 (F508del), characterised by impaired chloride secretion.

Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CF gene). It plays an important role in mucociliary transport along the respiratory mucosa. It also helps to regulate the amount of exocrine gland secretion.

The defect in the ion channel results in the production of hyper-viscous, adherent secretions which can obstruct the airways. Organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can grow in the sputum. The exocrine pancreas can undergo fibrotic scarring, cyst formation, and acinar tissue loss. The viscid secretions can lead to pancreatic duct obstruction. The flow of digestive enzymes to the duodenum is hence impaired.

Symptoms include sinusitis, steatorrhea, and abdominal pain. Distal intestinal obstruction is a complication due to difficulty in excreting intestinal contents. In neonates, it can present as meconium ileus.

Detection of high levels of trypsinogen is used in newborn screening. Chloride level >60mEq/L in the sweat of affected patients is diagnostic. Hyponatremic hypochloremic alkalosis is seen.

Postural drainage, short-term antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators can be used for medical management. The definitive treatment is lung transplantation.

The image below shows the features of the disease.
questions.learning: Phenylalanine at 508 position, chloride channel — The mutant gene of cystic fibrosis (CF gene) produces a mutant CFTR protein with the deletion of a phenylalanine residue at 508 (F508del), characterised by impaired chloride secretion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following blood groups can be given to a patient having Bombay blood group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oh

Among the given options, Oh (Bombay) blood group blood can be transfused to Bombay blood group patients.

The H antigen is present in all four blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). A rare blood group where there is an absence of the H antigen is known as the Bombay blood group. The absence of this H antigen results in the absence of A and B antigens. Their plasma contains anti-A, anti-B, and strong anti-H antibodies. Therefore, they do not react with anti-A, anti-B, and anti-AB antiserums, and get recognized as O blood group on cell typing.

However, the O blood group has an H antigen. Thus if a patient with the Bombay blood group is transfused with the O blood group blood, the anti-H antibodies in the Bombay blood group patient react with the H antigen present in the O blood group. This can lead to fatal transfusion reactions. Therefore, patients with the Bombay blood group require the same blood group during transfusion.

Other less common systems of blood grouping include MNSs, Lutheran, Kell, and Kidd systems of blood grouping.

ABO blood typing is performed by mixing the individual's red blood cells with antisera that contains the various agglutinins on a slide and observing for the presence of clumping or agglutination.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 73 old male smoker with a past history of coronary artery disease presents with blackening of the toes. An image of the foot is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atherosclerosis

The given clinical scenario of an elderly smoker with past history of coronary artery disease and gangrene of the first three toes is likely to have atherosclerosis.

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease in which there is a build-up of plaques inside arteries.  It is common after 50 years.These plaques are principally composed of lipids that induce an inflammatory reaction causing turbulent flow leading to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease(ASCVD). This results in atheroma formation in arteries throughout the body hampering the blood flow and leading to ischemia.

Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and elevated cholesterol. The infrarenal part of the abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, iliofemoral vessels, carotid bifurcation, and popliteal arteries are the common arteries involved. The presence of atherosclerotic disease in one part of the body suggests there could be blockade in other parts as well.

Patients with chronic limb ischemia present with rest pain and tissue loss such as gangrene and ulceration. An ischemic ulcer is painful, pale, and cyanotic in appearance with absent pulsations. It may be associated with transient ischemic attacks, chest pain, eye problems, mesenteric ischemia, and altered renal function.

Doppler or angiogram can be done to identify the block. It is important to evaluate these patients for intercurrent cardiac disorders.

Management involves cessation of smoking and modification of other risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. High-intensity statins should be given irrespective of cholesterol levels in ASCVD. Other drugs that can be used include pentoxifylline, aspirin, clopidogrel, and cilostazol. Surgical options include thrombectomy, endarterectomy, bypass grafting, and amputations if the limb is gangrenous.

Complications of atherosclerosis include

* Narrowing of the arteries: Coronary, cerebral, renal, mesenteric, iliofemoral. > 70% narrowing (severe) causes reduced blood flow.

* lschaemia, ulcerations, gangrene

* Embolism: From atheromatous plaques

* Aneurysm formation: Mainly abdominal aorta and also in peripheral arteries

Option A: Buerger’s disease is a progressive nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory disease that most often affects small- and medium-sized arteries, veins, and nerves of the upper and lower extremities.

* Typically presents in young male smokers, with symptoms beginning prior to age 40.

* Patients initially present with the foot, leg, arm, or hand.

* Claudication may progress to rest pain to calf claudication and eventually ischemic rest pain and ulcerations on the toes, feet, or fingers and even gangrene.

If the patient continues to smoke, the disease progresses into the collaterals, blocking them eventually, leading to severe ischemia which is called decompensatory peripheral vascular disease/ critical limb ischemia which presents as rest pain, ulceration, and gangrene.

Option C: Raynaud's disease usually occurs in females and affects bilateral upper limbs. Patients present with pallor/blanching (syncope), dusky cyanosis (asphyxia), and rubor/painful red de-engorgement (recovery). Peripheral pulses are normal.

Option D: Giant cell arteritis is characterized by giant cell infiltration of the arterial wall (giant cell arteritis) involving superficial temporal, facial, retinal, upper limb, coronary and vertebral arteries. Patients present with severe headaches, visual abnormalities, jaw claudication, and a tender superficial temporal artery.

Pearl PF1741: Ankle–brachial Pressure Index (ABPI)

The ankle-brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is the ratio of systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the arm.

The numerator is the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, or peroneal artery and the denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure.

ABPI Reading
Interpretation

>0.91 < 1.3
Normal

<0.9
Diagnostic of occlusive arterial disease in patients with symptoms of claudication or other signs of ischemia

0.5 to 0.9
Arterial obstruction often associated with claudication

<0.3
Critical limb ischemia (multilevel obstruction i.e any combination of iliac, femoral or tibial vessel disease and may be associated with non-healing ulcerations, ischemic rest pain, or pedal gangrene.

>1.4
Signifies poor compressibility of the arteries. Mostly due to calcification because of increased age, diabetes etc.

Note: A fall in the resting ABPI of more than 20% after exercise is indicative of arterial disease.
questions.learning: Atherosclerosis — The given clinical scenario of an elderly smoker with past history of coronary artery disease and gangrene of the first three toes is likely to have atherosclerosis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 56-year-old female has been diagnosed with gallstones and is undergoing a preanaesthesia checkup. She has been a diabetic since the last 15 years, but sugar levels are within the limits. Which category of physical status does she fit into?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ASA II

The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative fitness and estimate perioperative risk.

ASA II — mild systemic disease without substantive functional limitations.

Quick reference for ASA-PS classification:

• ASA I — normal healthy patient
• ASA II — mild systemic disease, no functional limitation (e.g., well-controlled diabetes or hypertension, controlled asthma, current smoker, social alcohol use, obesity with BMI 30–40, mild lung disease)
• ASA III — severe systemic disease, some functional limitation (e.g., poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, diabetes with vascular complications, morbid obesity, active hepatitis, ESRD on dialysis)
• ASA IV — severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g., recent MI/CVA <3 months, ongoing cardiac ischemia, sepsis)
• ASA V — moribund, not expected to survive without surgery
• ASA VI — brain-dead patient for organ donation
questions.learning: ASA II — The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative fitness and estimate perioperative risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs functions as a selective α₁-adrenergic receptor antagonist in clinical use?
questions.explanation: Prazosin is a prototype selective -adrenergic receptor antagonist. By selectively blocking receptors on vascular smooth muscle, it causes vasodilation, making it useful in treating hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Phenoxybenzamine (Option A) is a non-selective, irreversible alpha antagonist that blocks both and receptors; it is primarily used in the management of pheochromocytoma. Phentolamine (Option B) is also a non-selective antagonist but is reversible and used for short-term control of hypertensive crises. Idazoxan (Option D) is a selective receptor antagonist, used more in research than in routine clinical practice. The clinical advantage of Prazosin’s selectivity for is that it does not block the receptors on presynaptic nerve terminals, thereby avoiding the massive release of norepinephrine and the resultant severe tachycardia associated with non-selective agents. Prazosin is also associated with the "first-dose effect" of orthostatic hypotension
questions.learning: Prazosin is a prototype selective -adrenergic receptor antagonist. By selectively blocking receptors on vascular smooth muscle, it causes vasodilation, making it useful in treating hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Find out the true and false statements regarding paradoxical bronchoconstriction with ipratropium bromide: A. It particularly occurred when given by nebulizer B. It is due to antibacterial additives added with ipratropium C. This will not be seen when given by MDI D. This problem primarily is due to blockade of prejunctional M2 receptors E. This problem is not seen with tiotropium bromide
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A-T, B-T, C-F, D-T, E-T

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction can rarely occur with ipratropium bromide, especially when given via nebulization.

• Nebulized preparations may contain antibacterial preservatives (e.g., benzalkonium chloride) that can trigger bronchospasm.
• Blockade of prejunctional M₂ muscarinic receptors may increase acetylcholine release, causing bronchoconstriction.

Important points:

• This reaction is more common with nebulized ipratropium than with MDI formulations.
• Tiotropium is more selective for M₁ and M₃ receptors and spares M₂ receptors, so paradoxical bronchoconstriction is not typically seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with fatigue, pallor, weight loss, and heaviness in the left hypochondrium, for the past 2 months. Abdominal palpation reveals splenomegaly. His hemogram and peripheral smear results are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Hemogram: Hb - 10 gm/dL WBC count - 1,65,000/cu.mm (Leukocytosis) Platelet count - 3 lakhs/mm3 Peripheral smear: Metamyelocytes - 15% Promyeloblasts - 30% Myeloblasts - 45%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic myeloid leukemia

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).

In this condition, the peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and blasts. Hence, the histological picture is described to have garden party or college girl appearance.

The image given below shows the peripheral smear in CML showing a garden party or college girl appearance.

CML is a myeloproliferative disorder with a peak incidence in the 5th to 6th decades of life. It occurs due to the chimeric BCR-ABL gene.

Clinical features of CML:

* Hypermetabolism

* Fatigability

* Weakness

* Weight loss and anorexia

* Extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis causing -

* Splenomegaly

* Mild hepatomegaly

* Lymphadenopathy

Hematological findings include:

* Mild-to-moderate anemia

* Leukocytosis

* Platelets - usually increased

* DLC shows predominantly neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils and blasts (>10%)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Most effective test to confirm a diagnosis of GERD?
questions.explanation: While several tests are used to evaluate Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD), 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is the gold standard and the most effective test to definitively confirm the diagnosis. This test measures the frequency and duration of acid reflux episodes and, most importantly, correlates these episodes with the patient's reported symptoms. Upper GI endoscopy (Option B) is often the first step to look for complications like esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus, but many patients with GERD have "non-erosive" disease with a normal-looking endoscopy. CECT (Option C) and MRI (Option D) provide structural information but cannot measure physiological reflux activity. Therefore, because pH monitoring directly detects the presence of acid in the esophagus over a significant period, it remains the most accurate diagnostic tool. It is particularly useful for patients who do not respond to proton pump inhibitors or those being considered for anti-reflux surgery
questions.learning: While several tests are used to evaluate Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD), 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is the gold standard and the most effective test to definitively confirm the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis. Specimen revealed that she had gall bladder carcinoma infiltrating the muscularis layer. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extended cholecystectomy

In the given clinical scenario, gallbladder carcinoma with T1b lesions is detected incidentally after cholecystectomy. Treatment guidelines for the same are as follows:

• Up to stage Ia and stage Ib with negative margins, a standard cholecystectomy would suffice.
• Stage Ib with perineural, lymphovascular invasion, positive cystic duct margins, or poor differentiation, and stage II, extended cholecystectomy should be performed. Extended cholecystectomy involves the removal of the gall bladder, segments IVB and V of the liver, and lymph nodes along the hepatoduodenal ligament, with or without removal of the common bile duct (CBD).

However, the likelihood of nodal disease increases significantly with T1b lesions and perineural, lymphatic, or vascular invasion, therefore, extended cholecystectomy is generally recommended for all patients who are medically fit with T1b or greater level of invasion.
If the initial procedure was performed laparoscopically, the surgeon should examine the laparoscopic port sites. The finding of disease at the port sites is a sign of generalized peritoneal disease and carries a very poor prognosis. However, resection of port sites is no longer recommended.

Chemotherapy is not required in early gallbladder cancer. Radiation has no role.

Treatment of gallbladder carcinoma:

TNM staging
Treatment

T1a
Simple cholecystectomy

T1b, T2, T3
Radical cholecystectomy

T4
Unresectable, chemotherapy and palliative nonsurgical therapy are provided

N1
Regional lymphadenectomy

N2
Radical cholecystectomy plus hepatopancreatic duodenectomy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drug is not used for a patient diagnosed with sarcoidosis with multi organ involvement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fludrocortisone

The drug that is not used in the treatment of multisystemic sarcoidosis is Fludrocortisone.

The first-line drug for sarcoidosis is prednisolone.

Management of sarcoidosis:

* Asymptomatic patients- monitored for disease progression

* Localized/ limited cutaneous and ocular lesions- treated using topical steroids

* Multisystem involvement:

* Systemic steroids

* Other drugs like hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and infliximab are considered when the steroids are ineffective or not tolerated
questions.learning: Fludrocortisone — The drug that is not used in the treatment of multisystemic sarcoidosis is Fludrocortisone. The first-line drug for sarcoidosis is prednisolone.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following carbapenems has increased risk of causing seizures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Imipenem

Imipenem is the carbapenem that is associated with an increased risk of causing seizures, especially when high doses are given to patients with CNS lesions.

Excretion of imipenem is mainly renal and dosage modification is required to avoid seizures in renal failure patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 17-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of numbness and tingling in her fingers, especially triggered by stress or exposure to cold. She has no significant past medical history and is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and the provided image are pathognomonic for Raynaud’s phenomenon. This condition is characterized by episodic, reversible vasospasm of the digital arteries in response to cold or emotional stress. It classically follows a triphasic color change: white (vasospasm/ischemia), blue (deoxygenation/cyanosis), and red (reactive hyperemia/reperfusion). In a 17-year-old non-smoker with no underlying disease, this is likely "primary" Raynaud’s (Raynaud's disease). Buerger's disease (Option B) causes digital ischemia but typically presents in heavy male smokers and is characterized by permanent vessel inflammation rather than reversible spasms. Atherosclerosis (Option C) and Peripheral Arterial Disease (Option D) are common in older adults with risk factors like diabetes or hypertension and cause permanent claudication rather than episodic color changes in the fingers. Therefore, given the triggers and the classic visual pattern, Raynaud's phenomenon is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation and the provided image are pathognomonic for Raynaud’s phenomenon. This condition is characterized by episodic, reversible vasospasm of the digital arteries in response to cold or emotional stress.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old male who is a known case of bronchial asthma presented for a routine follow-up. PFT was done earlier—his FEV1 was 70%, which improved to 83% after bronchodilator nebulization. He was already on MDI Albuterol daily. On questioning, it seems like he is being symptomatic for at least 2 times per week and is waking up in the nights due to symptoms at least once per week. On examination, there are scattered rhonchi. What should be done?
options: Add Fluticasone MDI two times a day
Shift to MDI Salmeterol two times a day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Add Fluticasone MDI two times a day

Symptoms ≥2 times/week with nighttime awakening indicate persistent asthma, despite SABA use.

PFT shows reversibility, confirming asthma with inadequate anti-inflammatory control.

The correct step-up is adding an inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone) to treat airway inflammation.

| Severity | Symptoms | Treatment

| -------- | -------- | ---------

| Intermittent | <2/week | SABA

| Mild persistent | ≥2/week | Low-dose ICS

| Moderate persistent | Daily symptoms | ICS + LABA

| Severe | Continuous | High-dose ICS + LABA

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with lacy lesions in oral cavity and genitals. Her proximal nail fold has extended onto the nail bed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lichen planus

Based on the given history, the patient has mucous membrane changes and pterygium of nail. Both are features of lichen planus.

* Mucus membrane lesions are very common in lichen planus, occuring in almost 30–70% of cases. It is mostly seen on tongue and buccal mucosa and also on genitals and anal mucosa.

* White streaks forming a lacework in buccal mucosa is a characteristic feature and are known as Wickham’s striae.

Image: Wickham’s Striae on the buccal mucosa.
questions.learning: Lichen planus — Based on the given history, the patient has mucous membrane changes and pterygium of nail. Both are features of lichen planus. * Mucus membrane lesions are very common in lichen planus, occuring in almost 30–70% of cases.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Transport of iron into enterocytes is done by which of the following proteins:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Divalent metal transporter - 1

Transport of iron into enterocytes is done by divalent metal transporter-1 protein.

Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum. Iron in our gut exists in 2 forms, they are nonheme and heme iron.

Luminal nonheme iron is mostly in the Fe3+ (ferric) state and is reduced to Fe2+ (ferrous) iron by ferrireductases. Fe2+ iron is then transported across the apical membrane by divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1).

Given below is an image of iron absorption that shows divalent metal transporter-1 protein in intestinal mucosal cells.

Heme iron is moved across the apical membrane into the cytoplasm through heme transporters.

In the duodenal cells, Fe2+ iron can follow one of two pathways: transport to the blood or storage as mucosal iron. The nonstorage form of Fe2+ iron is transported from the cytoplasm into circulation by the protein ferroportin (Option B).

Once in circulation, Fe2+ is again oxidized back to Fe3+ iron by hephaestin and ceruloplasmin. The newly absorbed Fe3+ iron binds rapidly to transferrin (Option A), which delivers iron to red cell progenitors in the marrow.

Hepcidin (Option C), is a protein secreted from the liver that plays a major role in the regulation of iron absorption. When the body’s iron stores are adequate, it downregulates the expression of ferroportin and thereby decreases iron absorption.
questions.learning: Divalent metal transporter - 1 Transport of iron into enterocytes is done by divalent metal transporter-1 protein. Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statement refers best to the criteria for starting an urban community health center?
options: Caters to a population of 1-1.5 lakh
Referral centre for 2- 3 primary health centers
No sub-district and district hospitals present in the area
Should have a 100-bed facility in metro cities
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Should have a 100-bed facility in metro cities

An urban community health center (U-CHC) has a 100-bed facility in metro cities.

U-CHC acts as a referral center for 4–5 urban primary health centers (U-PHC). It is usually a 30–50 bedded facility that caters to a population of 2,50,000.

When it comes to metro cities, it caters to a population of 5,00,000 with a 100-bed facility. These hospitals will have surgeons, gynecologists, physicians, and pediatricians, along with x-ray and laboratory facilities.

The specialists at the community health center can refer a patient to the state-level hospital or the nearest medical college hospital directly. The subdistrict and district hospitals operate in addition to CHC to cater to the population.

Services of CHC:

• Care of routine and emergency cases in medicine and surgery
• Maternal, newborn, and child health
• Family planning
• All the national health program functions
• Physical medicine and rehabilitation services
questions.learning: Should have a 100-bed facility in metro cities — An urban community health center (U-CHC) has a 100-bed facility in metro cities. U-CHC acts as a referral center for 4–5 urban primary health centers (U-PHC).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents to you with a unilateral headache. It is associated with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. What is the drug of choice for acute management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sumatriptan

The clinical vignette is suggestive of an acute attack of migraine and the drug of choice for acute management is sumatriptan.

Migraine is the second most common cause of headaches and is seen more commonly in women. It presents as an episodic headache associated with nausea, vomiting, photosensitivity, and sensitivity to sound (phonophobia). Common triggers include bright lights, sounds, and hunger.

The release of vasoactive peptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) by the trigeminal nucleus cells is the theory used to explain the pathogenesis of the condition. The neurotransmitters serotonin and dopamine also play a part.

Triptans are 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptor agonists and they act by arresting the nociceptive nerve signaling in the trigeminovascular system. In addition, they cause cranial vasoconstriction. Cardiac side effects such as transient myocardial ischemia, coronary artery vasospasm, and myocardial infarction can occur in patients with risk factors for coronary artery disease. Other side effects include sweating, nausea, and serotonin syndrome when used in combination with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).

Ergotamine, an ergot alkaloid are serotonin receptor agonists which can be used to treat an acute attack. They produce long-lasting vasoconstriction and can result in gangrene of fingers and toes (ergotism). These drugs are contraindicated in sepsis, ischemic heart disease, and peripheral vascular disease.

Migraine can broadly be classified into:

• Migraine with aura
• Migraine without aura
• Chronic migraine

The migraine disability assessment score (MIDAS) can be used to assess the severity of the condition. Avoidance of recognized triggers is helpful to avoid symptoms. The various drugs used to treat an acute attack of migraine are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), triptans, gepants (rimegepant), ditans (lasmiditan), and dopamine receptor antagonists (domperidone).

In patients with ≥4 attacks in a month, prophylactic medications can be used. The various FDA-approved drugs include propranolol, timolol, flunarizine, and topiramate.

Other options:

Option A - Flunarizine is a calcium channel blocker that can be used in migraine prophylaxis. Side effects include weight gain, depression, and parkinsonism.

Option C - Propranolol is a non-selective β-receptor antagonist that can be used to treat hypertension, arrhythmias, and migraine prophylaxis. It is contraindicated in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) as it can cause bronchoconstriction. Side effects include fatigue, depression, and insomnia.

Option D - Topiramate is an FDA-approved drug for generalized tonic-clonic seizures, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and for migraine prophylaxis in adults. Adverse effects include somnolence, weight loss, and nervousness.
questions.learning: Sumatriptan — The clinical vignette is suggestive of an acute attack of migraine and the drug of choice for acute management is sumatriptan. Migraine is the second most common cause of headaches and is seen more commonly in women.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most frequent association of lung malignancy?
questions.explanation: Occupational lung diseases are significantly associated with various respiratory complications. Among the choices, Asbestosis (Option A) has the strongest and most frequent association with lung malignancy, including both bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma . In fact, individuals with asbestosis who also smoke have a synergistically increased risk (roughly 50–90 fold) of developing lung cancer. Silicosis (Option B) is associated with an increased risk of lung cancer and tuberculosis but is less frequently cited as the primary driver compared to asbestos. Bagassosis (Option C, from moldy sugarcane) and Byssinosis (Option D, from cotton dust) are hypersensitivity and reactive airway diseases that do not typically carry a direct, high-frequency link to lung cancer. Therefore, because of its powerful carcinogenic potential and widespread historical industrial use, asbestosis is the definitive choice for the strongest association with lung malignancy. Prevention involves strict workplace safety standards and total avoidance of fibers

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a tributary of the thoracic duct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right jugular trunk

The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body and drains lymph from both lower limbs, abdomen, left thorax, left upper limb, and the left side of the head and neck before emptying into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Its major tributaries include:

• Right and left lumbar trunks (via cisterna chyli)
• Intestinal trunk
• Left jugular trunk
• Left subclavian trunk
• Left bronchomediastinal trunk

The right jugular trunk does not drain into the thoracic duct. Instead, it usually drains into the right lymphatic duct or directly into the right venous angle.

Why Not the Other Options?

• Left lumbar trunk → Contributes to formation of the cisterna chyli.
• Right lumbar trunk → Contributes to formation of the cisterna chyli.
• Left jugular trunk → Drains into the thoracic duct near its termination.
• Right jugular trunk → Drains into the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator(SERM)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tamoxifen

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor (ER) modulator that is used for hormone receptor–positive breast cancers.

It exhibits selective agonistic and anatagonistic activity for ER receptors:

* Agonist activity at uterus, bone, liver, and pituitary

* Antagonist activity at breast and blood vessels

* It has potent antiestrogenic effects in breast tissues.

Estrogenic agonist action is seen in

* Endometrium: endometrial hypertrophy, vaginal bleeding and endometrial cancer.

* Coagulation system: thromboembolism risk.

* Bone metabolism: increase in bone mineral density.

* Liver: alteration of blood lipid profile.

Used for:

* Primary prophylaxis of breast cancer in high-risk women

* Reducing the risk of carcinoma in contralateral breast

* Reducing the risk of recurrence of carcinoma in ipsilateral and contralateral breasts

Dose: 20 mg once daily for 10 years (Earlier 5 years was the duration, but latest guidelines recommend 10 years).

Adverse effects:

* Hot flushes, most common adverse effect

* Endometrial carcinoma

* Thromboembolic events

* Reduced visual acuity, cataract, and retinal deposits

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: This image displays a brace that belongs to?
questions.explanation: The image displays a Taylor brace (Option C), which is a thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO). It is characterized by two long vertical metal bars (paraspinal bars) connected to a pelvic band, along with shoulder straps. This brace is traditionally used to restrict spinal flexion and extension, particularly in the management of stable vertebral fractures, Pott's disease (spinal tuberculosis), or Scheuermann's kyphosis. The Milwaukee brace (Option B) is a cervico-thoraco-lumbosacral orthosis that includes a neck ring, used for high-thoracic scoliosis. The Boston brace (Option A) is a low-profile, rigid plastic shell used primarily for lumbar or thoracolumbar scoliosis. The ASHE brace (Option D) is another spinal support but lacks the specific Taylor vertical-bar structure. Understanding these orthoses is essential for pediatric and spinal care. Therefore, the visual of the paraspinal metal bars with shoulder straps uniquely identifies the Taylor brace
questions.learning: The image displays a Taylor brace (Option C), which is a thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO). It is characterized by two long vertical metal bars (paraspinal bars) connected to a pelvic band, along with shoulder straps.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After how many days is the polymorphic rash of Varicella not contagious?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. After crust formation over lesions

Chicken pox or Varicella caused by Varicella zoster virus becomes non-contagious after the lesions have crusted.

* Varicella zoster virus is an α Herpes virus (Human Herpes Virus 3).

* Over half of primary infections occur before the age of 5 and 85% before puberty.

* The lesions are polymorphic - present at different stages in each site.

* In 2–4 days, a dry crust forms and soon separates, to leave a shallow pink depression which, in the absence of secondary infection, heals without scarring.

* Most common complication is secondary bacterial infection.

* Varicella confers lasting immunity and second attacks are uncommon.

* In histopathology, keratinocytes show ballooning degeneration creating multinucleated giant cells called Tzanck cells.

Characteristics of rash of chicken pox

* Superficial

* Pleomorphic

* Centripetal

* Unilocular

* Symmetrical

* Spares palms and soles, affects flexor surfaces and axilla

* Rapid evolution

* Dew drop on Rose-petal appearance

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a forensic examination of a shooting incident, a medical examiner discovers both shotgun pellets and rifle bullets at the crime scene. The examiner notes the differences in their design and function. Which statement about these ammunition types is not correct?
options: Shotgun cartridges contain multiple projectiles that spread upon firing.
Wads are used in all types of cartridges
Rifle bullets are generally elongated with a pointed tip
Rifle bullets and shotgun pellets are made of lead
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wads are used in all types of cartridges

This statement is not correct. Wads are characteristic of shotgun cartridges, where they separate the powder from the shot, seal gases, and help control pellet spread. Rifle cartridges do not use wads; instead, they contain a single bullet seated directly in the cartridge case with propellant.

A. Shotgun cartridges: Contain multiple pellets that disperse after firing—true.

C. Rifle bullets: Are typically elongated and pointed for stability and penetration—true.

D. Both rifle bullets and shotgun pellets are commonly made of lead (often jacketed in rifles)—true.
questions.learning: Wads are used in all types of cartridges — This statement is not correct. Wads are characteristic of shotgun cartridges, where they separate the powder from the shot, seal gases, and help control pellet spread.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The drug shown in the image below is administered for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malaria

The image given below shows artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), which is used in the treatment of falciparum malaria.

ACT consists of artesunate given for 3 days and sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine given for 1 day. It is supplied by the government of India under the national vector-borne disease control program (NVDCP).

It is given to all confirmed cases of Plasmodium falciparum infection, found positive by microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests. Primaquine with dose of 0.75 mg/kg of body weight is given on day 2 along with it. Artemether-lumefantrine is used for the treatment of falciparum malaria in the northeastern states of India.

This drug is not given in pregnancy and in children less than 5 kg of body weight.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient was referred by a doctor to a radiologist for a CT scan and the doctor was given money for the referral. What is this unethical act called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dichotomy

This unethical act of receiving a commission for referring a patient is referred to as Dichotomy.

Dichotomy is an unethical act wherein a doctor receives a gift, commission or money for referring, recommending, or procuring a patient for any medical, surgical or other treatments. Fee splitting is unethical in India.
