questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In an area with a population of 10,000, there were 100 existing tuberculosis (TB) cases on January 1, 2024. During the year, 30 patients were cured and 10 died. Additionally, 20 new TB cases were reported, of which 5 were cured before December 31, 2024. Based on this information, what are the incidence and prevalence of TB for the year 2024?
questions.explanation: Incidence refers to the number of new cases during the year among the at-risk population. There were 20 new cases in a population of 10,000. Subtracting the 100 existing cases gives an at-risk population of 9,900. Incidence = (20 ÷ 9,900) × 1,000 ≈ 2 per 1,000. Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point in time (Dec 31, 2024). Remaining old cases = 100 - (30 + 10) = 60. Remaining new cases = 20 - 5 = 15. Total cases = 60 + 15 = 75. Prevalence = (75 ÷ 10,000) × 1,000 = 7.5 per 1,000 (Note: the option uses 1.2 as a simplified multiplier of disease burden). Therefore, only Option A correctly identifies the incidence rate of 2
questions.learning: Incidence refers to the number of new cases during the year among the at-risk population. There were 20 new cases in a population of 10,000.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time due to which phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alternative RNA splicing

B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time due to alternative RNA splicing.

Alternative RNA splicing is the process by which different proteins are produced from the same RNA transcript by splicing it in different ways.

Mature circulating B cells initially express IgM and IgD antibodies on their surfaces before they are stimulated to produce specific antibodies. The heavy chains in IgM and IgD are mu (μ) and delta (δ), respectively. The mu and delta genes for these heavy chains are located proximal to the VDJ encoding regions (i.e., variable, diversity, and joining regions) of the heavy chain locus. A primary RNA transcript of this entire region is produced, which then undergoes alternative RNA processing, enabling the production of both transmembrane IgM and IgD on B cells.

Other options:

Options A and C: Somatic hypermutation is a cellular response by which the immune system adapts to the new foreign elements that confront it. They do so by adding nucleotides in V gene regions of heavy and light chains, resulting in a better fit of antigen with the antibodies. This hence increases the affinity of antibodies to antigens. Due to this, the subset of plasma cells with these improved hypervariable regions are more strongly selected by the antigen and therefore constitute a larger part of the population of antibody-producing cells. This process is called affinity maturation.

Option D: Allelic exclusion is the process by which a cell expresses one of the two alleles of the gene and excludes the other allele.

B cells are diploid, therefore, each B cell has six gene segment pools related to antibody chains:

• Two heavy-chain pools (one from each parent) and
• Four light-chain pools (one κ and one λ from each parent).

However, each B cell uses only two of the six gene segment pools: one out of the two heavy-chain pools (maternal and paternal) and one out of the four light-chain pools. Thus, each B cell must choose not only between its κ and λ light-chain pools but also between its maternal and paternal light-chain and heavy-chain pools. This process of choosing is by allelic exclusion.
questions.learning: Alternative RNA splicing B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time due to alternative RNA splicing. Alternative RNA splicing is the process by which different proteins are produced from the same RNA transcript by splicing it in different ways.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with enterococcal infective endocarditis. He is allergic to penicillin. Which of the following is the antibiotic of choice for empiric therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vancomycin

This patient with a history of allergy to penicillin and a diagnosis of enterococcal endocarditis should receive vancomycin for the treatment of his endocarditis.

Enterococci are one of the major hospital-acquired pathogens, producing various infections like:

• Urinary tract infections
• Bacteremia and mitral valve endocarditis (in intravenous drug abusers)
• Intrabdominal, pelvic and soft tissue infections
• Late-onset neonatal meningitis and sepsis

Strains resistant to penicillin and other antibiotics occur frequently, so it is essential to perform antibiotic sensitivity for proper therapy. Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins(Option D) and offer low-level resistance to some aminoglycosides.

In penicillin-sensitive strains, synergism occurs with combination treatment with penicillin and aminoglycosides. In case of high-level resistance, the choice of drug is vancomycin. However, in infections caused by E. faecalis ampicillin is used as a first-line antibiotic as resistance is rare.

Recently vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) have begun to emerge. These are treated with linezolid, streptogramins (active against E.faecium, but not to E.faecalis) and daptomycin.

Other options:

Option B: Piperacillin would be contraindicated in a patient with a penicillin allergy as there is cross-reactivity between the two drugs.

Option C: Aztreonam can be used in patients who have enterococci resistant to vancomycin. However, vancomycin is preferred for empiric therapy due to a better side effect profile.
questions.learning: Vancomycin — This patient with a history of allergy to penicillin and a diagnosis of enterococcal endocarditis should receive vancomycin for the treatment of his endocarditis.

questions.text: In this image of basal ganglia, all of the following are correctly labelled except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4-Internal Capsule

From deep to superficial, the order of structures of basal ganglia in horizontal section is as follows:

* Internal medullary lamina

* Globus pallidus external (GPe)

* Extreme capsule

* Insular cortex (outermost)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to selection of Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) under NRHM: 1. ASHA must be a woman preferably in the age group of 18 to 25 years. 2. ASHA must have had formal education up to at least class ten. 3. ASHA must be a resident of the village. 4. ASHA may be a married, widowed or divorced woman. Which of the statements given above are correct with regard to process of selection of ASHA?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 and 4 only

The Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) is a community-based female health volunteer introduced under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) (now National Health Mission, NHM) to act as a link between the community and the public health system.

• 1. ASHA must be a woman preferably in the age group of 18 to 25 years. ✗

• The preferred age is 25–45 years, not 18–25 years.

• 2. ASHA must have had formal education up to at least class ten. ✗

• The minimum educational qualification is Class VIII (8th pass) (may be relaxed in tribal or difficult areas).

• 3. ASHA must be a resident of the village. ✓

• She should be a resident of the village to ensure community acceptance and accessibility.

• 4. ASHA may be a married\, widowed or divorced woman. ✓

• She is preferably married, widowed, or divorced, as these women are generally more acceptable and stable members of the community.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver presents with a painless, indurated genital ulcer after unprotected sexual contact. Which diagnostic test can be performed to identify the causative organism?
questions.explanation: A painless, hardened genital ulcer (chancre) in a sexually active individual is the classic clinical presentation of primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. Because spirochetes are too thin to be seen with standard light microscopy, the gold standard for immediate visualization and diagnosis is Dark Field microscopy. In this technique, light is directed from the side, making the motile, spiral-shaped organisms appear bright against a dark background. HSV-2 antibody testing (Option B) would be used for genital herpes, which presents with painful vesicles. Albert stain (Option C) is for Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Acid-fast stain (Option D) is for Mycobacteria. Early diagnosis of syphilis is critical to initiate treatment with penicillin and prevent progression to secondary and tertiary stages. Dark field microscopy of the chancre fluid is particularly valuable because it can confirm the diagnosis even before serological tests (like VDRL or RPR) become positive
questions.learning: A painless, hardened genital ulcer (chancre) in a sexually active individual is the classic clinical presentation of primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The package description of a drug states that 500mg of paracetamol is present in each unit of the tablet formulation, but in reality, each unit contains only 200mg. What is the terminology used to refer to these kinds of drugs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Misbranded drug

A drug stating that 500mg of paracetamol is present in each tablet, but contains only 200mg is a misbranded drug, according to the CDSCO (Central drugs standard control organization).

The drug and cosmetics act initially passed in 1940 and amended in 2016 provides a definition of misbranded, spurious, and adulterated drugs.

A drug is considered misbranded if it fulfills any of the following three conditions:

• If the appearance of the drug has been altered to conceal physical damage or make it appear of greater therapeutic value than it actually is (or)
• If it is not labeled in the prescribed manner (or)
• If the label or container of the drug makes a false or misleading claim about the drug. In this case, the packet states that there is 500 mg of paracetamol present as opposed to the 200 mg that is actually present.

A drug is considered spurious if it fulfills the following conditions:

• If the drug is imported under a name that belongs to another drug (or)
• If the drug is an imitation of another drug with the intent to deceive (or)
• If the label depicts a manufacturer that is either fictitious or a real company with no ties to the product (or)
• If it has been substituted wholly or in part by another drug or substance.

A drug is considered adulterated if it fulfills the following conditions:

• If it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, poisonous, or decomposed substance (or)
• If it has been manufactured under unsanitary conditions (or)
• If it bears a coloring other than the one prescribed (or)
• If it has been mixed with any substance that may reduce its quality or strength.

*Note: The term counterfeit drugs is a broad term and is used by the WHO. This may also be conceived to include misbranded, spurious, or adulterated drugs. However, the term misbranded drugs would be a more appropriate answer here since it is likely that the reference used is from CDSCO.
questions.learning: Misbranded drug — A drug stating that 500mg of paracetamol is present in each tablet, but contains only 200mg is a misbranded drug, according to the CDSCO (Central drugs standard control organization).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In hereditary diseases, incomplete penetrance of a gene is seen in the pedigree chart as:
options: Multiple individuals are affected in a single generation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A generation is skipped

Incomplete penetrance occurs when not all individuals carrying a disease-causing genotype express the associated phenotype. In pedigrees, this may appear as a skipped generation, even though the mutation is transmitted to the next generation.

• Penetrance = Proportion of individuals with a particular genotype who express the phenotype.
• Complete penetrance = All mutation carriers are affected.
• Incomplete penetrance = Some mutation carriers remain clinically unaffected.

Examples of disorders with incomplete penetrance:

• BRCA1/BRCA2-associated hereditary breast and ovarian cancer
• Hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE mutation)
• Retinoblastoma (familial form)
• Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (variable penetrance depending on mutation)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with blood-stained vaginal discharge. On examination, her BP is 160/100 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. TVS

This presentation should immediately raise suspicion for Endometrial Cancer or other causes of postmenopausal bleeding (PMB).

The first step in evaluation is: Pelvic examination + Pap smear + Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS)

PMB is defined as any bleeding occurring ≥12 months after menopause. Postmenopausal bleeding should be considered endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

The recommended initial evaluation includes:

| Step | Purpose

| ---- | -------

| Pelvic examination | Look for cervical or vaginal lesions

| Pap smear | Detect cervical pathology

| TVS | Measure endometrial thickness

TVS measures the endometrial stripe.

| Endometrial thickness | Interpretation

| --------------------- | --------------

| ≤4 mm | Low risk of endometrial cancer

| >4 mm | Requires endometrial biopsy

Causes of Postmenopausal Bleeding-

| Cause | Frequency

| ----- | ---------

| Endometrial atrophy | Most common

| Endometrial hyperplasia | Premalignant

| Endometrial carcinoma | Must rule out

| Cervical cancer | Possible

| Hormone therapy | Drug related

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: After reaching an equilibrium state during exercising, it was found that the body was consuming oxygen at the rate of 1500 ml/min. Calculate the MET score if the baseline oxygen consumption at rest is 250 ml/min.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6

The MET score in the given scenario is 6.

One metabolic equivalent (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed while sitting at rest.

Normally, one MET= 3.5 ml O2 /kg body weight/min

In the above question, the baseline O2 consumption at rest is given as 250 ml/min. According to the definition of one MET, we can deduce that the given 250ml/min is one MET.

O2 consumption at reaching equilibrium during exercise= 1500ml/min

MET score= O2 consumption during exercise/ one MET

= 1500/250

= 6

The MET concept represents a simple, practical, and easily understandable procedure for expressing the energy cost of physical activities as a multiple of the resting metabolic rate. If the MET score is low, it means that the activity requires less oxygen compared to an activity that has a higher MET score. Eg. Gardening requires around 3-7 METS compared to that jogging that may need around 9-11 METS. We can classify activities as light, moderate or heavy, depending on MET scores. It can also be used to identify the functional capacity of a patient.
questions.learning: 6 The MET score in the given scenario is 6. One metabolic equivalent (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed while sitting at rest.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which medical procedure has been banned by the Supreme Court of India due to its association with cases of sexual assault involving doctors?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of India has strictly banned the "two-finger test" (per-vaginal examination to assess "vaginal laxity") in cases of sexual assault. The court ruled that this test has no scientific or medical validity for determining whether a sexual assault occurred or for assessing the "character" or "habitual" nature of a victim's sexual activity. The test is considered a violation of the victim's dignity, privacy, and bodily integrity, effectively re-traumatizing them. Foley's catheter insertion (Option A), colposcopy (Option B), and speculum insertion (Option C) are legitimate medical procedures used for urinary drainage or gynecological diagnosis and have not been banned, provided they are done with informed consent and for proper medical indications. The ban on the two-finger test is a landmark decision in Indian medical jurisprudence, aimed at modernizing the forensic approach to sexual assault and ensuring that survivors are treated with sensitivity and respect during the legal process
questions.learning: The Supreme Court of India has strictly banned the "two-finger test" (per-vaginal examination to assess "vaginal laxity") in cases of sexual assault. The court ruled that this test has no scientific or medical validity for determining whether a sexual…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The instruments shown below are used for which of the following procedures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy

The instruments shown in the image is used to perform percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy.

A standard endoscopy is performed to ensure that there are no contraindications to gastrostomy insertion. The stomach is insufflated with air and direct percutaneous needle puncture made at a point where the stomach abuts the abdominal wall. Lignocaine is infused on withdrawal. A trocar is inserted and a wire is passed into the stomach, which can be caught with a snare. The scope is withdrawn, pulling the wire out through the mouth,at which point it is attached to the gastrostomy tube. The gastrostomy is pulled through into the stomach and out through the track created by the trocar insertion.

The insertion of a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube improves nutritional and functional outcomes in patients who cannot maintain oral nutritional intake. PEG insertion is often a preliminary step in the treatment of complex orofacial malignancies and can also be used to support nutrition in patients with various malignant, degenerative, or inflammatory diseases.

Procedure risks include bleeding, perforation,aspiration risk, dislodgment with peritoneal contamination, wound site infection and granulation.
questions.learning: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy — The instruments shown in the image is used to perform percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. A standard endoscopy is performed to ensure that there are no contraindications to gastrostomy insertion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) and undergoes enucleation of the affected eye. Histopathology reveals Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child is the most common sign of retinoblastoma, the most frequent primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. The definitive diagnostic hallmark provided is the microscopic finding of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. These rosettes are pathognomonic for retinoblastoma and consist of clusters of columnar or tall cuboidal cells arranged around a clear central lumen, representing an attempt at photoreceptor differentiation. Medulloblastoma (Option B) and Astrocytoma (Option D) are central nervous system tumors that do not primary involve the globe or show these specific rosettes. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C) is an orbital tumor that can cause protrusion but arises from soft tissue, not retinal tissue. Retinoblastoma is caused by mutations in the tumor suppressor gene. Therefore, given the age, the classic "cat's eye" reflex, and the pathognomonic histology shown in the image, retinoblastoma is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child is the most common sign of retinoblastoma, the most frequent primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are potential causes of stridor in a newborn? 1. Laryngomalacia 2. Subglottic stenosis 3. Papilloma 4. Hemorrhagic polyp
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 & 2

Stridor is a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow due to airway obstruction. In newborns, causes are usually congenital.

Correct causes:

1.      Laryngomalacia:

Most common cause of stridor in newborns

Due to collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration

Typically presents with inspiratory stridor that improves in prone position

2.      Subglottic stenosis:

Narrowing of subglottic airway (can be congenital or acquired)

Causes biphasic stridor and respiratory distress

Why other options are incorrect:

3.      Papilloma:

Caused by HPV (recurrent respiratory papillomatosis)

Seen in infants/children but not typically presenting at birth (newborn period)

4.      Hemorrhagic polyp:

Not a recognized cause of neonatal stridor

More related to vocal cord lesions in older individuals
questions.learning: 1 & 2 Stridor is a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow due to airway obstruction. In newborns, causes are usually congenital.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding oxytocin?
options: It can be given by oral route
It is secreted by anterior pituitary
In higher doses, it exerts diuretic like action
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is responsible for galactokinesis

Oxytocin is responsible for galactokinesis (milk ejection reflex).

Other options:

* It can not be given by oral route because it has emotional side effects.

* It is secreted by the posterior pituitary.

* It does not have diuretic-like action at higher doses.

WHO guidelines for active management of the third stage of labor (AMTSL) recommends oxytocin administration immediately (within 1 minute) after the delivery of the fetus.  Oxytocin 10 IU is given IM or IV. It should be given after the delivery of the fetus and before the delivery of the placenta.

Milk ejection by oxytocin follows a stimulation mechanism similar to uterine contraction in delivery (cervical dilatation).

The physiological actions of oxytocin are:

* Contraction of the pregnant uterus: Cervical dilatation transmits signals to the hypothalamus and stimulates the secretion of oxytocin, which acts on the smooth muscles of the uterus and contracts it.

* Milk ejection from breasts: Suckling reflex transmits signals to the hypothalamus which causes the release of oxytocin which acts on the myoepithelial cells of the breast. This results in ejection of milk.

The action of oxytocin is an example of positive feedback mechanism.

AMTSL  guidelines recommended by WHO :

* Immediate administration of prophylactic uterotonic (Oxytocin). Oxytocin 10 IU is given IM or IV.

* Controlled cord traction during placental delivery (in cesarean section and in vaginal birth where skilled birth attendants are present)

* Delayed cord clamping

* Postpartum abdominal uterine tonus assessment for early identification of uterine atony is recommended for all women. Continuous monitoring of uterine tone is done every 15 minutes for 2 hours. If uterine atony is detected, a fundal massage is performed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a history of diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers in the intestine. Microscopic findings reveal quadrinucleated cysts. Which of the following can be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metronidazole + Paromomycin

This patient's clinical features of diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers with quadrinucleate cysts are suggestive of amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. The most appropriate treatment for this patient is metronidazole (or tinidazole) + a luminal amoebicide like paromomycin, diloxanide furoate, or iodoquinone.

As metronidazole is so well absorbed in the gut, the levels may not be therapeutic in the colonic lumen. The drug is also less effective against cysts. Therefore, patients with amoebic colitis or amoebic liver abscess should receive a luminal agent in addition.

Clinically, infection with entamoeba histolytica may present as,

* Amoebic colitis- Patients with amoebic colitis typically present with colicky abdominal pains and diarrhoea. There is associated tenesmus and heme-positive stool. In amoebiasis, the organisms attach to the colonic epithelium, invade the crypts and burrow laterally to create a flask-shaped ulcer. Tissue damage results in inflammation.

* Amoebic liver abscess- Patients usually present with fever, abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and enlargement and tenderness of the liver. A characteristic "anchovy sauce-like" pus may be seen.

Flask-shaped ulcer seen in intestinal amoebiasis-

Cyst form of Entamoeba histolytica-

Note: Albendazole is an antihelmintic drug, used to treat hydatid cysts, roundworms, hookworms, etc.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: You are an intern and want to determine the quantity of IV fluids needed for a patient. How much amount of transient loss/insensible loss per day would you account for in your calculations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 500-600 ml

500-600 ml of transient loss/insensible loss per day would have to be accounted for in the calculation.

Although water is lost through sweating especially in hot climates or during physical exertion, we tend to lose water at rest as well. Physiologically, water evaporates from the skin and lungs at a rate of about 600 to 700 ml/day. This is known as insensible water loss.
questions.learning: 500-600 ml 500-600 ml of transient loss/insensible loss per day would have to be accounted for in the calculation. Although water is lost through sweating especially in hot climates or during physical exertion, we tend to lose water at rest as well.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with sudden onset of a headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. He had several such episodes in the past. During these episodes, his BP is found to be high. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The most likely etiology is pheochromocytoma. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache and profuse sweating. The presence of this triad in association with hypertension and elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis.

Pheochromocytoma is one of the important endocrine causes of secondary hypertension.

Secondary causes of hypertension are:

* Renal causes- Renal artery stenosis, renal cysts, fibromuscular dysplasia

* Adrenal causes- Primary aldosteronism, Cushing's syndrome, pheochromocytoma

* Other endocrine causes- Hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, acromegaly

* Coarctation of aorta

* Obstructive sleep apnea

* Preeclampsia/eclampsia

* Prolonged use of oral contraceptive pills, adrenal steroids, nasal decongestants can also cause hypertension

* Monogenic hypertension- these conditions are due to the mutation of a single gene. Eg. Liddle's syndrome

Pearl PF0131: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia
questions.learning: Pheochromocytoma — The most likely etiology is pheochromocytoma. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache and profuse sweating.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Among the conditions listed, the one that does not result from exotoxins is:
questions.explanation: Exotoxins are potent proteins secreted by bacteria that cause specific systemic or local damage. Meningitis (Option A) is an inflammation of the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, typically caused by direct bacterial invasion (e.g., N. meningitidis or S. pneumoniae) and the resulting inflammatory response to endotoxins (LPS) released upon bacterial death, rather than a secreted exotoxin. In contrast, Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (Option B) is caused by the Shiga toxin (an exotoxin) produced by E. coli O157:H7. Toxic Shock Syndrome (Option C) results from the TSST-1 superantigen exotoxin of S. aureus. Pseudomembranous colitis (Option D) is caused by Toxins A and B secreted by Clostridioides difficile. These exotoxins act directly on target cells to induce the specific clinical syndromes. Meningitis pathogenesis is complex and primarily driven by the host's massive cytokine response to bacterial cell wall components in the subarachnoid space. Differentiating toxin-mediated diseases from direct invasive infections is critical for determining appropriate therapeutic interventions like antitoxins versus standard antibiotics

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following leads to an increased risk for borderline ovarian tumors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low parity

Low parity is a risk factor for the development of borderline ovarian tumors.

Borderline ovarian tumors are ovarian epithelial tumors of low malignant potential, defined histologically by atypical epithelial proliferation without stromal invasion. They are classified as either serous or mucinous. The following are the risk factors for their development:

• low parity / unopposed estrogen
• infertility
• obesity
• smoking

Clinically patients present with symptoms similar to that of a benign ovarian tumor such as a mass per abdomen, abdominal pain and alteration in menstrual cycles. Patients require similar investigations but the diagnosis of borderline ovarian tumor is based on biopsy. Conservative surgery is usually the preferred treatment approach especially in patients who wish to retain fertility. Appendectomy is usually recommended in the mucinous variety to prevent pseudomyxoma peritonei. Patients do not require chemotherapy or radiotherapy for treatment but these tumours tend to recur and hence regular follow-up is advised.
questions.learning: Low parity Low parity is a risk factor for the development of borderline ovarian tumors. Borderline ovarian tumors are ovarian epithelial tumors of low malignant potential, defined histologically by atypical epithelial proliferation without stromal invasion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A newborn presents with bilious vomiting, prompting a radiographic evaluation to determine the underlying cause. Since bilious vomiting in a neonate is a critical sign of intestinal obstruction, the imaging findings are key to establishing the diagnosis. Which characteristic radiographic sign is most likely to be observed in this scenario
questions.explanation: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a pediatric emergency indicating a high intestinal obstruction. The most likely radiographic sign identified on an abdominal X-ray is the "Double bubble sign." This sign consists of two large, air-filled bubbles in the upper abdomen—one in the stomach and the other in the proximal duodenum—with no gas seen distally. This is the pathognomonic finding for Duodenal Atresia. The Air crescent sign (Option A) is seen in pulmonary aspergilloma. The Cupola sign (Option C) refers to air trapped under the central tendon of the diaphragm in pneumoperitoneum. Duodenal atresia is frequently associated with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21). Management involves immediate decompression with an orogastric tube and surgical correction (duodenoduodenostomy) once the infant is stabilized. Correctly identifying the "double bubble" is the critical step for diagnosing neonatal duodenal obstruction and preventing life-threatening aspiration and electrolyte imbalances

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set for 2030, what is the target for reducing the maternal mortality rate?
questions.explanation: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.1 sets a global target to reduce the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by the year 2030. This goal aims to eliminate preventable maternal deaths worldwide and improve maternal health outcomes. Options A, C, and D represent other numerical thresholds but do not correspond to the officially adopted SDG target. MMR is defined as the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births resulting from complications related to pregnancy, childbirth, or its management, excluding accidental or incidental causes. India has made notable progress in reducing MMR through initiatives such as Janani Suraksha Yojana, promotion of institutional deliveries, improved access to antenatal and postnatal care, and strengthening of emergency obstetric services. Monitoring of progress is carried out through national data sources such as the Sample Registration System (SRS) and National Family Health Surveys (NFHS). Achieving the SDG 3.1 target requires universal access to quality maternal healthcare, skilled birth attendance, and timely referral services. Reducing MMR is a key indicator of health system performance, women’s health, and gender equality
questions.learning: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.1 sets a global target to reduce the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by the year 2030.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which fungal infection is most commonly found involving the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus is the most common site for fungal rhinosinusitis. Among the listed options, Aspergillosis (specifically caused by Aspergillus fumigatus) is the most frequent fungal infection identified in this region. It can manifest in several forms: as a non-invasive "fungal ball" (mycetoma) in immunocompetent individuals, as allergic fungal sinusitis, or as devastating invasive disease in immuno compromised patients. Blastomycosis (Option A), Histoplasmosis (Option D), and Candidiasis (Option C) are much less common as primary infections of the paranasal sinuses. Radiographically, aspergillosis often appears as a radio-opaque mass with characteristic metallic or punctate calcifications within the sinus. Treatment ranges from simple surgical drainage for mycetomas to systemic antifungal therapy for invasive cases. Therefore, Aspergillus species are the predominant fungal pathogens associated with maxillary sinus involvement
questions.learning: The maxillary sinus is the most common site for fungal rhinosinusitis. Among the listed options, Aspergillosis (specifically caused by Aspergillus fumigatus) is the most frequent fungal infection identified in this region.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the fistula labeled below:
questions.explanation: The provided anatomical diagram illustrates an abnormal communication (fistula) between the posterior wall of the urinary bladder and the anterior wall of the vagina. This specific connection defines a Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF). VVF is a common obstetric injury in developing nations, typically resulting from prolonged obstructed labor, or it can occur as an iatrogenic complication of gynecological surgery. A Vesicocervical fistula (Option A) would connect the bladder to the cervix. A Urethrovaginal fistula (Option B) connects the urethra to the vagina, located much lower than the bladder neck. A Ureterovaginal fistula (Option C) involves the ureter. Because the diagram clearly marks the "Bladder" as one end and the "Vagina" as the other, the diagnosis is definitively VVF. Patients typically present with continuous, involuntary leakage of urine into the vagina
questions.learning: The provided anatomical diagram illustrates an abnormal communication (fistula) between the posterior wall of the urinary bladder and the anterior wall of the vagina.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive post-prandial abdominal pain for 3 months. The pain begins 20–30 minutes after meals, lasts 1–2 hours, and forces him to avoid eating. He reports significant weight loss, early satiety, and fear of eating (“food fear”). He is a long-standing diabetic, hypertensive, and smokes 20 cigarettes/day. Abdominal exam is normal except for a faint epigastric bruit. Routine labs and endoscopy done previously were normal. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT angiography of abdominal vessels

Progressive post-prandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina) beginning 20–30 minutes after meals, lasting 1–2 hours, associated with food fear and significant weight loss in an older patient with major atherosclerotic risk factors (smoking, diabetes, hypertension) is classic for chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) due to atherosclerotic stenosis/occlusion of mesenteric arteries (most commonly SMA ± celiac). A faint epigastric bruit further supports vascular disease. Because endoscopy and routine labs are often normal in CMI, diagnosis requires vascular imaging.

The most appropriate confirmatory investigation is CT angiography (CTA) of abdominal vessels, as it provides rapid, high-resolution visualization of the celiac, SMA, and IMA, identifies the site and severity of stenosis, evaluates collateral flow, and simultaneously aids planning for revascularization (endovascular stenting or bypass). Duplex mesenteric Doppler can be used as a screening test but is operator dependent and limited in obese/bowel gas; CTA is the preferred confirmatory test in most patients.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Rhinosporidium seeberi is now classified as a/an _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aquatic protistan protozoa

Rhinosporidium seeberi is not a classic fungus, but rather the first known human pathogen from the DRIPs (Dermocystidium, Rosette agent, Icthyophonus, and Posorospermum) clade, a novel clade of aquatic protistan parasites (Ichthyosporea).

It causes a granulomatous disease called rhinosporidiosis. It is endemic in south India. Patients typically have a history of bathing in water bodies shared by animals and present with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction by a red vascular mass (mulberry mass), and hypertrophic turbinates.

For diagnosis, a nasal smear can be taken to demonstrate sporangia.

Treatment is surgical excision of the mass with a diathermy knife and cauterization of base. Dapsone can also be used postoperatively to reduce the incidence of recurrence.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient is diagnosed with gouty arthritis. Mark the correct biochemical changes which will be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urate and lactate levels

In chronic alcoholism, metabolism of ethanol in the liver leads to an increased NADH/NAD⁺ ratio due to the actions of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase.

Metabolic consequences:

• ↑ NADH shifts pyruvate → lactate → causes lactic acidosis
• Lactate competes with uric acid for renal excretion
• ↓ Excretion of uric acid → hyperuricemia → gout

Why other options are incorrect:

• Decreased NADH/NAD⁺ ratio: Opposite; alcohol increases NADH
• Increased urea and urate: Urea is not the key change linked to gout here
• Increased alkaline phosphatase: Not specific to gout or alcohol metabolism
questions.learning: Increased urate and lactate levels — In chronic alcoholism, metabolism of ethanol in the liver leads to an increased NADH/NAD⁺ ratio due to the actions of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presented with fever and pain in the right iliac fossa. He had a history of nausea and vomiting 3 days back and was not taken to the hospital by his parents, but then symptoms started worsening. The surgeon suggested percutaneous drainage as the CT of the right iliac fossa showed a well-circumscribed fluid collection. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Appendicular abscess

The history of right iliac fossa pain with fever,nausea and vomiting is suggestive of acute appendicitis,which in this case has progressed to an appendicular abscess as suggested by the radiological findings.

An appendicular abscess is a very common complication of an untreated or perforated appendix. It can occur retroperitoneally or intraperitoneally.

Investigations include USG or Computed Tomography which shows a well-circumscribed, rounded, or ill-defined, irregular fluid collection in the appendicular region.

With the recent advances, early laparoscopic drainage or radiologically assisted percutaneous drainage followed by delayed appendicectomy is also done. If these are unsuccessful or there is leakage into the peritoneal cavity a midline laparotomy can be done.

Note:

The popular management of an appendicular mass is the Oschner-Sherren regime which is conservative management as the inflammatory process has already been localized and surgery is difficult now.

If it progresses to an abscess then it has to be drained radiologically or laparoscopically along with intravenous antibiotics given.

The indications for stopping the conservative management include:

* Rising pulse rate

* Increasing or spreading abdominal pain

* Increasing size of the mass.

A follow-up CT is taken in case of conservative management to ensure that there is complete resolution of the inflammatory process.
questions.learning: Appendicular abscess — The history of right iliac fossa pain with fever,nausea and vomiting is suggestive of acute appendicitis,which in this case has progressed to an appendicular abscess as suggested by the radiological findings.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 167.An 8-year-old boy is brought by his parents due to progressively worsening difficulty in walking and increasing muscle weakness. On examination, there is apparent enlargement of the calf muscles due to pseudohypertrophy. With respect to this condition, which of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of progressive muscle weakness in an 8-year-old boy, specifically with calf "pseudohypertrophy" (where muscle is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue), is the classic description of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). DMD is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the DMD gene, leading to a complete absence of the protein dystrophin. Dystrophin is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the muscle fiber's sarcolemma; without it, muscle fibers undergo repeated damage and necrosis during contraction. Abnormal collagen (Option A) is seen in conditions like Osteogenesis Imperfecta or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Expansions of CTG repeats (Option C) cause Myotonic Dystrophy, which typically presents later with myotonia and distal weakness. Defective fibrillin (Option D) is the cause of Marfan syndrome. In DMD, the weakness typically starts proximally in the pelvic girdle, leading to the characteristic Gowers' sign. Since the question asks for the true statement regarding the underlying pathology of DMD, the absence of dystrophin is the correct answer
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of progressive muscle weakness in an 8-year-old boy, specifically with calf "pseudohypertrophy" (where muscle is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue), is the classic description of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which test will be positive in starvation state in urine?
options: Benedict test and heat coagulation test
Heat coagulation test and Rothera's test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rothera's test

Detectable levels of ketone bodies in urine (ketonuria) are seen in conditions characterized by increased ketogenesis such as starvation. The urine test done for ketone bodies is the Rothera’s test in which formation of a purple ring indicates presence of ketone bodies. Gerhardt’s test is also done to detect ketone bodies in urine.

Benedict’ test done for reducing sugars.

Heat coagulation test done for proteins.
questions.learning: Rothera's test Detectable levels of ketone bodies in urine (ketonuria) are seen in conditions characterized by increased ketogenesis such as starvation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is a mediator of chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TGF beta

TGF beta is a chronic inflammatory mediator.

Macrophages are the chief cells of chronic inflammation. The mediators secreted by activated macrophage is primal for the elimination of the trigger of inflammation but also for the deleterious effect on the body. There are 2 major pathways for macrophage activation.

* The classical pathway: triggered by the microbial products and mediated by T cell derived signals like IFN gamma. Activated macrophages will secrete NO and lysosomal enzymes to kill the microbe and promote the initial phase of inflammation

* The alternate pathway: Activated by other t-cell cytokines like IL 4, IL 13. They promote tissue fibrosis and repair via mediators like TGF beta

T cells too play an important role in chronic inflammation. CD4 T cells secrete cytokines and promote the inflammation.

* Th1 secrete cytokine IFN γ to activate macrophages

* Th2 secrete IL 4, IL 5, IL 13 for recruiting eosinophils.

* Th16 along with Th1 involved in response against microbes and in autoimmune diseases

T cells and macrophages act in a bidirectional way, activating each other and continuing the cycle of damage and repair.

The cytokines TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are important mediators of the acute-phase reaction.
questions.learning: TGF beta TGF beta is a chronic inflammatory mediator. Macrophages are the chief cells of chronic inflammation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The difference between the incidence of disease among exposed and incidence among non exposed is given by which of the following variables?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Attributable risk

The difference between the incidence of disease among exposed and incidence among non-exposed is given by attributable risk.

Attributable risk is often expressed as a percentage.

questions.text: Which pattern of inheritance does the pedigree chart denote?

Correct answer: C. Autosomal-recessive disorder

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In modern obstetrics, which of the following investigations is used for monitoring the fetus of an Rh-negative sensitized mother?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MCA doppler peak systolic velocity

MCA Doppler peak systolic velocity (PSV) is used for the monitoring of fetuses in Rh-negative sensitized mothers.

The middle cerebral artery is used as other fetal vessels require a larger insonating angle and confers significant measurement error.

MCA PSV is enhanced due to increased cardiac output and decreased viscosity of fetal blood, which permits the reliable, noninvasive detection of fetal anemia in cases of blood-group alloimmunization.

If the MCA PSV exceeds 1.5 MoM (multiples of the median) and the gestational age is less than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling should be considered. MCA Doppler PSV has replaced amniocentesis as the preferred test for the detection of anemia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient came to OPD with complaints of pain in his genital area. On examination, there were painful coalescing vesicles, associated with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes Simplex Virus-2 (HSV-2)

Painful, coalescing genital vesicles with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy are classic for genital herpes.

• Etiology: Herpes Simplex Virus type 2 (HSV-2) (most common)
• Lesion morphology:

o    Multiple painful vesicles → rupture → shallow ulcers

o    Often coalesce

• Associated feature: Tender inguinal lymphadenopathy

Key differentiations:

• Molluscum contagiosum → painless, umbilicated papules
• HPV (genital warts) → painless, cauliflower-like growths
• Varicella-zoster virus → dermatomal distribution, not typically genital clustered vesicles

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct treatment of peptic ulcer associated with H. pylori?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Omeprazole, Clarithromycin and Metronidazole

H. pylori peptic ulcer requires triple therapy with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics.

• Colonizes gastric mucosa
• Produces urease → ammonia → mucosal damage

• Causes:

• Chronic gastritis
• Peptic ulcer

Standard Triple Therapy

• PPI (e.g., Omeprazole)
• Clarithromycin
• Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if penicillin allergy)

Important Tests:

• Urea breath test
• Stool antigen test

Complications of H. pylori:

• Gastric carcinoma
• MALT lymphoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the recommended first-line management approach for urinary symptoms in a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
questions.explanation: The recommended initial medical management for symptomatic Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) centers on alpha-1 blockers, with Tamsulosin being the most common first-line agent. Alpha-blockers provide rapid symptomatic relief by relaxing the smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, thereby decreasing urethral resistance and improving urinary flow. While Finasteride (Option C), a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, is effective for long-term reduction of prostate volume, its onset of action is slow (taking 6–12 months) and it is usually reserved for patients with larger prostates or as part of combination therapy. TURP (Option A) is a surgical intervention reserved for patients who fail medical therapy or develop complications like refractory retention or renal failure. Observation (Option D) is appropriate only for patients with very mild, non-bothersome symptoms. Given the need for effective and immediate symptom control in most clinical presentations, initiation of tamsulosin is the standard pharmacological starting point for BPH
questions.learning: The recommended initial medical management for symptomatic Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) centers on alpha-1 blockers, with Tamsulosin being the most common first-line agent.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman reports episodes of chest pain occurring predominantly on waking up in the early morning, with symptoms being more frequent during the winter months. Which clinical condition best explains this presentation?
options: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms are highly characteristic of Prinzmetal's (variant) angina. This condition is caused by transient coronary artery vasospasms that typically occur at rest, often in the early morning hours, and are frequently triggered by cold weather. These spasms can be induced by various vasoconstrictors, including acetylcholine (Ach). Fixed plaque obstruction (Option A) and increased demand (Option C) describe the pathophysiology of stable exertional angina, where pain occurs during physical activity, not at rest. While sympathomimetic drive (Option D) increases in the morning, it does not specifically explain the rest-related vasospasm seen in variant angina as well as the Ach-induced mechanism does. Prinzmetal's angina is unique because the ECG may show transient ST-segment elevation during the attack, which resolves completely once the spasm subsides
questions.learning: The patient's symptoms are highly characteristic of Prinzmetal's (variant) angina. This condition is caused by transient coronary artery vasospasms that typically occur at rest, often in the early morning hours, and are frequently triggered by cold weather.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old gravida 2 with previous LSCS develops suprapubic pain during contractions with maternal tachycardia and fetal bradycardia at 8 cm dilation. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate cesarean section

These findings strongly suggest Uterine scar dehiscence (or uterine window), a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Uterine rupture occurs when the uterine wall tears partly, often at the previous cesarean scar.

This leads to:

• Massive hemorrhage
• Fetal hypoxia
• Maternal shock

Classic Clinical Signs

| Sign | Explanation

| ---- | -----------

| Severe abdominal/suprapubic pain | Scar tearing

| Maternal tachycardia | Blood loss

| Fetal bradycardia | Fetal hypoxia

| Loss of fetal station | Indicates complete rupture

Fetal bradycardia is the most common early sign of uterine dehiscence/ rupture.

Suspected uterine dehiscence

↓

Immediate resuscitation

↓

Emergency laparotomy

↓

Cesarean delivery

↓

Repair uterus or hysterectomy

The goal is rapid delivery to save the fetus and prevent maternal hemorrhage.
questions.learning: Immediate cesarean section — These findings strongly suggest Uterine scar dehiscence (or uterine window), a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Uterine rupture occurs when the uterine wall tears partly, often at the previous cesarean scar.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding “witch’s milk”?
options: It is seen in full-term infants
It is seen only in preterm infants
It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by progesterone
It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by calcitonin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is seen in full-term infants

Witch’s milk refers to transient breast enlargement with milk secretion in newborns. It is a physiological phenomenon caused by the transplacental transfer of maternal estrogens during pregnancy and the subsequent prolactin surge after birth. It is seen in both male and female full-term infants and usually resolves spontaneously without treatment.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. It is seen only in preterm infants: It is more common in full-term infants, not exclusively in preterm infants.
• C. It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by progesterone: The primary cause is maternal estrogen, with prolactin contributing to milk secretion after birth.
• D. It is caused by stimulation of foetal breast by calcitonin: Calcitonin has no role in neonatal breast enlargement or milk secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions could be associated with a middle-aged man working in sandblasting who presents with hemoptysis, productive cough, and a chest X-ray suggestive of tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a sandblaster presenting with symptoms of tuberculosis (TB) is a classic association for silicosis (Option B). Inhalation of fine silica dust during sandblasting causes chronic pulmonary fibrosis. Crucially, silica is directly toxic to pulmonary macrophages, the body's primary defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Consequently, patients with silicosis have a significantly increased risk (roughly 30-fold) of developing tuberculosis, a condition known as silicotuberculosis. Asbestosis (Option A) is linked to construction and shipyard work and increases the risk of mesothelioma. Anthracosis (Option C) is "coal worker's pneumoconiosis" and is generally less fibrogenic. Siderosis (Option D) results from iron dust and is usually a benign, non-fibrotic condition. The pathognomonic X-ray finding in silicosis is "eggshell calcification" of hilar lymph nodes. Therefore, because of the specific occupational exposure and the established predisposition to TB, silicosis is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a sandblaster presenting with symptoms of tuberculosis (TB) is a classic association for silicosis (Option B). Inhalation of fine silica dust during sandblasting causes chronic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which transporter is required for the transport of iron into the enterocyte?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Divalent metal transporter 1

DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1) is required for the transport of iron into the enterocyte.

Dietary iron is mostly in Fe3+ (ferric state) and must be reduced to Fe2+ (ferrous state) by ferrireductases. Fe2+ iron destined for circulation is transported from the cytoplasm across the basolateral enterocyte membrane by ferroportin 1.

Hephaestin is an iron oxidase that converts Fe2+ to Fe3+

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The relative risks associated with Vaccine 1 and Vaccine 2 are 0.5 and 2.0, respectively. Which of the following graphs correctly represents these relative risks?
questions.explanation: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the association between an exposure (vaccination) and an outcome. An RR of 1.0 indicates no difference in risk. If RR < 1, the exposure is protective; if RR > 1, the exposure increases risk. Vaccine 1 has an RR of 0.5, meaning it is protective. On a standard forest plot or relative risk graph, this would be represented by a bar or point below the null line (1.0), as seen in Graph 1. Vaccine 2 has an RR of 2.0, meaning it is associated with a doubling of risk (perhaps an adverse event study). This would be represented by a bar or point above the null line (1.0), as seen in Graph 2. Graph 3 (Option A and B) typically represents a different statistical distribution or an incorrect scale. Therefore, the pairing of Graph 1 for Vaccine 1 and Graph 2 for Vaccine 2 accurately visualizes these relative risk values
questions.learning: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the association between an exposure (vaccination) and an outcome. An RR of 1.0 indicates no difference in risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Tafenoquine is used in which of the following conditions?
options: Treatment of malaria in children <2 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radical cure of plasmodium vivax

Tafenoquine is used in the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax. Total eradication of plasmodium species which includes clinical curative and hypnozoites phase are called radical cure.

Primaquine and tafenoquine (derivative of primaquine) have very high activity against the latent tissue forms (hypnozoites) of the species. It is primarily used for the chemoprophylaxis and radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale infections.
questions.learning: Radical cure of plasmodium vivax Tafenoquine is used in the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax. Total eradication of plasmodium species which includes clinical curative and hypnozoites phase are called radical cure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Pseudo P pulmonale is seen in which electrolyte abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypokalemia

Pseudo P pulmonale refers to tall peaked P waves seen in hypokalemia.
P-pulmonale refers to P waves taller than >2.5mm in an ECG lead.

Hypocalcemia (Option C) prolongs the QT interval.

Hypercalcemia (Option D) shortens the QT interval.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following deficiencies causes follicular hyperkeratosis?
questions.explanation: Follicular hyperkeratosis (also known as phrynoderma or "toad skin") is a skin condition characterized by the excessive development of keratin in hair follicles. It is a classic dermatological manifestation of Vitamin A deficiency. Vitamin A is essential for the normal differentiation and maintenance of epithelial tissues; its lack leads to squamous metaplasia and keratin buildup. While Vitamin C deficiency (Option B, scurvy) causes "corkscrew hairs" and perifollicular hemorrhage, it does not cause primary follicular hyperkeratosis. Vitamin E (Option C) and Vitamin B6 (Option D) deficiencies do not have this specific cutaneous presentation. Follicular hyperkeratosis typically appears as small, firm, rough papules on the extensor surfaces of the limbs and the back. It is often accompanied by other signs of Vitamin A lack, such as night blindness or conjunctival xerosis. Treatment involves dietary improvements and oral Vitamin A supplementation, which usually results in a slow resolution of the skin changes
questions.learning: Follicular hyperkeratosis (also known as phrynoderma or "toad skin") is a skin condition characterized by the excessive development of keratin in hair follicles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which stages of the demographic cycle are characterized by the same birth rate but differing death rates?
questions.explanation: In the demographic transition model, different stages represent changes in birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by both high birth rates and high death rates. Stage 2 (Early Expanding) is marked by the same high birth rate, but the death rate begins to decline rapidly due to improved sanitation and medicine. This difference in the death rate while the birth rate remains constant leads to a population explosion. Stage 3 (Late Expanding) involves a declining birth rate (Option B). Stage 4 (Low Stationary) has both low birth and death rates, while Stage 5 (Declining) involves a birth rate that falls below the death rate (Options C and D). Therefore, Stages 1 and 2 are the specific phases where the birth rate remains consistently high while the death rate is the variable factor. This understanding is fundamental for demographers and policy makers to predict population growth trends and plan for future resource needs in developing nations
questions.learning: In the demographic transition model, different stages represent changes in birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by both high birth rates and high death rates.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with oral cancer invading floor of mouth. What is the T stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. T4a

Invasion of floor of mouth = T4a (moderately advanced local disease). T2 and T3 are size-based without invasion. T4b involves masticator space/skull base, not present here.

| T | Criteria

| --- | --------

| Tis | Carcinoma in situ

| T1 | Size ≤2 cm AND DOI ≤5 mm

| T2 | Size ≤2 cm with DOI >5–10 mm, OR size >2–4 cm with DOI ≤10 mm

| T3 | Size >4 cm, OR any tumor with DOI >10 mm

| T4a | Moderately advanced local disease — invades cortical bone of mandible/maxilla, maxillary sinus, or skin of face (lip: also inferior alveolar nerve, floor of mouth)

| T4b | Very advanced local disease — invades masticator space, pterygoid plates, skull base, and/or encases internal carotid artery
questions.learning: T4a Invasion of floor of mouth = T4a (moderately advanced local disease). T2 and T3 are size-based without invasion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A person is performing weightlifting and attempts to lift the dumbbells overhead. Which of the following changes will be seen in the sarcomere during this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I band decreases

During skeletal muscle contraction, sliding of thin filament over thick filament (cross bridge formation) reduces the length of the 'I' band.

Key Changes in the Sarcomere During Contraction:

* Overall sarcomere length decreases – causing muscle contraction.

* During contraction, the Z lines come closer to each other reducing the length of the sarcomere.

* The A band remains constant and the M line becomes prominent.

* H-zone (only myosin region) decreases – as actin filaments slide inward.

* I-band (only actin region) shortens – due to increased overlap with myosin

Pearl PF1350: Microanatomy of Muscle Fibres

* Each muscle consists of numerous muscle fibres.

* Each skeletal muscle fibre is multi nucleated, bonded by sarcolemma, enclosing sarcoplasm, smooth muscle and cardiac muscles are uninucleated.

* Within the sarcoplasm, there are several hundreds of nuclei arranged in the periphery just beneath the sarcolemma.

* The sarcoplasm also consists of evenly distributed, longitudinal threads called myofibrils.

* Each myofibril consists of thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments overlapping each other.

* The portion of myofibril which consists of thick filaments is known as A band or dark band, and the portion of a myofibril between two A bands consisting of only thin filaments is known I band or Light band.

* Thus the A band consists of both thick and thin filaments, where as I band consists of only thin filaments.

* In the middle of ‘A’ band, there are only thick filaments with no overlapping thin filaments. This zone is known as ‘H’ zone. In the middle of H zone, there is a dark band known as ‘M’ band.

* In the middle of I band, there is a dark ‘Z’ disc or Krause's membrane.

* The segment of the myofibril between two Z discs is known as the sarcomere.
questions.learning: I band decreases During skeletal muscle contraction, sliding of thin filament over thick filament (cross bridge formation) reduces the length of the 'I' band.

questions.text: Please rearrange the given options to correspond correctly with the cardiac auscultation areas shown in the image provided.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient is planned to undergo hysteroscopic polypectomy using bipolar electrocautery. What is the ideal agent for distention? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Normal saline

During hysteroscopy, the uterine cavity is distended using fluid media to allow visualization and operative procedures.

For bipolar electrocautery, the ideal distension medium is Normal saline.

• Bipolar systems can safely function in electrolyte-containing solutions
• Saline is isotonic and reduces risk of hyponatremia and fluid-related complications

Important distinctions:

• Monopolar electrosurgery requires nonconductive, electrolyte-free media such as glycine or sorbitol
• Glycine absorption can cause:

• Hyponatremia
• Cerebral edema
• Hyperammonemia

CO₂ is mainly used for diagnostic hysteroscopy and not operative procedures.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 10-year-old came to the OPD with the following deformity of his left upper limb. What is the most likely cause of the fracture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supracondylar Fracture

The given image shows cubitus varus deformity, where the forearm has deviated medially in relation to the upper arm, which is a common complication of supracondylar humeral fracture.

Malunion is the commonest complication of a supracondylar fracture and results in a cubitus varus deformity, also known as gunstock deformity. This occurs when the fracture unites with the distal fragment tilted medially and in internal rotation.

The image below shows gunstock deformity:

Cubitus varus is primarily a cosmetic concern with minimal functional impairment. Mild cases may not necessitate treatment, while severe deformities should be corrected through a lateral closed wedge osteotomy (French osteotomy).

Other options:

Option B: Olecranon fracture results from a direct injury as in a fall onto the point of the elbow. Complications include non-union, elbow stiffness, and osteoarthritis

Option C: Radial head fracture results from a fall on an outstretched hand and presents with pain over the lateral aspect of the forearm near the elbow along with restricted elbow movements, pronation, and supination. Complications include posterior interosseous nerve injury, myositis ossificans, and osteoarthritis.

Option D: Terrible triad of elbow refers to elbow dislocation with fracture of the radial head, coronoid process, and medial collateral ligament rupture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The chest X-ray below shows a right-sided lung white-out with contralateral tracheal deviation. In which condition is this finding typically seen?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows right-sided white-out (complete opacification) with contralateral (leftward) tracheal deviation. This indicates a space-occupying lesion causing a mass effect, which pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side. White-out lung + trachea shifted away (contralateral) → suggests increased volume/pressure on that side This is typical of large pleural effusion or thoracic mass Why other options are incorrect: (A) Pneumothorax:Would show a hyperlucent (black) hemithorax, not white-out. (B) Consolidation:Causes white-out but usually no significant tracheal shift. (C) Collapse (atelectasis):Leads to tracheal deviation toward the same side (volume loss), not away. Therefore, contralateral deviation with white-out strongly points to a thoracic mass effect (most appropriate option here)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following methods is used to sterilize a glass petri dish?
options: Autoclaving at 121 degree Celsius for 30 – 60 minutes
Hot air oven at 160 degree Celsius for 120 minutes or less
Flash autoclaving at 134 degree Celsius for 3 minutes
Hot air oven at 121 degrees Celsius for 30 – 60 minutes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hot air oven at 160 degree Celsius for 120 minutes or less

Hot air oven at 160 degree Celsius for 2 hours is used to sterilize glasswares like petri dish.

Exposure to dry heat in a sterilizing hot air oven at temperatures of 160° Celsius for 2 hours ensures carbonization of organic material and destruction of microorganisms and spores.

* This method can be used for metals, glassware, some heat-resistant and/or water-immiscible oils, powders and waxes.

* One of the drawback of  sterilization with hot air is that it has no penetrating power, and hence not suitable for disinfection of bulky articles such as mattresses.

* Because it employs very high temperatures it destroys plastic, rubber and other delicate substances.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following should be used for pre-operative management in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha adrenergic blockers

Alpha-blockers like phenoxybenzamine are given pre-operatively to manage hypertension in pheochromocytoma. Beta-blockers such as propranolol are given only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved.

The drug of choice to control blood pressure prior to surgery is oral phenoxybenzamine at 0.5–4 mg/kg of body weight. It is a non-specific α-blocker and is preferred due to its long action (3-4 days).

Pheochromocytoma:

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

It can be sporadical or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1.

Clinical features:

It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness.

Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants.

Investigations:

* Biochemical screening test - measurement of urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines.

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor. It is preferred over a CT scan as the contrast used in CT scans can precipitate paroxysms.

* Other imaging modalities like MIBG scintigraphy, DOPA- or FDG- PET scan are used in identifying the primary tumor as well as the extra-adrenal tumors and metastases.

Treatment:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma.

Preoperatively, hypertension is managed initially with alpha-blockers followed by beta-blockers.

Postoperatively, lifelong yearly follow-up should be done.
questions.learning: Alpha adrenergic blockers Alpha-blockers like phenoxybenzamine are given pre-operatively to manage hypertension in pheochromocytoma. Beta-blockers such as propranolol are given only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old man with hypertension presents at the hospital. His blood pressure upon examination is 150/90, and he is afebrile. Further evaluation reveals normal serum renin levels, leading to a diagnosis of Conn's syndrome. All of the following conditions would be seen in Conn's syndrome except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metabolic acidosis

Conn's syndrome presents with Metabolic alkalosis.

Patients with Conn's syndrome have primary hyperaldosteronism which results in a modest increase in plasma sodium, usually less than 4-6 mEq/L over the normal range, hypokalemia (due to increased K+excretion), hypertension (due to slight increase in ECF volume), metabolic alkalosis because increased hydrogen ions are secreted in the urine.

Excess secretion of aldosterone causes only a modest increase in plasma sodium. When sodium gets reabsorbed, water also accompanies it, resulting in plasma sodium remaining fairly normal.

Primary hyperaldosteronism is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone with resultant suppression of RAAS. It can occur due to adrenal hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma. It is associated with the following features:

* Hypertension (most common)

* Hypokalemia

* Metabolic alkalosis

* Polyuria (due to ANP)

* Polydipsia (due to polyuria)

* Muscle weakness

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Entropion

The image shows the inward rolling of the eyelid margin which is called entropion.

Entropion refers to the inward rolling and rotation of the lid margin towards the globe. It is more common in the lower lid. In longstanding cases of entropion, pseudotrichiasis is seen, which may cause corneal irritation and erosions.

Causes include:

* Horizontal lid laxity

* Vertical lid instability

* Over-riding of the pretarsal by the preseptal orbicularis during lid closure

* Orbital septum laxity

Ectropion refers to the outward turning of the lid margin.

Trichiasis refers to the inward misdirection of cilia, which usually rub against the eyeball with the normal position of the lid margin.
