questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with a 0.3-cm nodule on the left nasolabial fold. It was excised and a pathological examination was done. The image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Basal cell carcinoma

The given clinical scenario of a nodule on the nasolabial fold and the histopathological image showing peripheral palisading is likely to be basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing malignant tumor, with locally invasive characteristics. It affects the pilosebaceous skin.

Ultraviolet radiation exposure is the strongest predisposing factor. Other risk factors include exposure to arsenic, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and ionizing radiation.

It mainly affects the elderly or middle-aged men who are excessively exposed to sun, common in the age group 40-80 and white-skinned people.

Macroscopically, it is categorized as localized and generalized. Nodular, nodulocystic (nodular and nodulocystic together account for 90% of BCC), pigmented, and nevoid are the localized cancers while superficial multifocal and superficial spreading, infiltrative, and cicatrizing are the generalized types. Nodular type is described as pearly waxy nodules at the margins. A central depression with umbilication or ulceration and rolled-out edges are characteristic of BCC.

The below gross image shows pearly, rolled-out borders suggestive of basal cell carcinoma.

Histopathologic features show ovoid cells in nests with a single palisading layer. The outer layer of cells is in the active division and thus incomplete excision can lead to being more aggressive. The below image shows the histopathology of BCC.

Sites near the eye, nose, and ear and size >2 cm are considered to be high risk. Direct invasion at these sites can reach the cranium.

Management is by Moh's microscopic surgery. Non-surgical measures such as topical 5-fluorouracil, and imiquimod are useful. Metastasis is extremely rare.

Other options:

Option B: Melanoma is a malignancy, commonly seen in young adults, arising from melanocytes and involves the skin, mucosa, retina, and leptomeninges. Microscopically, malignant changes are seen in the basal epidermis with breach and invasion of the dermis as shown below.

Option C: Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common malignant tumor, seen more commonly in men. Microscopically, the proliferation of irregular masses of squamous epithelium is seen. The image is shown below.

Option D: Nevus are aggregates of melanocytes at the dermis or dermo-epidermal junction. It can get transformed into malignant melanoma and the features suggestive of malignant transformation are a change in size, shape, color, thickness, satellite lesions, and tingling/ itching/serosanguinous discharge.
questions.learning: Basal cell carcinoma — The given clinical scenario of a nodule on the nasolabial fold and the histopathological image showing peripheral palisading is likely to be basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the given diagram of LV pressure-volume loop, point C represents
questions.explanation: In a left ventricular (LV) pressure–volume loop, point C represents the moment when the aortic valve opens. This occurs at the end of isovolumetric contraction, when the pressure inside the left ventricle rises high enough to exceed the pressure in the aorta. As a result, the aortic valve opens and the ejection phase begins, allowing blood to flow into the aorta. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Mitral valve closes : This event occurs at the beginning of isovolumetric contraction (point B), when ventricular pressure just exceeds left atrial pressure—not at point C. (C) Aortic valve closes : This happens at the end of ventricular ejection (point D), when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, marking the start of isovolumetric relaxation. (D) Mitral valve opens : This occurs after isovolumetric relaxation (point A), when ventricular pressure drops below left atrial pressure, allowing ventricular filling. Thus, point C corresponds to aortic valve opening, making (B) the correct answer
questions.learning: In a left ventricular (LV) pressure–volume loop, point C represents the moment when the aortic valve opens. This occurs at the end of isovolumetric contraction, when the pressure inside the left ventricle rises high enough to exceed the pressure in the aorta.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common pulmonary manifestation of SLE?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pleuritis

The most common pulmonary manifestation of SLE is pleuritis, with or without pleural effusion.

The most common manifestations of different systems involved in SLE are:

• Musculoskeletal- arthritis and arthralgia
• Skin- photosensitivity
• Kidneys- proteinuria
• Neurologic- cognitive impairment
• Cardiac- pericarditis
• Pulmonary- pleuritis
• Hematologic- anemia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes to you with increased cough, increased breathlessness, and decreased exercise capacity. Chest X-ray shows pulmonary fibrosis. Which drug can be administered in the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pirfenidone

Of the given options, Pirfenidone is used in the condition of pulmonary fibrosis.

Pirfenidone is a novel anti-fibrotic agent approved for treating Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) in patients with mild to moderate disease. It inhibits the progression of fibrosis and loss of lung function in patients with IPF via its antifibrotic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties.

Pirfenidone inhibits growth factors involved in connective tissue proliferation and is also approved for use in acute exacerbations of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Other options:

Option A: Bortezomib is a first-generation inhibitor of proteasome-mediated protein degradation that has a role in the treatment of multiple myeloma.

Option B: Roflumilast is a phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor used in severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder(COPD).

Option C: Imatinib is used as a targeted treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia by targeting the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase fusion protein.
questions.learning: Pirfenidone Of the given options, Pirfenidone is used in the condition of pulmonary fibrosis. Pirfenidone is a novel anti-fibrotic agent approved for treating Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) in patients with mild to moderate disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes with a history of high fever for 5 days and altered sensorium. He also gave a history of two seizure episodes one day ago. Peripheral smear shows the following findings. What is the drug of choice in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Artesunate

The given scenario of high fever. altered sensorium and seizures and peripheral smear showing rings (headphones appearance) points towards the diagnosis of severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria, and the drug of choice for this condition is artesunate.

Artesunate-based combination therapy is given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary.

If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is given at a dose of 3.2 mg/kg stat IM, followed by 1.6 mg/kg QD, or quinine dihydrochloride is given at a dose of 20 mg of salt/kg infused over 4 hours, followed by 10 mg of salt/kg infused over 2–8 hours.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include more than two convulsions in 24 hours, unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 mins after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought by her mother with concerns about asymmetrical breast development. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reassure and reassess

Breast asymmetry is a common physiological finding during puberty. In adolescent girls with isolated asymmetrical breast development and no red-flag features (e.g., mass, pain, skin changes, nipple discharge, or lymphadenopathy), the appropriate management is reassurance and follow-up, as breast development usually becomes symmetrical over time.

Why not the other options?

• A. Biopsy of the larger breast: Not indicated in physiological pubertal breast asymmetry.
• B. Mammography: Not recommended in adolescents due to dense breast tissue and low likelihood of malignancy.
• D. Breast ultrasound: Reserved for a palpable breast mass or other suspicious clinical findings, not for isolated asymmetry.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a group of 60 patients diagnosed with COVID-19, 12 deaths were recorded. What is the case fatality rate in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is a proportion used to measure the severity or virulence of a disease. It is calculated as the ratio of the total number of deaths from a disease to the total number of diagnosed cases of that same disease, expressed as a percentage. Formula: CFR = (Number of deaths / Total diagnosed cases) x 100. Substituting the provided values: CFR = (12 deaths / 60 cases) x 100 = 0.2 x 100 = 20%. CFR is useful for measuring the risk of death in acute infectious diseases like COVID-19 or cholera. It can vary between different epidemics based on host health, medical care quality, and the pathogen's strain. The Case Survival Rate (CSR) would be 100 minus the CFR, which in this case is 80%. Options B, C, and D are incorrect mathematical results

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum in developed countries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia

Chlamydia is at present the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatarum in developed countries.

Ophthalmia neonatarum also called neonatal conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva occurring in an infant <30 days after birth.It should be ruled out in any infant having discharge or watering within the first week of birth.

Causes include:

1. Chlamydia(Option A): neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis caused by serotypes D-K is at present the most common cause in developed countries.
2. Gonorrhoea(Option B): effective prophylaxis against gonococcal infection and its subsequent decline has almost eliminated it's incidence in developed countries.
3. Staphylococcus aureus(Option D), Haemophilus species, Streptococcus haemolyticus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae are other less commonly seen causes of ophthalmia neonatarum
4. Herpes simplex ophthalmia neonatrum rarely occurs and is caused by Herpes simplex type 2 virus from the mother.
5. Chemical conjunctivitis(Option C) is caused by the application of prophylactic antibiotics or silver nitrate at the time of birth.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 11-14 weeks

The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is 11-14 weeks.

Twin pregnancies should ideally be dated when the crown–rump length (CRL) measurement is between 45 and 84 mm (i.e. 11 + 0 to 13 + 6 weeks of gestation).

Chorionicity should be ideally determined between 11 + 0 and 13 + 6 weeks of gestation (the earliest time to identify chorionicity is 7 weeks). This is done using the membrane thickness at the site of insertion of the amniotic membrane into the placenta. The T‐sign (in monochorionic twins) or lambda sign (in dichorionic twins) can be seen here. As the determination of chorionicity is most accurate when the amnion and chorion have not yet been fused, the first‐trimester scan in twin pregnancy is highly important.

Markers of dichorionicity include 4 layers of membranes between the twins, membrane thickness >2mm, different sex of twins, 2 different placentas, and positive twin peak sign.

Women with an uncomplicated dichorionic twin pregnancy should have a first‐trimester scan, a detailed second‐trimester scan, and scans every 4 weeks thereafter.

Women with uncomplicated monochorionic twins should have a first‐trimester scan and then scans every 2 weeks from 16 weeks onwards. This is done in order to detect TTTS and TAPS in a timely manner.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A newborn is seen to have an abnormal lump in the lower back. Identify the condition from the MRI given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meningocele

The MRI given represents meningocele.

Meningocele involves the midline protrusion of the meninges. A fluctuant midline mass, that may transilluminate is present in the lower back along the vertebral column. Meningomyelocele involves the protrusion of the spinal cord with the meningeal covering. Neurological dysfunction is more common in these open defects.

Spina bifida occulta refers to fusion defects of the posterior part of the vertebral body. There is no associated protrusion of the spinal cord or meninges. These neonates are usually asymptomatic, without any neurological signs. They present only with a tuft of hair over the lower back.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Regarding ASHA, all are true except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malaria slide preparation

Preparation of malaria slides is the responsibility of health worker male (HWM), not ASHA.

Roles and responsibilities of ASHA:

A. Health education:  The ASHA provides information and awareness to the community regarding nutrition, basic sanitation and hygienic practices, healthy living and working conditions, and timely utilization of health and family welfare services.

B. Maternal and child health:

1. Facilitate utilization of health services such as immunization, antenatal and postnatal checkup and supplementary nutrition, sanitation and other services provided by the government.
2. Provide counseling to women on birth preparedness, safe delivery, breastfeeding and complementary feeding, immunization, contraception, and prevention of common infections.
3. Escort/accompany pregnant women and children requiring treatment or admission to the nearest health center.
4. Upon graded training, provide newborn care and management of common childhood illnesses.

C. Primary care:

1. Provide primary care for minor ailments like diarrhea and fever and provide first aid for injuries.
2. Provide DOTS under RNTCP.
3. Depot holder of essential provisions such as oral rehydration therapy, iron and folic acid tablets, chloroquine, disposable delivery kits, oral pills, condoms, etc.

D. Sanitation:

1. Work with village health and sanitation committee to create a comprehensive village health plan.
2. Promote the construction of household toilets under total sanitation campaign

E. Notification: ASHA will inform births, deaths, and any disease outbreaks to the sub-center or PHC.
questions.learning: Malaria slide preparation Preparation of malaria slides is the responsibility of health worker male (HWM), not ASHA. Roles and responsibilities of ASHA: A.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: C wave of JVP represents:
options: Tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction

'C' wave in JVP represents tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

Characteristics of JVP :

• a wave corresponds to atrial systole which causes regurgitation of some blood into the great veins.
• c wave occurs due to the increase in atrial pressure caused by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
• x descent occurs due to the fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to pulling of valve leaflets.
• v wave is seen at the end of ventricular contraction and occurs due to the slow venous filling which causes an increase in atrial pressure.
• y descent occurs due to the passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle.
questions.learning: Tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction 'C' wave in JVP represents tricuspid bulge into right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about cancer treatment according to the Colombo plan?
options: Help with PET scan units for diagnosis of cancer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Setting up cobalt therapy units

Aid to set up cobalt therapy units for cancer treatment at medical institutions in India was a part of the Colombo plan.

The Colombo Plan is a regional organization that upholds the concept of a collective intergovernmental effort to strengthen the economic and social development of member countries in the Asia-Pacific region.

It was formed at a meeting of the commonwealth foreign ministers with the headquarters at Colombo in January 1950. It comprises 20 developing countries within the region and 6 non-regional members - Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, the UK, and USA. It involves foreign aid and technical assistance for the economic and social development of the region.

The contribution of Canada in supplying cobalt therapy units to medical institutions in India was an important item of aid under the Colombo plan. AIIMS New Delhi was established with financial assistance from New Zealand under the Colombo plan. Cobalt therapy is a form of radiotherapy that uses cobalt-60, a radioactive isotope, to generate high-energy gamma rays for treating cancer. Cobalt therapy units were an important tool for cancer treatment in the mid-20th century, and their provision under the Colombo plan significantly improved cancer treatment capabilities in India.
The Colombo Plan has evolved over the years and now focuses on a broader range of development goals, including education, public administration, agriculture, and industry. This reflects the changing needs of the Asia-Pacific region and the importance of a comprehensive approach to development.

Other Options:

Option A (Help with PET scan units for diagnosis of cancer): While PET scan units are important for cancer diagnosis, they were not part of the Colombo plan's cancer treatment initiatives in India.

Option B (Human resource strengthening): Although the Colombo plan aims to improve the economic and social development of member countries, human resource strengthening in the context of cancer treatment is not explicitly mentioned as part of the plan.

Option C (Setting up chemotherapy units): The Colombo plan's focus in cancer treatment was on providing aid for cobalt therapy units, not chemotherapy units.
questions.learning: Setting up cobalt therapy units Aid to set up cobalt therapy units for cancer treatment at medical institutions in India was a part of the Colombo plan.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a wedding dinner, 140 of 200 attendees develop sudden vomiting within 3 hours. The outbreak investigation team interviews attendees about foods consumed and calculates attack rates for each item. Which study approach is most appropriate in this setting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retrospective cohort study

This is a classic point-source foodborne outbreak in a well-defined, closed group with a known denominator. There are 200 attendees, and investigators can ascertain exposure history to specific food items for both those who became ill and those who did not. In such settings, the most appropriate analytic approach is a retrospective cohort study.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory investigations reveal hyperammonemia along with increased urinary orotic acid levels. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia combined with elevated urinary orotic acid is diagnostic of Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, also known as Type 2 Hyperammonemia. This X-linked disorder prevents the conversion of carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine into citrulline within the mitochondria. The resulting buildup of carbamoyl phosphate shunts into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, leading to high orotic acid levels. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1) deficiency (Option A) causes hyperammonemia but with normal orotic acid levels because the cycle is blocked before that point. Orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase deficiency (Option C) results in orotic aciduria and anemia, but ammonia levels remain normal. Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency (Option D) causes hyperammonemia with elevated citrulline/argininosuccinate rather than orotic acid. Thus, OTC deficiency is the only condition matching this metabolic profile
questions.learning: Hyperammonemia combined with elevated urinary orotic acid is diagnostic of Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, also known as Type 2 Hyperammonemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident with a head injury. He is conscious, but when questioned about the incident, his responses are irrelevant despite fluent speech. Which area of the brain is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of fluent but irrelevant speech characterizes Wernicke's aphasia, also known as receptive aphasia. This condition results from a lesion in Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. These patients can produce speech with normal rate and rhythm, but they lack comprehension of language, leading to "word salad" answers. A lesion in the pre-central gyrus (Option A) would cause motor weakness or paralysis on the contralateral side rather than a language disorder. Damage to the inferior frontal gyrus (Option B) causes Broca's aphasia, where speech is non-fluent and effortful, though comprehension is relatively preserved. Brain stem injuries (Option D) would typically involve severe motor/sensory deficits or altered consciousness rather than an isolated fluent aphasia. Thus, the disconnect between speech production and meaningful content localizes the injury to the superior temporal gyrus
questions.learning: The patient's presentation of fluent but irrelevant speech characterizes Wernicke's aphasia, also known as receptive aphasia. This condition results from a lesion in Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus delivers a full-term infant. Which of the following complications is the newborn at risk of developing due to maternal diabetes?
questions.explanation: Infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) are at a high risk for several neonatal complications. The most common acute metabolic issue is neonatal hypoglycemia (Option D) . During pregnancy, the fetus is exposed to high maternal glucose, which crosses the placenta and triggers fetal pancreatic hypertrophy and hyperinsulinemia. After birth, the maternal glucose supply is suddenly cut off, but the baby's insulin levels remain high, leading to a rapid drop in blood sugar. IDMs are also at risk for hypocalcemia (not hypercalcemia, Option C) and various congenital heart defects, most notably ventricular septal defects or transposition of the great arteries (Tetralogy of Fallot, Option B, is less specifically linked than these). Hyperglycemia (Option A) would not occur in a hyperinsulinemic neonate. Therefore, close monitoring of blood glucose levels in the immediate postpartum period is mandatory for all IDMs to prevent neurological injury from hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) are at a high risk for several neonatal complications. The most common acute metabolic issue is neonatal hypoglycemia (Option D) .

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with persistent dull pain in the upper abdomen. He gives a history of a severe episode of abdominal pain five weeks ago following heavy alcohol consumption. On examination, he is jaundiced and has a firm, palpable mass in the epigastric region. A CT scan reveals a well-circumscribed, fluid-filled lesion near the pancreas. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a firm epigastric mass developing four to six weeks "after an episode of acute pancreatitis" (heavy drinking event) is the classic presentation for a "Pancreatic Pseudocyst". A pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue rather than a true epithelial lining. The dull pain and jaundice result from the cyst compressing adjacent structures like the bile duct. Choledochal cysts (Option B) are congenital dilations of the bile duct and would usually present earlier in life. Gastric duplication cysts (Option C) and mesenteric cysts (Option D) are much rarer and would not be temporally related to a clear episode of pancreatitis. Most pseudocysts resolve with conservative management. However, if they are large, symptomatic, or infected, they may require drainage (endoscopic or surgical cystogastrostomy)
questions.learning: The clinical history of a firm epigastric mass developing four to six weeks "after an episode of acute pancreatitis" (heavy drinking event) is the classic presentation for a "Pancreatic Pseudocyst".

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which neuromuscular blocking agent undergoes Hofmann elimination?
questions.explanation: Atracurium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is unique because it undergoes Hofmann elimination. Hofmann elimination is a spontaneous, non-enzymatic chemical degradation that occurs at physiological temperature and pH. Because this process is independent of kidney and liver function, atracurium (and its isomer cisatracurium) is the drug of choice for inducing muscle relaxation in patients with renal or hepatic failure. Pancuronium (Option A), Rocuronium (Option B), and Vecuronium (Option C) are primarily cleared by the liver or kidneys; their duration of action is significantly prolonged in patients with organ dysfunction, increasing the risk of prolonged paralysis. A byproduct of atracurium's degradation is laudanosine, which can theoretically cross the blood-brain barrier and cause seizures at very high concentrations. Cisatracurium is often preferred as it produces less laudanosine and does not cause histamine release. Understanding these specific metabolic pathways is fundamental for choosing safe anesthetic agents for medically complex surgical patients
questions.learning: Atracurium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is unique because it undergoes Hofmann elimination. Hofmann elimination is a spontaneous, non-enzymatic chemical degradation that occurs at physiological temperature and pH.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Paradoxical bronchoconstriction seen with ipratropium bromide is due to all except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypertonic saline

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction with ipratropium bromide is seen with a hypotonic nebulizer solution and not hypertonic saline.

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction with ipratropium bromide is seen especially when given by a nebulizer and may be due to the following factors:

• Hypotonic nebulizer solution
• Antibacterial additives like benzalkonium chloride and EDTA
• It may be also due to prejunctional M2 receptor blockade on the cholinergic nerves present in the airway. These prejunctional M2 receptors normally inhibit acetylcholine release into the synapse. So their blockade can cause increased Ach release and bronchoconstriction.

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction is not reported with tiotropium bromide or any other long-acting muscarinic antagonists. Tiotropium is selective for M3 and M1 receptors and therefore less likely to produce prejunctional M2 receptor blockade.

Other adverse effects of inhaled muscarinic antagonists:

• A bitter taste is seen with ipratropium
• Nebulization with ipratropium bromide may precipitate glaucoma in elderly patients. This is due to the direct effect of the drug on the eyes and can be easily prevented by using a mouthpiece instead of a facemask.
• Long-acting agents can cause dryness of the mouth.
• In elderly patients, urinary retention may be seen occasionally.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male underwent bilateral laparoscopic hernia repair for inguinal hernia. Postoperatively, he complained of pain in the right thigh. Which of the following nerve entrapment leads to this symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh

Entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh is the most likely cause of pain in this patient with history of laparoscopic hernia repair.

The laparoscopic approach is preferred for bilateral or recurrent inguinal hernias. Transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) repair and total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair are the methods commonly used.

The nerves commonly injured in laparoscopic repair are the genitofemoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves of the thigh. Patients present with acute neuropathic pain along the dermatomal distribution. Injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve results in meralgia paresthetica.

Treatment consists of rest, ice, NSAIDs, physical therapy, and possible local corticosteroid and anesthetic injection. Drugs like gabapentin can be used.

In laparoscopic TAPP repair, to reduce the chances of nerve injury during mesh placement, tacks are ideally placed above the iliopubic tract to avoid nerve injury.

Other options:

Option A: Ilioinguinal nerve may be commonly injured during open hernia repair. It leads to sensory disturbances and pain over the skin of the genitalia and upper medial thigh.

Option B: Iliohypogastric nerve can be injured while making an incision in the right iliac fossa during hernia surgery.

Option C: Femoral nerve can be compressed by retroperitoneal tumors or hemorrhage in patients on anticoagulants or bleeding diathesis. It presents as wasting and weakness of the quadriceps femoris muscle making the patient difficult to walk. Pain and paraesthesia are seen along the region of the distribution of the nerve.
questions.learning: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh Entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh is the most likely cause of pain in this patient with history of laparoscopic hernia repair.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient develops bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea after receiving intravenous irritant substances. These clinical features are mediated by a specific reflex mechanism. Which reflex is primarily responsible for these physiological responses?
questions.explanation: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is characterized by the clinical triad of bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea (or shallow breathing). It is triggered by the stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors (C-fibers) located in the ventricular walls of the heart. Chemical irritants, certain drugs, or myocardial ischemia can activate these receptors, leading to an increase in parasympathetic (vagal) outflow and a decrease in sympathetic tone. The Bainbridge reflex (Option B) is the opposite; it causes an increase in heart rate in response to increased venous return and atrial stretch. The Cushing reflex (Option C) is a physiological response to increased intracranial pressure, characterized by hypertension, irregular breathing, and bradycardia. While both Cushing and Bezold-Jarisch involve bradycardia, the specific combination of hypotension and apnea following IV irritant administration is diagnostic for the Bezold-Jarisch reflex. This reflex can be particularly significant during anesthesia or in the early stages of a myocardial infarction
questions.learning: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is characterized by the clinical triad of bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea (or shallow breathing). It is triggered by the stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors (C-fibers) located in the ventricular walls of the heart.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a likely symptom of a panic attack?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Suicide attempt

A suicide attempt is not a likely symptom of a panic attack.

A panic attack is characterized by a sudden onset of overwhelming fear or severe discomfort, which can persist for several minutes to hours.Recurrent panic attacks are termed panic disorders.

Panic attacks can occur in other disorders, particularly in specific phobias, social phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unexpected panic attacks occur at any time and are not associated with any identifiable situational trigger. Attacks in patients with social and specific phobias are usually expected in response to a specific stimulus.

Some panic attacks do not fit into unexpected or expected attacks, and these attacks are referred to as situationally predisposed panic attacks. They may or may not occur on exposure to a specific trigger, or may occur immediately after exposure or after a considerable period of time.

Four or more of the following should be present to label it a panic attack:

* Racing or pounding heart, palpitations

* Sweating

* Involuntary shaking/trembling

* Shortness of breath or smothering sensation

* Choking sensation

* Pain or discomfort in the chest region

* Upset stomach or nausea

* Sensation of light-headedness/dizziness/ faintness

* Hot flashes or chills

* Tingling or numbness (paresthesias)

* Depersonalization (disconnected from oneself) or derealization (detached from reality)

* Sense of losing control over oneself  or “going crazy”

* Overwhelming fear of death

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient who has been diagnosed with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history/history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma has a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mismatch repair

Mismatch repair will be defective in a patient with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history/history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma (HNPCC)

Mismatch repair is a DNA repair mechanism that corrects single-nucleotide mismatches, insertions, and deletions introduced by the DNA polymerase during DNA replication.

HNPCC or Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition. It occurs due to defects in DNA mismatch repair genes like MLH1 and MSH2. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability. HNPCC is associated with a high risk of colon cancer. It may also be associated with a risk of developing carcinomas of the endometrium, stomach, small bowel, ovary, pancreas, and transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter and renal pelvis.

The diagnostic criteria for HNPCC are referred to as the Amsterdam criteria or the 3-2-1-0 rule. It includes:

• Three or more relatives with HNPCC-associated cancer (colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, cancer of the small bowel, ureter, or renal pelvis), one of whom is a first-degree relative of the other two.
• At least two successive generations affected
• At least one case diagnosed before age 50 years
• Familial adenomatous polyposis excluded
• Tumors verified by pathologic examination.

Other options:

Option B: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum have a defect in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.

Option C: Defect in base excision repair pathway is seen in patients with MUTYH-associated polyposis.

Option D:  Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia are examples of diseases seen in patients with point mutations.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 38-year-old banker with a history of chronic heartburn suddenly experiences excruciating pain in the epigastric region of the abdomen. Emergency surgery is performed upon admission. Intraoperative findings reveal a ruptured ulcer located on the posterior wall of the stomach. Where will a surgeon first expect to find leaked stomach contents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Omental bursa

The posterior wall of the stomach lies directly anterior to the lesser sac (omental bursa), a subdivision of the peritoneal cavity. When a posterior gastric ulcer perforates, the gastric contents first enter the lesser sac (omental bursa) rather than the greater sac.

Anatomical relationships:

• Anterior stomach wall → greater sac
• Posterior stomach wall → lesser sac (omental bursa)

Boundaries of the lesser sac:

• Anterior: stomach and lesser omentum
• Posterior: pancreas and posterior abdominal wall
• Communication with greater sac: through the epiploic (omental) foramen of Winslow

Other options:

• Greater peritoneal sac: involved in anterior gastric perforation.
• Cul-de-sac of Douglas: lowest peritoneal recess in females.
• Paracolic gutters: channels that allow spread of peritoneal fluid later.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Following total thyroidectomy, a patient started having difficulty in breathing, and repeated attempts to extubate were unsuccessful. The most probable cause is ___
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

The clinical picture of breathing difficulty and unsuccessful attempts at extubation after total thyroidectomy is suggestive of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

Thyroid surgery may cause injury to both external (ELN) and recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN). The upper part of the RLN is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery. Unilateral RLN injury may be asymptomatic but in a few may cause hoarseness of voice.

The relation of RLN with the inferior thyroid artery is shown in the image below:

Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy can also occur postoperatively and the presentation is acute. Other causes of it include carcinoma of the cervical esophagus, carcinoma thyroid, and cervical lymphadenopathy. All the intrinsic muscles are paralyzed in this condition.

The vocal cords lie in the median or paramedian position due to the unopposed action of the cricothyroid muscles. This leads to dyspnoea and stridor, necessitating emergency tracheostomy.

For long-standing cases of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, there are two main treatment options. One approach involves performing a tracheostomy with a speaking valve. Alternatively, cord lateralizing procedures can be considered, such as transverse cordotomy, partial arytenoidectomy, injection of botulinum toxin, thyroplasty type II, or re-innervation procedures.

Transverse cordotomy (Kashima operation) involves excising laterally the soft tissue at the junction of the membranous cord and the vocal process of the arytenoid with laser.

Partial arytenoidectomy involves excising the medial part of the arytenoid with a laser.

Thyroplasty type II creates a lateral expansion of the larynx which is similar to vocal cord lateralization.

Reinnervation procedures innervate paralyzed posterior cricoarytenoid muscle by implanting a nerve-muscle pedicle of sternohyoid or omohyoid muscle with its nerve supply from ansa hypoglossi.
questions.learning: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury — The clinical picture of breathing difficulty and unsuccessful attempts at extubation after total thyroidectomy is suggestive of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman who has done strenuous exercise complains of Involuntary urine voiding during work out. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI) is defined as the involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as strenuous exercise, coughing, sneezing, or laughing. It results from a failure of the urethral sphincter mechanism, often due to weakened pelvic floor muscles or urethral hypermobility. Urge incontinence (Option A) involves a sudden, uncontrollable need to void followed by leakage, often due to detrusor overactivity. Neurogenic incontinence (Option C) results from nerve damage (e.g., spinal cord injury) affecting bladder control. Mixed incontinence (Option D) is a combination of both stress and urge symptoms. SUI is very common in women, particularly after multiple vaginal deliveries. Management initially involves conservative measures like Kegel exercises (pelvic floor muscle training) and lifestyle modifications. For severe cases that fail conservative therapy, surgical options like the mid-urethral sling (TVT/TOT) are highly effective. Identifying the specific trigger (exercise vs. urgency) is the key to correct classification and treatment
questions.learning: Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI) is defined as the involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as strenuous exercise, coughing, sneezing, or laughing.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which type of hanging does weight of the head, arms and chest act as a constricting force?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Partial

The weight of the head, arms, and chest acts as a constricting force in partial hanging.

Types of hanging:

* Complete hanging: Here the weight of the entire body acts as a constricting force.

* Partial hanging: The bodies are partially suspended, the weight of the head (5-6 kgs), arms, and chest act as a constricting force.

* Typical hanging: In this, the ligature runs from the midline above the thyroid cartilage symmetrically upward on both sides of the neck to the occipital region. A knot of the ligature is on the backside of the neck.

* Atypical hanging: The knot of the ligature is anywhere other than on the backside of the neck. Usually, the knot is near the mastoid process or angle of mandible. Occasionally, it may be under the chin.

In India, the knot is tied under the angle of the right jaw. On drawing the bolt, the person drops to the length of the rope. The sudden stoppage of the moving body associated with the position of the knot causes the head to be jerked violently.

Judicial hanging:

* The face of the person is covered with a dark mask, stand on a platform above trapdoors,which open downwards when the blot is drawn.

* Rope is looped around the neck and the person is allowed to drop for 5-7 meters according to weight, age and build.

* Sudden stop causes fracture dislocation at the level C-2, C-3 or C-3/C-4 vertebra and rupture between pons and medulla (hangman fracture).

* Death is instantaneous, but the heartbeat may continue for 15-20 minutes and spasmodic muscle jerking may occur for a considerable time.

* Asphyxial signs are not seen in correctly performed judicial hangings.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient undergoes surgery of the lateral part of the base of the skull. Postoperatively, the patient presents with aspiration but does not have a change in voice. Which of the following is the reason?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior laryngeal nerve injury

In the given clinical scenario, the patient experiences aspiration but does not exhibit any change in voice following base of skull surgery. This suggests an injury to the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN).

In SLN injury, only the cricothyroid muscle is involved which is used only in high-pitch vocalization, normal speech will not be affected. SLN also provides sensory supply to the mucosa above vocal cords, hence its lesion would lead to increased susceptibility to aspiration.

Other options:

Option B: The glossopharyngeal nerve does not provide sensory or motor supply to the larynx.

Option C and D: The patient also has normal vocalization which rules out recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) and high vagal injury. RLN supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, therefore an RLN lesion would lead to disordered vocalization. A high vagal injury would mean that both the SLN and RLN functions are affected, therefore that can also be ruled out.
questions.learning: Superior laryngeal nerve injury — In the given clinical scenario, the patient experiences aspiration but does not exhibit any change in voice following base of skull surgery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which is the most accurate test for evaluating the effectiveness of treatment in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)?
questions.explanation: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is defined by the translocation, creating the fusion gene. Monitoring treatment success, particularly with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like imatinib, requires measuring the "Minimal Residual Disease" (MRD). "RT-PCR" (Option C) is the "most accurate and sensitive test" for this purpose because it can detect one leukemic cell among to normal cells. It quantifies the transcript levels of , allowing for the assessment of Major Molecular Response (MMR). CBC (Option A) only assesses hematological response, which is the least sensitive measure. Cytogenetic testing (Option B) for the Philadelphia chromosome and FISH (Option D) are used for diagnosis and to assess "Complete Cytogenetic Response," but they are much less sensitive than RT-PCR for detecting very low levels of residual disease. Achieving a deep molecular response as measured by RT-PCR is the primary goal of modern CML therapy to prevent disease progression to blast crisis
questions.learning: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is defined by the translocation, creating the fusion gene. Monitoring treatment success, particularly with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like imatinib, requires measuring the "Minimal Residual Disease" (MRD).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the term used for a disease that is not native to a country and is introduced from another country?
questions.explanation: In epidemiology, an exotic disease (Option D) is one that is not normally present in a given country or geographical region but is introduced from an external source (abroad). The 25-year-old male diagnosed at an Indian airport upon arrival represents an imported or exotic case. An endemic disease (Option A) is one that is constantly present in a specific population or region (e.g., malaria in parts of India). An epidemic (Option B) is a sudden, large-scale outbreak of a disease in a specific area. A zoonotic disease (Option C) is one that is transmitted from animals to humans, such as rabies or anthrax . Exotic diseases are a major focus of international health regulations and airport quarantine measures to prevent the domestic spread of "new" pathogens. Therefore, because the condition originated outside the country's borders, "exotic" is the correct epidemiological classification for this imported case
questions.learning: In epidemiology, an exotic disease (Option D) is one that is not normally present in a given country or geographical region but is introduced from an external source (abroad).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient comes with complaints of progressive weakness as the day progresses. He is found to have antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which is the most common ocular finding in this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ptosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myasthenia gravis and ptosis is the most common ocular feature of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction most commonly caused by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The disorder is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles where the weakness increases during repeated use and may improve following rest.

Ptosis and diplopia are common initial complaints due to early involvement of the lids and extraocular muscles (EOMs). Of them, Ptosis is a more common manifestation than diplopia. Ptosis in myasthenia gravis is insidious, bilateral, and frequently asymmetrical.

Investigations of myasthenia gravis include:

1. Ice pack test -This tests for a transient improvement of the ptotic eyelid on placing an ice pack for 2 minutes, as  the cold inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase.
2. Tensilon (Edrophonium) test - This tests for a transient improvement in the weakness on administration of a short-acting anticholinesterase such as edrophonium.
3. Antibody testing - for Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies, MuSK protein antibodies helps support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology technician is performing quality control on this device. Which biological indicator can be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Geobacillus stearothermophilus

Biological indicators (spore tests) are the gold standard for monitoring the effectiveness of sterilization because bacterial spores are the most resistant forms of microorganisms. Spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus are used to test steam sterilization (autoclaves) due to their high resistance to moist heat.

An autoclave sterilizes using steam under pressure (121°C, 15 psi, 15–20 minutes). The biological indicator for verifying successful sterilization is Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores. If these spores are killed, effective sterilization has been achieved.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bacillus subtilis: Previously used for dry heat and ethylene oxide sterilization (largely replaced by Bacillus atrophaeus).
• C. Bacillus globigii (Bacillus atrophaeus): Biological indicator for ethylene oxide gas and dry heat sterilization, not autoclaves.
• D. Bacillus pumilus: Biological indicator for ionizing radiation (gamma irradiation).
questions.learning: Geobacillus stearothermophilus Biological indicators (spore tests) are the gold standard for monitoring the effectiveness of sterilization because bacterial spores are the most resistant forms of microorganisms.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the context of a national public health program targeting anemia, which initiative implements the “6×6×6 strategy”?
questions.explanation: The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, launched in 2018, aims to reduce the prevalence of anemia across the life cycle. It is famously defined by its comprehensive "6x6x6 strategy". This refers to: 1. Target Beneficiaries: Including children (6-59 months, 5-9 years), adolescents, women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. 2. Interventions: Such as prophylactic iron-folic acid supplementation, deworming, and counseling. 3. Institutional Mechanisms: Like intra-ministerial coordination and a national digital portal. Poshan Abhiyan (Option B) is a broader overarching mission for holistic nutrition but is not synonymous with this specific 6x6x6 framework. Kishori Shakti Yojana (Option C) targets adolescent girls specifically rather than this multi-tiered approach. AMB aims for a 3% annual reduction in anemia prevalence, a more ambitious target than previous programs. Its success relies on strengthening the supply chain and community mobilization through frontline workers. Anemia Mukt Bharat represents a significant shift toward data-driven, life-cycle-based public health interventions in India
questions.learning: The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, launched in 2018, aims to reduce the prevalence of anemia across the life cycle. It is famously defined by its comprehensive "6x6x6 strategy".

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements: • Statement 1- Contemplation – A person who smokes is thinking of quitting smoking • Statement 2- Precontemplation – A person is considering starting morning walks and the benefits to their health • Statement 3- Maintenance phase – A person quit smoking one year back and has not smoked since then • Statement 4- Action phase – A person with obesity says they can’t do anything, as it runs deep in their family
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Statement 1 and 3 are correct

The Stages of Change (Transtheoretical Model):

A behavioral change framework (Prochaska & DiClemente) describing readiness to change across sequential stages.

Stages of Change

• Precontemplation

• No intention to change
• Unaware / denial / resistance
• Example: “Smoking isn’t a problem for me.”

• Contemplation

• Aware of problem, thinking about change
• Ambivalence present
• Example: “I should quit, but it’s hard.”

• Preparation

• Intends to act soon
• Small initial steps taken
• Example: “I’ll quit next month; I’ve reduced cigarettes.”

• Action

• Active behavior change
• High effort and risk of relapse
• Example: Recently stopped smoking

• Maintenance

• Sustained change (>6 months)
• Focus on preventing relapse
• Example: Abstinent for months, avoiding triggers

• Relapse

• Return to old behavior
• Common and part of the cycle

Contemplation involves awareness and thinking about change (Statement 1 correct), while precontemplation reflects lack of intent to change; considering health benefits fits early contemplation rather than denial. (hence statement 2 is incorrect)

Maintenance refers to sustained behaviour change for >6 months, as in quitting smoking for one year (Statement 3 correct).

The action phase involves active behaviour change; expressing helplessness reflects precontemplation, making Statement 4 incorrect.
questions.learning: Statement 1 and 3 are correct — The Stages of Change (Transtheoretical Model): A behavioral change framework (Prochaska & DiClemente) describing readiness to change across sequential stages.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the type of transport across the cell membrane given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facilitated diffusion

The given image shows the transport of a molecule across a membrane with the help of a carrier protein. This form of transport is called facilitated diffusion.

When carrier proteins help in the movement of substances in the direction of their chemical or electrical gradients (downhill movement), no energy input is required and the process is called facilitated diffusion.

Glucose transporters or GLUTs are examples of transport proteins in the cell membrane responsible for the transfer of glucose into the cells by facilitated diffusion. Facilitated diffusion involves the passage of molecules or ions inside the cell membrane by binding to a carrier/ transport protein.

Other options -

Option A. Simple diffusion - It is along the concentration gradient but is not carrier-mediated. In the cell, examples of molecules that can use simple diffusion to travel in and out of the cell membrane are water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen. They pass directly through the cell membrane along the concentration gradient, without the use of energy.

Option C. Primary active transport - It is a form of cellular transport requiring energy in the form of hydrolysis of ATP to ship and transfer molecules against gradient differences. The important examples of primary active transport include sodium-potassium ATPase, proton pump, and calcium ATPase.

Option D. Secondary active transport - In this form of transport, two or more substances are transported together across the membrane with help of a carrier molecule. As one of the substances (e.g., sodium) diffuses down its electrochemical gradient, the energy released is used to drive another substance (e.g., glucose) against the gradient. It does not require energy directly from ATP.
questions.learning: Facilitated diffusion — The given image shows the transport of a molecule across a membrane with the help of a carrier protein. This form of transport is called facilitated diffusion.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following are symptoms of Gradenigo syndrome?
options: Ear discharge, retro-orbital pain, and diplopia
Nasal discharge, retro-orbital pain, and diplopia
Ear discharge, retro-orbital pain, and headache
Retro-orbital pain, Diplopia, and hearing loss
questions.explanation: Gradenigo syndrome is a classic clinical triad caused by petrous apicitis, an infection of the apex of the petrous temporal bone, most often arising as a complication of otitis media. The triad consists of: 1. Ear discharge (otorrhea): Persistent discharge due to ongoing middle ear infection. 2. Retro-orbital pain: Deep pain behind the eye caused by irritation of the ophthalmic division (V₁) of the trigeminal nerve in Meckel’s cave. 3. Diplopia: Double vision due to abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) palsy, as the nerve passes through Dorello’s canal, leading to lateral rectus muscle paralysis. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Option B: Nasal discharge is incorrect; the infection is otogenic, not sinonasal. 2. Option C: Headache may occur but this option misses diplopia, a hallmark feature. 3. Option D: Hearing loss can be associated with otitis media, but ear discharge is essential to establish the otogenic origin. Diagnosis is confirmed with CT/MRI of the temporal bone, and management requires aggressive intravenous antibiotics, with surgical drainage if there is no response or complications develop
questions.learning: Gradenigo syndrome is a classic clinical triad caused by petrous apicitis, an infection of the apex of the petrous temporal bone, most often arising as a complication of otitis media.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A young individual sustains a head injury following a road traffic accident and subsequently develops marked behavioral changes. These include excessive curiosity, compulsive touching of objects, rapid memory loss, a tendency to place non-food items in the mouth, and inappropriate sexual behaviors such as genital manipulation. Damage to which brain structure is most likely responsible for this presentation?
options: Gray matter around the aqueduct of Sylvius
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation described is diagnostic of Klüver-Bucy syndrome, which results from bilateral lesions or injury to the anterior temporal lobes, specifically involving the amygdala. The hallmark symptoms include hyperorality (mouthing objects), hypersexuality (genital squeezing or inappropriate behavior), visual agnosia (excessive curiosity/touching to identify objects), and docility or diminished fear response. Rapid forgetfulness also points to temporal lobe involvement. Option A, the periaqueductal gray, is involved in pain modulation and defensive behavior, not complex social/sexual changes. Option C, the lateral hypothalamus, regulates hunger; its lesion causes anorexia. Option D, the anterior cingulate gyri, are involved in emotional processing and attention, but lesions there do not produce the specific Klüver-Bucy triad. In the context of a road traffic accident, traumatic brain injury with bilateral temporal contusions is the most likely cause. Management is primarily supportive, focusing on behavioral stabilization and safety due to the patient's lack of social inhibition and poor judgment
questions.learning: The clinical presentation described is diagnostic of Klüver-Bucy syndrome, which results from bilateral lesions or injury to the anterior temporal lobes, specifically involving the amygdala.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can be given without dose modification in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
questions.explanation: Linagliptin is unique among the DPP-4 inhibitors because it is primarily excreted via the enterohepatic system (bile and feces) rather than the renal route. Consequently, it does not require any dose adjustment regardless of the severity of renal impairment or CKD. Saxagliptin (Option B), conversely, is eliminated renally and requires a reduction in dose once the glomerular filtration rate falls below a certain threshold. Repaglinide (Option C), a meglitinide, is mostly metabolized by the liver, but current guidelines still suggest cautious titration in severe renal failure. Glyburide (Option D) is a second-generation sulfonylurea that is metabolized into active metabolites excreted by the kidneys ; it is generally contraindicated in CKD due to the high risk of prolonged, severe hypoglycemia. For clinicians managing diabetes in renal patients, Linagliptin offers a significant advantage by maintaining safety and efficacy without the need for complex dosage modifications based on fluctuating creatinine levels
questions.learning: Linagliptin is unique among the DPP-4 inhibitors because it is primarily excreted via the enterohepatic system (bile and feces) rather than the renal route.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries passes through the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Splenic artery

The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament is a double layer of peritoneum that extends between the left kidney and the spleen. It contains the splenic artery and splenic vein, along with the tail of the pancreas. This anatomical relationship is of major surgical importance during splenectomy, as inadvertent injury to the tail of the pancreas may result in pancreatic fistula or pancreatitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Left gastric artery: Travels within the lesser omentum (hepatogastric ligament) along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
• C. Common hepatic artery: Runs in the superior border of the pancreas and gives rise to the proper hepatic artery, which enters the hepatoduodenal ligament, not the splenorenal ligament.
• D. Superior mesenteric artery: Arises from the abdominal aorta and passes behind the neck of the pancreas into the root of the mesentery; it is not contained within any peritoneal ligament.
questions.learning: Splenic artery — The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament is a double layer of peritoneum that extends between the left kidney and the spleen. It contains the splenic artery and splenic vein, along with the tail of the pancreas.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · Basics Of Cell Cytoskeleton
questions.text: Which of the following are present in the intercalated disc of cardiac muscle? 1. Fascia adherens 2. Desmosome (Macula adherens) 3. Gap junction 4. Tight junction (Zonula occludens)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

Intercalated discs are specialized junctions that connect adjacent cardiac muscle cells, providing both mechanical strength and electrical coupling required for synchronized cardiac contraction. They contain–

• Fascia adherens: anchors actin filaments and transmits contractile force.
• Desmosomes (macula adherens): provide strong mechanical attachment, preventing separation of cardiomyocytes during contraction.
• Gap junctions: allow rapid passage of ions between cells, enabling electrical coupling and synchronized depolarization.

Why not the other options?

• B. Gap junction only: Ignores the mechanical junctions essential for maintaining tissue integrity.
• C. Tight junction included: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are absent in cardiac intercalated discs.
• D. Includes tight junctions: Incorrect because tight junctions are characteristic of epithelial cells, not cardiac muscle.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 Intercalated discs are specialized junctions that connect adjacent cardiac muscle cells, providing both mechanical strength and electrical coupling required for synchronized cardiac contraction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a bimanual examination used to elicit Hegar's sign, a probable sign of pregnancy typically detected between 6–8 weeks of gestation. It is characterized by the softening of the lower uterine segment, which allows the cervix and the body of the uterus to feel like separate structures upon palpation. This softening results from hormonal changes increasing vascularity and edema. Chadwick’s sign (Option A) is the bluish discoloration of the cervix. Goodell’s sign (Option B) is the softening of the cervix itself. Piskacek’s sign (Option D) involves asymmetric enlargement of the uterus due to lateral implantation. The specific technique shown—pressing the cervix from below and the fundus from above to feel the thin, soft isthmus—is the definitive method for identifying Hegar's sign
questions.learning: The image demonstrates a bimanual examination used to elicit Hegar's sign, a probable sign of pregnancy typically detected between 6–8 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 58-year-old develops sudden hypotension and a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border 3 days after an anterior STEMI. There are pulmonary crackles and elevated JVP. The most appropriate immediate confirmation test in this condition is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urgent echocardiography with Doppler

Sudden hypotension with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border 3 days after an MI strongly suggests a mechanical complication, most classically ventricular septal rupture causing an acute left-to-right shunt with pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. The fastest and most definitive bedside confirmation is urgent transthoracic echocardiography with color Doppler to demonstrate the septal defect and shunt.

Learning Points

• Post-MI mechanical complications often occur 3 to 5 days after infarction.
• Ventricular septal rupture causes a new harsh holosystolic murmur best heard at the LLSB, shock, and pulmonary edema.
• Best immediate confirmation is urgent echo with color Doppler.
• Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe MR with a new systolic murmur at the apex and flash pulmonary edema, and echo is also the key test.

Management is urgent stabilization and early surgical or percutaneous intervention.
