questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He gives a history of having consumed shellfish and raw seafood a day before. The causative agent showed the Kanagawa phenomenon on Wagatsuma agar. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vibrio parahaemolyticus

Kanagawa Phenomenon is shown by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. The Kanagawa phenomenon is hemolysis on wagatsuma agar.

On Wagatsuma agar (High salt blood agar), pathogenic strains of V. parahaemolyticus are hemolytic, while non-pathogenic strains are non-hemolytic. This is due to a heat-stable hemolysin.

V. parahaemolyticus causes food poisoning due to the consumption of contaminated seafood, after an incubation period of 12–24 hours. The common sources of infection are raw seafood like mollusks and crustaceans. No enterotoxin like cholera toxin has been identified, it causes enteritis by invasion of the intestinal epithelium.

Clinically, patients present with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, fever, and watery or bloody diarrhea. Fecal leukocytes are often seen in stool samples. Enteritis subsides spontaneously in 1–3 days with no specific treatment. Adequate hydration and electrolyte balance should be restored.

V. parahaemolyticus is a capsulated bacterium. It shows bipolar staining and has a tendency to pleomorphism. It is characterized by peritrichous flagella on solid media and polar flagella on liquid media and it gives a negative string test.

Pathogenic strains of V. parahemolyticus are hemolytic on Wagatsuma agar, while non-pathogenic strains are non-hemolytic. This is called the Kanagawa phenomenon and is due to a heat-stable hemolysin.
questions.learning: Vibrio parahaemolyticus Kanagawa Phenomenon is shown by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. The Kanagawa phenomenon is hemolysis on wagatsuma agar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles are ectoderm-derived?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ciliaris

Why Ciliaris?

The ciliaris muscle is derived from neural crest cells. It is an intraocular smooth muscle that controls lens accommodation.

Why the Others Are Wrong

| Option | Embryological Origin | Why Wrong

| ------ | -------------------- | ---------

| A — Cardiac muscle | Mesoderm (splanchnic/lateral plate) | Completely mesodermal

| B — Smooth muscle of gut | Mesoderm (splanchnic lateral plate) | Not ectoderm

| C — Erector pili | Mesoderm | Common trap — it's a skin muscle but still mesodermal

| D — Ciliaris | Neural crest | Correct

The two key ones to remember:

• Ciliaris — accommodation (Neural crest)
• Sphincter and dilator pupillae — neuroectoderm

Erector pili is the classic distractor — students assume "skin = ectoderm," but the smooth muscle itself comes from mesoderm (specifically, mesenchyme).
questions.learning: The ciliaris muscle is derived from neural crest cells. It is an intraocular smooth muscle that controls lens accommodation.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Frotteurism is __________
options: Obtaining sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of opposite sex
Desire to seek surgery to become member of opposite sex
Sexual gratification by rubbing his private parts against another person
Exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sexual gratification by rubbing his private parts against another person

• Frotteurism is obtaining sexual gratification by contact with another person (rubbing his private parts against female buttocks, breasts, thighs etc. in crowds etc). It is punishable under Section 292 BNS (290 IPC, with a fine of up to 200 Rs). Under the BNS, it is permissible to be fined up to Rs. 1000.
• Eonism (also known as Transvestism) is a sexual perversion where a person's whole personality is dominated by a desire to be identified as a member of the opposite sex. Usually seen in males who obtain sexual pleasure by wearing female clothes. There is no hormonal/genital abnormality.
• Transsexualism: It is the desire to become members of the opposite sex and seek surgery for anatomical alterations.
• Exhibitionism:  It involves behaviours over a period of 6 months or more, involving the exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger. This is a punishable offence. Section 296 BNS (294 IPC with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine.)
Under the BNS, this is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months, or a fine of Rs. 1000, or with both.
questions.learning: Sexual gratification by rubbing his private parts against another person • Frotteurism is obtaining sexual gratification by contact with another person (rubbing his private parts against female buttocks, breasts, thighs etc. in crowds etc).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is presented with a staggering gait and nystagmus after a road traffic accident. Which lobe of cerebellum is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flocculonodular

Staggering gait with nystagmus indicates involvement of the vestibulocerebellum.

The flocculonodular lobe controls balance, posture, and eye movements via vestibular connections.

Lesions cause truncal ataxia, vertigo, and nystagmus with a positive Romberg sign.

Anterior lobe causes limb ataxia, and vermis affects axial posture without prominent eye signs.

| Structure | Function | Lesion Feature

| --------- | -------- | --------------

| Flocculonodular | Balance + eye movement | ⭐ Ataxia + nystagmus

| Anterior lobe | Posture | Gait disturbance

| Posterior lobe | Fine movement | Limb ataxia

| Vermis | Trunk control | Truncal instability
questions.learning: Flocculonodular Staggering gait with nystagmus indicates involvement of the vestibulocerebellum. The flocculonodular lobe controls balance, posture, and eye movements via vestibular connections.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient with maxillofacial trauma, airway protection is a critical priority because facial injuries can compromise airway patency. Among the various options available for airway control in this setting, which technique is considered the most appropriate for securing the airway?
questions.explanation: In severe maxillofacial trauma, airway management becomes extremely challenging due to bleeding, edema, disrupted anatomy, and possible obstruction by fractured bones or soft tissue. In such cases, conventional airway methods like orotracheal intubation may be difficult or even impossible, especially if: 1. The mouth cannot be opened (trismus/fracture) 2. There is profuse bleeding or debris 3. There is a risk of worsening injury Under these conditions, tracheostomy provides a definitive and secure airway by bypassing the upper airway entirely. It ensures direct access to the trachea, making ventilation reliable even in distorted facial anatomy. Why other options are wrong: (C) Orotracheal intubation : May not be feasible in severe facial trauma (B) Laryngeal mask airway : Not a definitive airway; poor seal, aspiration risk (D) Mask ventilation : Ineffective due to facial disruption
questions.learning: In severe maxillofacial trauma, airway management becomes extremely challenging due to bleeding, edema, disrupted anatomy, and possible obstruction by fractured bones or soft tissue.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An old man presents with dyspnea and swelling of his feet. On examination, rales are heard and he is found to have an enlarged heart on chest x-ray. Which of the following will delay the progression?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Captopril

The given scenario is suggestive of heart failure. ACE inhibitors like captopril are the first-line drugs to prevent further cardiac remodeling and prevent the progression of disease.

Heart failure is a complex clinical syndrome that occurs because the ventricle is unable to fill with or eject blood. The important etiologies of heart failure include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, high output states, such as beriberi, thyrotoxicosis, and severe anemia.

Clinical features of heart failure include dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, pedal edema, anorexia, pallor, elevated JVP, ascites, and hepatomegaly.

Heart failure is classified based on the ejection fraction:

• Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) - left ventricular ejection fraction is ≥50%
• Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction (HFmEF) - left ventricular ejection fraction 40-50%
• Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) - left ventricular ejection fraction is ≤40%

The mainstay management of heart failure is medical therapy and device therapy is reserved for refractory cases. The type of medications used in medical therapy are:

• Drugs with symptomatic and mortality benefits provide symptomatic relief and reduce mortality risk by preventing cardiac remodeling. It includes -

• Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) - a combination of sacubitril and valsartan
• Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors - ramipril, enalapril
• β-blockers - metoprolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol
• Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist - spironolactone, eplerenone
• Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2 inhibitor) - dapagliflozin

• Drugs with only symptomatic benefits provide only symptomatic relief and have no effect on reducing mortality risk. It includes -

• Loop diuretics - furosemide
• Digoxin

Unfortunately, evidence of the clinical benefits of most therapies is restricted to HFrEF. Pharmacological therapy used in HFpEF is mainly diuretics.

Non-pharmacological therapy includes implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICD), cardiac resynchronization using biventricular pacing, etc. These treatments are not found to be effective in HFpEF.
questions.learning: Captopril — The given scenario is suggestive of heart failure. ACE inhibitors like captopril are the first-line drugs to prevent further cardiac remodeling and prevent the progression of disease.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: CT scan of a patient with laryngeal carcinoma is shown below. What is the staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T4N1M0

The given CT image depicts a mass invading the thyroid cartilage as pointed by the red arrows. This indicates a tumor (T) stage of T4. Among the given options, T4N1M0 is the only option with a T4 staging and hence the best answer.

Laryngeal cancer is more commonly seen in men. Alcohol, tobacco, and previous radiation to the neck region are some of the risk factors for the development of laryngeal cancer. The most common type is squamous cell carcinoma.

Larynx is divided into three regions - supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis. In the TNM system: T indicates the extent of the tumor, N indicates lymph node involvement, and M indicates distant metastasis.

TNM classification of laryngeal carcinoma:

Tumor (T)

• T1: Only one site/subsite is involved (one named structure) with both vocal cords mobile.

• T1a: Only one vocal cord involved
• T1b: Involvement of both vocal cords

• T2: Spread to adjacent sites/subsites

• T2a: Both vocal cords are mobile
• T2b: Slight impairment in the mobility of vocal cord

• T3

• Fixed vocal cord
• Involvement of pre-epiglottic space, para-glottic space, post-cricoid space, or inner cortex of thyroid

• T4a: Local invasion.

• Anteriorly: Thyroid cartilage, thyroid gland, strap muscles
• Superiorly: Tongue muscles
• Inferiorly: Trachea
• Posteriorly: Esophagus

• T4b: Unresectable

• Involvement of prevertebral space, carotid sheath, or mediastinum

Regional lymph nodes (N)

• Nx: Cannot be assessed
• No: No regional lymph node metastasis
• N1: Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, ≤3cm
• N2: Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, >3cm but <6cm or multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes or bilateral lymph nodes none more than 6cm
• N3: Metastasis in a lymph node more than 6cm

Distant metastasis (M)

• Mx: Metastasis cannot be assessed
• Mo: No distant metastasis
• M1: Distant metastasis
questions.learning: T4N1M0 — The given CT image depicts a mass invading the thyroid cartilage as pointed by the red arrows. This indicates a tumor (T) stage of T4.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle movements are related to the Abducens nerve?
questions.explanation: The Abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI) is purely a motor nerve that innervates a single extraocular muscle: the lateral rectus. The primary function of the lateral rectus muscle is to abduct the eye, moving it laterally away from the midline. The medial rectus (Option B), superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique (Option D) are all innervated by the Oculomotor nerve (CN III). The superior oblique muscle (Option C) is innervated by the Trochlear nerve (CN IV). A classic mnemonic for eye muscle innervation is , where 6 refers to the abducens and 4 to the trochlear. Clinical paralysis of the abducens nerve results in the inability to abduct the affected eye, leading to convergent strabismus (esotropia) and horizontal diplopia (double vision) that worsens when looking toward the side of the affected muscle. This nerve has a long intracranial course, making it susceptible to damage from increased intracranial pressure
questions.learning: The Abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI) is purely a motor nerve that innervates a single extraocular muscle: the lateral rectus. The primary function of the lateral rectus muscle is to abduct the eye, moving it laterally away from the midline.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A woman visits the gynaecology OPD for a scheduled ANC check-up. A 1st-trimester scan reveals that her child has anencephaly. This occurs due to the inability of neural tube closure at what weeks of intrauterine life?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4th week

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. Neural tube defects (NTDs) result from the failure of the neural tube to close spontaneously between the 3rd and 4th week of in utero development.

Anencephaly is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation.  Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP).

The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.

* Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog.

* Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies. 400 μg of folic acid is given starting preconceptionally and continud throughout pregnancy(In cases with no prior history).

The major NTDs include the following:

* Spina bifida occulta

* Meningocele

* Myelomeningocele

* Encephalocele

* Anencephaly

* Caudal regression syndrome

* Dermal sinus

* Syringomyelia

* Diastematomyelia (split spinal cord)

* Lipoma involving the conus medullaris or filum terminale

* Iniencephaly
questions.learning: 4th week Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. Neural tube defects (NTDs) result from the failure of the neural tube to close spontaneously between the 3rd and 4th week of in utero development.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presented with a skin lesion as shown below. Biopsy shows the presence of multiple neutrophilic foci in the stratum corneum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis

The given image represents plaque psoriasis. The characteristic histopathological finding in psoriasis consists of multiple neutrophilic foci in the parakeratotic stratum corneum i.e Munro’s microabscesses and spongiform neutrophils in the spinous layer of the epidermis i.e spongiform pustules of Kogoj.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin with systemic manifestations. Plaque psoriasis is the most common type. The nails are frequently involved and punctate pitting is the most common finding seen. Psoriasis is associated with Koebner or isomorphic phenomenon. It describes the appearance of new lesions along the site of trauma (linear lesions)

* The peak on occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.

* The lesions are red, scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.

* They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.

* They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

Topical application of steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and emollients is the mainstay of management. Phototherapy and oral methotrexate, acitretin, and cyclosporine can also be used.

Pearl PF1460: Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

I. In Mild Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* Coal tar

* Dithranol

* Potent topical steroid

* Vitamin D analogue

Second line

* Local NB-UVB or PUVA

* Excimer laser

II. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* NB-UVB or PUVA

Second line

* Apremilast

* Ciclosporin

* Fumaric acid esters (where available)

* Methotrexate

Third line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Ustekinumab

III. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis with Psoriatic Arthritis

First line

* Apremilast

* Methotrexate

Second line

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Ustekinumab

Third line

* Combination therapy

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What does a linear accelerator (LINAC) produce in radiation therapy?
questions.explanation: A linear accelerator (LINAC) is the standard device for external beam radiation therapy. It functions by accelerating electrons to high energies using microwave technology. These high-energy electrons can be used directly to treat superficial tumors or directed onto a metal target to generate high-energy X-rays (photons) for treating deep-seated malignancies. Alpha and beta rays (Option A) are products of natural radioactive decay. Gamma rays (Option B) are emitted from isotopes like cobalt-60, not generated by a LINAC. Neutrons and positrons (Option D) are utilized in specialized neutron therapy or PET imaging, respectively. Therefore, the primary therapeutic outputs of a modern LINAC are precisely controlled X-ray beams and electron beams tailored to the tumor's depth
questions.learning: A linear accelerator (LINAC) is the standard device for external beam radiation therapy. It functions by accelerating electrons to high energies using microwave technology.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, and investigations reveal elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels and renal calculi. Which investigation should be performed next?
questions.explanation: The combination of abdominal pain (potentially from peptic ulcers or pancreatitis), renal calculi, and elevated Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) levels in a middle-aged female strongly suggests Primary Hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most often caused by a single parathyroid adenoma. Once the biochemical diagnosis is established, the most appropriate next step for localizing the overactive gland is a Technetium (Tc)-99m sestamibi scan. This nuclear imaging test is highly sensitive for identifying parathyroid adenomas, as they retain the tracer longer than normal thyroid tissue. USG thyroid (Option A) can visualize the thyroid but is less specific for parathyroid localization. A Dexa scan (Option C) is useful to assess bone density in hyperparathyroidism but is not a localization study. A radioactive iodine uptake test (Option D) is used to evaluate thyroid function in hyperthyroidism, not parathyroid disease. Localization is essential for surgical planning, as it allows for a minimally invasive parathyroidectomy
questions.learning: The combination of abdominal pain (potentially from peptic ulcers or pancreatitis), renal calculi, and elevated Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) levels in a middle-aged female strongly suggests Primary Hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Drug of choice for long-term management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) to reduce disease activity and flares is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the cornerstone of long-term treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is recommended for nearly all patients unless contraindicated. Hydroxychloroquine exerts its effect by inhibiting lysosomal antigen processing and Toll-like receptor (TLR-7 and TLR-9) signaling, thereby decreasing autoantigen presentation and cytokine production.

• Hydroxychloroquine is the drug of choice for long-term maintenance therapy in SLE because it:

• Reduces disease flares
• Improves skin and joint manifestations
• Prevents disease progression
• Improves long-term survival
• Lowers thrombotic risk, especially in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies

Why not the other options?

• B. Methotrexate: Used as a steroid-sparing agent for lupus arthritis or skin disease but is not the first-line maintenance drug for all SLE patients.
• C. Cyclophosphamide: Reserved for severe organ-threatening lupus (e.g., lupus nephritis, neuropsychiatric lupus) because of significant toxicity.
• D. Ibuprofen: Provides symptomatic relief of pain and arthritis but does not modify disease activity or prevent flares.
questions.learning: Hydroxychloroquine Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the cornerstone of long-term treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is recommended for nearly all patients unless contraindicated.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a criteria for severe acute malnutrition?
options: Weight for height less than -3 SD
Weight for age less than -3 SD
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight for age less than -3 SD

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) according to the WHO criteria is the weight for height (not age) less than minus -3 SD.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children of ages 6 to 59 months is defined by the WHO as any of the following:

• Weight-for-length (or height) below −3 SD of the WHO child growth standards
• Presence of bipedal edema
• Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) <11.5 cm.

Management of SAM is given below:
questions.learning: Weight for age less than -3 SD Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) according to the WHO criteria is the weight for height (not age) less than minus -3 SD.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The posterior end of the marked structure is present at the level of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eustachian tube

The marked structure shown is the inferior turbinate. The posterior end of the inferior turbinate is present at the level of the opening of the eustachian tube.

The eustachian tube connects the nasopharynx and the tympanic cavity in the middle ear. It is usually collapsed and opens during activities such as yawning or swallowing. Its function is to maintain the pressure in the middle ear cavity and drain any secretions from the middle ear. It opens approximately 1.25 cm behind the posterior end of the inferior turbinate, in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.

The inferior turbinate is the largest turbinate located in the lower part of the lateral nasal wall. The Woodruff’s plexus is located inferior to the posterior end of the inferior turbinate and is responsible for posterior epistaxis in adults.

Other options:

Option B: Sphenopalatine foramen is situated at the posterior end of the middle turbinate.

Option C: Odontoid process is a protuberance of the Axis (C2 vertebra). Part of the axis is located much lower in the neck and not associated with the nasal cavity.

Option D: Sphenoidal sinus opens into the nasal cavity at the superior meatus.
questions.learning: Eustachian tube — The marked structure shown is the inferior turbinate. The posterior end of the inferior turbinate is present at the level of the opening of the eustachian tube.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The children in a school underwent a health check-up whose ages were 2,3,4,4,5,6,7,8. What is their median age?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4.5

The median age here is 4.5 years.

In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value. In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values.

Here: elements: 2,3,4,4,5,6,7,8, therefore median = (4+5)/2= 4.5
questions.learning: 4.5 The median age here is 4.5 years. In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of fever with chills. MRCP image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary sclerosing cholangitis

The presence of fever and chills, along with the MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic beading is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Option B: Caroli's disease is a rare congenital condition characterized by irregular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal extrahepatic duct system. It is common in both sexes and mostly presents before the age of 30 years with abdominal pain, cholangitis, or end-stage liver disease. MRCP shows irregular, cystic dilation of the large proximal intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal common bile duct.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an autoimmune condition characterized by inflammatory strictures involving the intra and extra-hepatic biliary tree. It is a progressive condition that leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis.

MRCP or ERCP will show demonstrate multifocal, diffuse dilatation and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary trees, this pattern is a beading or chain of lakes appearance. Pseudodiverticula of extrahepatic bile ducts are pathognomic of PSC. MRCP is useful in diagnosis and surveillance, while ERCP is reserved for the treatment of dominant strictures and to exclude malignancy.

The below image shows a cholangiogram of primary sclerosing cholangitis:

The common age group of primary sclerosing cholangitis is 30-45 years. Men are affected twice as commonly as women. Two-thirds of these cases are associated with ulcerative colitis. It is also associated with Riedel’s thyroiditis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. 10–20% of patients develop cholangiocarcinoma.

Clinical features of a patient with PSC include pruritis, fever, chills, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, and weight loss.

Liver function tests show a cholestatic pattern with an elevation of ALP and GGT and smaller rises in the aminotransferases. Bilirubin values may be variable.

Liver biopsy excludes other causes of cholestatic liver disease and defines the stage of PSC. It shows onion skin concentric periductal fibrosis. With disease progression, periportal fibrosis occurs, progressing to bridging necrosis, and eventually biliary cirrhosis.

Currently, there is no known effective medical therapy. Surgical management involving resection of extrahepatic biliary tree and hepaticojejunostomy has shown reasonable effects. For patients with advanced liver disease, liver transplantation is the only available option.

Other options:

Option C: Oriental cholangitis, also known as recurrent pyogenic cholangitis is characterized by recurrent attacks of cholangitis due to bile stasis and stone formation. Patients between 30-40 years and both sexes are equally affected. It is caused due to infections (liver flukes, E.coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Proteus). Patients present with Charcot's triad (intermittent fever, pain, and jaundice). MRCP shows intra or extrahepatic calculi, dilatation of ducts, and strictures.

Option D: Biliary carcinoma  (cholangiocarcinoma) most commonly affects patients >60 years and presents with fever, abdominal pain, weight loss, and features of obstructive jaundice. MRCP shows irregular narrowing of the bile duct involved by the tumor, with asymmetric upstream dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts.
questions.learning: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — The presence of fever and chills, along with the MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic beading is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the type of tympanoplasty shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 3

The columella tympanoplasty is type 3 as per the Wullstein's classification of tympanoplasty.

While performing this procedure, the diseased ear would have already lost the malleus and incus, and hence the graft is placed over the stapes superstructure. Therefore, it is also called myringostapediopexy.

Type
Defect and repair

Type I
Perforation of tympanic membrane which is repaired with a graft (myringoplasty)

Type II
Perforation of tympanic membrane with erosion of malleus. The graft is placed on the incus or remnant of the malleus.

Type III
Malleus and incus are absent. The graft is placed directly on the stapes head (myringostapediopexy)

Type IV
Only the footplate of stapes is present. The graft is placed between the oval and round windows on the stapes footplate

Type V
The stapes footplate is fixed but the round window is functioning. The graft is placed in contact with a new window created on the fenestra in the horizontal semicircular canal

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The standardized age mortality ratio is an indicator for which of the following?
options: Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution
Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard sex distribution
Removal of bias due to different age group population in different countries
To eliminate age structure of different countries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution

The age standardized mortality ratio (SMR) is an indicator of the death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution. It is obtained by indirect standardization and cannot be used to compare multiple groups with different age structures.

Standardized death rate (SDR) obtained by direct standardization enables comparisons of mortality rates between populations with different age compositions by eliminating the confounding effect caused by variations in age structures (Options C and D). This adjustment process can also account for factors such as sex, race, and parity.

Standardization can be achieved through two methods: direct or indirect. In both cases, a standard population is selected as a reference, characterized by known numbers in each age and sex group.

The direct method of standardization requires age-specific death rates (ASDR) along with the corresponding subgroup sizes. By applying these rates to the standard population, the expected deaths across all age groups can be calculated assuming that both populations share the same age-specific death rates. Dividing the total expected deaths by the standard population yields the SDR.

The calculated standardized death rate in direct standardization can be compared with different population groups with different age group compositions.

Indirect standardization allows adjustment when age-specific rates are either unavailable or unstable due to small numbers. Examples of indirect standardization methods include standardized mortality ratio (SMR), life table analysis, survival analysis, regression analysis, and multivariate analysis.

SMR estimates expected deaths, assuming that the study group experiences the same death rates as a standard population.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old lady underwent thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma. Postoperatively she developed muscle cramps, perioral and peripheral paresthesia, and carpopedal spasm. Which one of the following interventions is appropriate?
options: Nerve conduction velocity in both upper and lower limbs and administer methylcobalamin
EMG of both lower limbs and administer oral prednisolone
Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate
Measure serum bicarbonate and administer intravenous bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate

Hypocalcemia due to postoperative hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of thyroidectomy. It typically presents within 24–72 hours with perioral numbness, paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, tetany, and positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum ionized calcium, and symptomatic hypocalcemia requires immediate intravenous calcium gluconate.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nerve conduction velocity in both upper and lower limbs and administer methylcobalamin: Nerve conduction studies and methylcobalamin are indicated for peripheral neuropathy, not acute postoperative tetany.
• B. EMG of both lower limbs and administer oral prednisolone: EMG and prednisolone have no role in hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy.
• D. Measure serum bicarbonate and administer intravenous bicarbonate: Bicarbonate is used for metabolic acidosis, not for neuromuscular symptoms caused by hypocalcemia.
questions.learning: Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate Hypocalcemia due to postoperative hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of thyroidectomy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During rounds, you come across the urinalysis report of the 30-year-old male diagnosed with Fabry's disease. What type of urinary casts would you expect to see in the report?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maltese cross cast

Maltese cross urinary casts are seen in a patient diagnosed with Fabry's disease.

Urine analysis in Fabry’s disease may reveal oval fat bodies and birefringent glycolipid globules under polarized light showing a maltese cross appearance. It can also be seen in nephrotic syndrome.

The image below shows Maltese cross appearance under polarized light:

Maltese cross appearance elsewhere:

• Short-range shotgun wound
• Peripheral smear of babesiosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer, recently bitten by fleas in a storage area, presents with high fever, painful inguinal lymphadenopathy, vomiting, diarrhea, and hypotension. Smears from the lymph node discharge show bacteria with bipolar staining. Which staining method should be used to help confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of flea bites and the clinical triad of high fever, painful lymphadenopathy (buboes), and systemic shock (hypotension) is pathognomonic for Bubonic Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis. A hallmark microbiological feature of Yersinia is its bipolar staining, where the ends of the bacilli stain more intensely, giving them a "safety-pin" appearance. Wayson's stain is the specific diagnostic technique used to demonstrate this bipolar staining pattern in clinical samples. Neisser and Albert's stains (Options A and C) are used to visualize the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. McFadyean's stain (Option D) is a specialized polychrome methylene blue stain used to detect the capsules of Bacillus anthracis. Therefore, because Wayson's stain is specifically designed for the rapid identification of the "safety-pin" morphology of the plague bacilli, it is the definitive choice for this farmer's diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s history of flea bites and the clinical triad of high fever, painful lymphadenopathy (buboes), and systemic shock (hypotension) is pathognomonic for Bubonic Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which molecule is universally known to serve as a methyl-group donor in various biochemical reactions?
questions.explanation: S-Adenosyl Methionine (SAM) is the universal activated methyl donor in biological systems. It is formed from the amino acid methionine and ATP. SAM provides the methyl group for hundreds of critical biochemical reactions, including the methylation of DNA, the synthesis of creatine, and the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine. After donating its methyl group, it is converted to S-adenosyl homocysteine. Glucose-6-phosphate (Option A) is a central intermediate in glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. Acetyl CoA (Option B) is the primary donor of acetyl groups and the fuel for the TCA cycle. S-Adenosyl Serine (Option D) is not a standard biochemical methyl donor. SAM’s unique high-energy sulfonium bond makes the methyl group highly reactive, which is why it is the definitive "universal" donor for methylation across all kingdoms of life
questions.learning: S-Adenosyl Methionine (SAM) is the universal activated methyl donor in biological systems. It is formed from the amino acid methionine and ATP.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following aneuploidies is most likely to be missed in prenatal neonatal screening? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Klinefelter’s Syndrome

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is commonly missed during prenatal and neonatal screening because affected individuals often lack obvious congenital abnormalities at birth.

Typical features appear later in life and may include:

• Tall stature
• Small firm testes
• Infertility
• Gynecomastia
• Reduced facial/body hair
• Learning or behavioral difficulties

In contrast:

• Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18 usually present with characteristic dysmorphic features and congenital anomalies detectable prenatally or neonatally.
• Turner syndrome often presents with cystic hygroma, lymphedema, or cardiac defects.

Thus, Klinefelter syndrome is more likely to remain undiagnosed until adolescence or adulthood.
questions.learning: Klinefelter’s Syndrome Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is commonly missed during prenatal and neonatal screening because affected individuals often lack obvious congenital abnormalities at birth.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman is evaluated for primary infertility. Hysterosalpingography was done and reveals the finding shown below. What is the anomaly seen in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Septate uterus

The anomaly seen in the given hysterosalpingogram is suggestive of a septate uterus.

A septate uterus is characterized by the presence of a septum in the endometrial cavity due to the failure of the medial segments of the Müllerian ducts to regress. This creates a permanent septum within the uterine cavity. The septum can project partially from the fundus or can extend completely to the cervical os. On HSG, the septate uterus is seen as widely diverging horns with an intercornual angle <75 degrees.

HSG provides information about the interior of the uterine cavity and not the exterior. Therefore, it cannot reliably differentiate between a septate uterus and a bicornuate uterus. A septate uterus has a smooth fundal contour whereas a bicornuate uterus has an indented fundus.

Transvaginal 3-D ultrasonography (3D TV USG) helps to differentiate between the bicornuate uterus and a septate uterus and is recommended for the assessment of patients with a suspected uterine anomaly. MRI is an accurate investigation to diagnose the septate uterus. Hysteroscopy combined with laparoscopy can confirm both the internal and the external contour of the uterus.

Hysteroscopic septoplasty is a preferred treatment option for the septate uterus. It refers to the resection of the uterine septum under hysteroscopic guidance. There is a reduced risk of pelvic adhesions, scarring and the necessity of cesarean sections for future pregnancies with the hysteroscopic approach, compared with transabdominal approaches.
questions.learning: Septate uterus — The anomaly seen in the given hysterosalpingogram is suggestive of a septate uterus. A septate uterus is characterized by the presence of a septum in the endometrial cavity due to the failure of the medial segments of the Müllerian ducts…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with facial edema progressing to generalized edema. Urinalysis shows heavy proteinuria, light microscopy appears normal, and electron microscopy demonstrates effacement of podocyte foot processes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (accounting for about 80% of cases). It classically presents with sudden-onset edema, starting peri-orbitally (facial) and progressing to anasarca. The diagnosis is confirmed by three key pathological findings: massive proteinuria, a completely normal appearance on light microscopy (hence the name "minimal change"), and the pathognomonic effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes visible only on electron microscopy. FSGS (Option A) shows focal scarring on light microscopy and is more common in adults or steroid-resistant cases. Membranous glomerulonephritis (Option C) shows basement membrane thickening. PSGN (Option D) is a nephritic syndrome (hematuria/hypertension), not a pure nephrotic syndrome. MCD is highly responsive to steroid therapy, which is the standard of care. Therefore, the electron microscopy findings provide the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Minimal Change Disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (accounting for about 80% of cases). It classically presents with sudden-onset edema, starting peri-orbitally (facial) and progressing to anasarca.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A USG can detect lymph node metastases in a patient with breast cancer and clinically negative lymph nodes by what percentage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 50 – 60%

A USG can detect lymph node metastasis in a patient with clinically negative lymph nodes by 50-60%.

The clinical determination of axillary lymph node metastases has an accuracy of only 33%.

Ultrasound (USG) is more sensitive than physical examination alone in determining axillary lymph node involvement during the preliminary staging of breast carcinoma.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or core biopsy of sonographically indeterminate or suspicious lymph nodes can provide a more definitive diagnosis than USG alone.

Ultrasonography can also be utilized to image the regional lymph nodes in patients with breast cancer. The sensitivity for the status of axillary nodes ranges from 35% to 82% and specificity ranges from 73% to 97%.

The features of a lymph node involved with cancer on USG include:

• Cortical thickening
• Change in shape of the node to a more circular appearance
• Size larger than 10 mm
• Absence of a fatty hilum
• Hypoechoic internal echoes
questions.learning: 50 – 60% A USG can detect lymph node metastasis in a patient with clinically negative lymph nodes by 50-60%. The clinical determination of axillary lymph node metastases has an accuracy of only 33%.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Oil drop cataract is seen in?
questions.explanation: An "oil-drop" cataract is a pathognomonic early sign of Galactosemia, an inborn error of metabolism. Because the body cannot process galactose, dulcitol (galactitol) accumulates in the lens. This creates an osmotic gradient that pulls fluid into the lens fibers, resulting in a central opacity that resembles a drop of oil when viewed through a slit lamp. Wilson's disease (Option B) is associated with a sunflower cataract. Gaucher's disease (Option C) and Tay-Sachs disease (Option D) are lysosomal storage disorders; Gaucher's may show pinguecula-like spots, while Tay-Sachs is famous for the "cherry-red spot" on the retina. Importantly, oil-drop cataracts are often reversible if a galactose-free diet is implemented early in infancy. Detecting this sign is critical, as it can be the first diagnostic clue to a potentially life-threatening systemic metabolic condition
questions.learning: An "oil-drop" cataract is a pathognomonic early sign of Galactosemia, an inborn error of metabolism. Because the body cannot process galactose, dulcitol (galactitol) accumulates in the lens.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A doctor asks a patient about her age, and the patient responds, "You know doctor, I'm from a village, I was married at a very young age of 12 years and my husband was just 5 years older than me. Then I had two kids when I was around 18 or something. Now I am 38, but I look like their older sister". What is most likely thought disorder displayed by patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Circumstantiality

Circumstantiality best describes this patient’s thought disorder, as she provides irrelevant and unnecessary details when asked her age before eventually giving the actual answer.

Circumstantiality refers to a formal thought disorder in which a patient gives irrelevant and unnecessary details. This is before finally getting to the point or the correct answer. It may be seen in schizophrenia, obsessional disturbances, and certain cases of dementia. An example is given below.

Doctor: "How did you get that bruise?"

Patient: "I woke up and had a cup of coffee, read the newspaper, and went for a walk. It was a wonderful day in the park. I returned home and watched the TV. I took a nap in the afternoon after lunch. I slipped and fell in the bathroom. The fall gave me this bruise."

A formal thought disorder is a disturbance in the formulation of thoughts and their expression. It is characterized by loosened associations, illogical constructs, and neologisms. Derailment, neologism, perseveration, and thought blocking are some examples.

Other options:

Option A: Clang association is a formal thought disorder where the thoughts are associated with the sound of words through rhyming, rather than the meaning of the words. It is usually seen in schizophrenia or mania. An example is "I am Sam...I like jam...I travel in a tram"

Option B: Flight of ideas refers to a rapid succession of multiple associations, where the thoughts appear to abruptly shift from one idea to another. It is usually seen in mania. An example is "I like mangoes, the weather is nice, India is great"

Option D: Tagentiality is a formal thought disorder where the patient says something that is related to the general topic. Although, the actual answer is not given. An example is as below.

Doctor: "How has your appetite been lately?"
Patient: "I usually have dinner with my wife, but now I eat alone"

Pearl PF1257: Disorders of thought and perception

DISORDERS OF THOUGHT

DISORDER OF STREAM OF THOUGHT

(A) Disorder of tempo

(i) Flight of Ideas

Continuous flow of rapid speech that jumps from topic to topic

•

"I like mangoes, the weather is nice, India is great"

(ii) Retardation of thinking

Slow speed of speech and a prolonged latent period before a response

•

"I went to the market (pause)......... the shop was closed"

(iii) Circumstantialities

Inclusion of irrelevant details and going on in a roundabout manner, but their thought ultimately reaches the answer

•

Doctor: "How did you get that bruise?"

•

Patient: "I woke up and had a cup of coffee, read the newspaper and went for a walk. It was a wonderful day in the park. I returned home and watched the TV. I took a nap in the afternoon after lunch. I slipped and fell in the bathroom. The fall gave me this bruise."

(iv) Clang associations

Jumping from one word to another irrelevant rhyming word

•

I am Sam...I like jam...I travel in a tram"

(B) Disorder of continuity

(i) Perseveration

Repetition of out of context words, phrases, or ideas beyond the point of relevance.

•

Q1. What's your name?: "Rahul"

•

Q2. Where are you from?: "Rahul"

•

Q3. How old are you?: "Rahul"

(ii) Thought blocking

A sudden disruption of thought or a break in the flow of ideas

•

"I went to the market (extreme silence)...................."

DISORDER OF FORM OF THOUGHT

(i) Tangentiality

In response to a question, the patient gives a reply that is appropriate to the general topic but does not answer the question exactly. The speech moves away from the actual answer.

• Doctor: "Have you had any trouble sleeping lately?"
• Patient: "I usually sleep in my bed, but now I'm sleeping on the sofa"

(ii) Derailment

A breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of goal-directedness. The words make sentences, but the sentences do not make sense.

• "Some people just don't understand why I had breakfast in America during the first world war"

(iii) Neologisms

Bringing in new words that do not exist.

• The world is not 'gooder' for people like me"

(iv) Desultory thoughts

Speech is grammatically correct, however, sudden unrelated ideas force their way in from time to time.

• My actual problem is that the people never understand me and my stomach feels like an empty bucket"

(v) Word salad

Using a mixture of unintelligible meaningless words and sentences

• Tree bus rain food home car tiger"

DISORDER OF POSSESSION OF THOUGHT

(A) Obsession and compulsion

(i) Obsessions

Recurrent and persistent thoughts, impulses. or images that cause distress to oneself.

• Fear of dirt or contamination
• Fear of becoming ill
• Constant thoughts of a certain number
• Need for symmetry or exactness
• Worry about whether something has been done "right"
• Forbidden sexual or religious thoughts

(ii) Compulsions

Repetitive behaviors or actions that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession

• Washing hands
• Blinking eyes
• Counting items, such as currency
• Checking to see if doors are locked
• Arranging items in a certain way
• Requiring constant approval from people around them

(B) Thought alienation

(i) Thought insertion

Thoughts are being inserted into the patient's mind and they recognize them as being foreign and coming from without any stimulus

•

"I have repeated thoughts of killing my neighbors and I believe aliens are putting these ideas into my head at night"

(ii) Thought withdrawal

Delusion that someone or something is removing from one's mind and the patient has no power over this.

•

"Lately, I am losing all my memories and I believe that the 'government agents' are stealing them when I go to sleep"

(iii) Thought broadcasting

Belief that one's thoughts are quietly escaping from one's mind and that other people might be able to access them and hear or see them.

•

"I believe my exact thoughts appear on the TV and the internet and I think I can broadcast them globally"

(iv) Thought echo

Patient hears the 'echo' of his own thoughts in the form of a voice after he has made the thought.

•

"I thought of making a sandwich in the morning and surprisingly a voice, from nowhere, told me to make a sandwich out loud"

DISORDER OF CONTENT OF THOUGHT

(i) Phobias

Persistent fear of an object or situation, typically disproportional to the actual danger posed, in which the sufferer goes to great lengths in avoiding it

•

Arachnophobia - fear of spider

•

Barophobia - fear of gravity

•

Cynophobia - fear of dogs

•

Hemophobia - fear of blood

•

Nosocomephobia - fear of hospitals

(ii) Religious preoccupations

Thoughts involving religious themes or subject matter.

•

"I get instructions from God on how to make my country great"

(iii) Ideas of hopelessness

Thoughts of complete despair where the patient strongly believes that the circumstances will never get better for him.

•

"I am never going to pass my final exams, no matter how hard I study"

(iv) Antisocial urges

Thoughts of indulging in some behaviors or actions that harm or lack consideration for the well being of others.

•

"I have these urges to go rob a bank or blackmail my neighbors for their money"

(v) Derealization

Alteration in the perception or experience of the external world so that it seems unreal

•

"The world and everything around is nothing but just a dream"

(vi) Depersonalization

Feeling as if one is disconnected from reality, feeling detached from one's own thoughts and one's own physical body

•

"I sometimes drift into a dream-like state where I lose contact with my own self"

(vii) Delusions

False beliefs that are strongly held and unchangeable in the face of refuting evidence and that are not consistent with the person's educational, social and cultural background.

The three main criteria for a belief to be considered a delusion are:

•

Certainty (held with complete confidence)

•

Incorrigibility (not changeable by proof to the contrary)

•

Impossibility or falsity of content (implausible, bizarre or patently untrue)

DISORDERS OF PERCEPTIONS

•

Illusion: Misinterpretation of real external stimuli.

•

Hallucination: False sensory perception, externally.

•

Pseudohallucination: False sensory perception from within and having an insight.
questions.learning: Circumstantiality Circumstantiality best describes this patient’s thought disorder, as she provides irrelevant and unnecessary details when asked her age before eventually giving the actual answer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked A in the image below gives rise to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Falciform ligament

The structure marked A is ventral mesentery. The falciform ligament is a derivative of the ventral mesentery.

Mesenteries are double layers of the peritoneum that enclose an organ and connect it to the body wall. They provide pathways for vessels, nerves, and lymphatics to and from the abdominal viscera.

• Ventral mesentery: Only the foregut has a ventral mesentery. It is attached to the terminal part of the esophagus, the stomach, and the upper part of the duodenum. The ventral mesentery is derived from the septum transversum. When the liver grows into the mesenchyme of the septum transversum, it divides the ventral mesentery into 2 parts:

• Lesser omentum- extends from the lower portion of the esophagus, the stomach, and the upper portion of the duodenum to the liver
• Ligaments of the liver- all ligaments of the liver (falciform ligament, right and left triangular ligaments, and coronary ligaments), except ligamentum teres

• Dorsal mesentery: The foregut, midgut, and hindgut have a dorsal mesentery. This connects the organs to the posterior abdominal wall. It runs from the lower end of the esophagus to the cloacal region of the hindgut. It has the following special names in different regions:

• Dorsal mesogastrium (or greater omentum)- stomach
• Dorsal mesoduodenum- duodenum
• Mesentery proper- jejunum and ileum
• Mesoappendix- appendix
• Transverse mesocolon- transverse colon
• Sigmoid mesocolon- sigmoid colon
• Gastrosplenic ligament (stomach to the spleen), lienorenal ligament (spleen to the left kidney), and gastrophrenic ligament (stomach to diaphragm) are derived from the dorsal mesentery.
questions.learning: Falciform ligament — The structure marked A is ventral mesentery. The falciform ligament is a derivative of the ventral mesentery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following layers is responsible for maintaining the hydration and transparency of the cornea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endothelial cells

The hydration level and transparency of the cornea is maintained mainly by the endothelial cells of the cornea.

The endothelium possesses Na+/K+ ATPase, which keeps the corneal stroma in a relatively dehydrated state. This helps maintain corneal transparency. Endothelial cells decrease in number with age. If the cornea becomes overhydrated, it begins to scatter light and gradually begins to lose its transparency

Other factors contributing to the transparency of the cornea are as follows:

• Regular arrangement of corneal lamellae (Maurice theory)
• The peculiar refractive index of corneal lamellae (Goldmann theory)
• Avascularity of the cornea
• A balance between the intraocular pressure (IOP) and swelling pressure

The different layers of the cornea are as follows:

• Epithelium
• Bowman’s membrane
• Stroma (substantia propria)
• Dua’s layer (pre-Descemet’s layer)
• Descemet’s membrane
• Endothelium

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the given image, the tendon marked by the arrow is?
questions.explanation: The tendon indicated in the image lies on the radial (lateral/thumb) side of the anterior wrist, which corresponds to the flexor carpi radialis (FCR). This tendon becomes prominent when the wrist is flexed, especially during a clenched fist. The flexor carpi radialis originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and inserts into the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals. Functionally, it is responsible for flexion and abduction of the wrist. Due to its position, the FCR tendon is located just lateral to the palmaris longus, which lies more centrally. In the image, the marked tendon is clearly not in the midline, ruling out palmaris longus, and instead is positioned toward the radial side, confirming it as flexor carpi radialis. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Palmaris longus → Midline tendon 2. Flexor carpi ulnaris → Ulnar (medial) side 3. Flexor digitorum superficialis → Deep tendon

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic liver disease presented with jaundice and melena. On examination, there is ascites and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is not part of the management of his encephalopathy?
options: Beta blocker to stop variceal bleed
Ascitic tap to rule out SBP

Correct answer: A. Beta blocker to stop variceal bleed

• Jaundice → hepatocellular dysfunction
• Melena → variceal bleed (precipitating factor)
• Ascites → portal hypertension
• Hepatosplenomegaly → chronicity

Most important: This patient is at high risk of hepatic encephalopathy (HE)

Hepatic encephalopathy management focuses on identifying precipitating factors like GI bleed, SBP, and renal failure. Ascitic tap is essential to rule out SBP, and evaluation for hepatorenal syndrome is required.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-week-old neonate was brought to the hospital with complaints of non-bilious vomiting. During the examination, the physician noted a firm, olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, which moved during feeding. What is the likely diagnosis for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

The clinical scenario of projectile non-bilious vomiting with an olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, which moved during feeding, is suggestive of Idiopathic Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis.

Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk.

Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right(not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting.

Metabolic abnormality:

* Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e. Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

* Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

* Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway.

* The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions.

* Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia.

* Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body loses more H+ ions through urine.

Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm. The cervix sign and nipple sign are signs seen on USG.

* Double-layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called Nipple sign.

* The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the cervix sign.

Management:

* The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality has to be corrected before proceeding to surgery.

* The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy remains the standard surgical procedure for its treatment.

Other options:

Option A: Esophageal atresia is a congenital condition where the oesophagus fails to properly connect to the stomach, leading to feeding difficulties and potential aspiration. It is often associated with a fistula between the oesophagus and trachea, requiring surgical correction.

Option C: Duodenal atresia is a congenital obstruction of the duodenum, often causing vomiting and inability to pass stool shortly after birth. It is commonly associated with a "double bubble" sign on abdominal X-rays due to the accumulation of air in the stomach and duodenum.

Option D: Intussusception is a condition where a part of the intestine folds into an adjacent segment, causing obstruction, pain, and potential blood in the stool. It commonly affects infants and young children and can be treated with an enema or surgery if needed.

Pearl PF1850: Radiological findings in various GI disorders

Duodenal atresia: Double bubble sign

Jejunal and ileal atresia: Multiple air-fluid levels (plain erect X-ray abdomen) presenting as triple bubble sign.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Single enlarged gastric gas bubble - single bubble sign

Sigmoid volvulus: Coffee bean sign

Achalasia cardia: Bird-beak sign
questions.learning: Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis — The clinical scenario of projectile non-bilious vomiting with an olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, which moved during feeding, is suggestive of Idiopathic Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT imaging reveals a renal mass, and the aldosterone–renin ratio (ARR) is elevated. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The combination of hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, a high Aldosterone-Renin Ratio (ARR), and a localized adrenal mass is highly suggestive of an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn’s Syndrome). In cases of confirmed unilateral adrenal disease in a surgical candidate, laparoscopic adrenalectomy is the definitive treatment of choice as it can cure the underlying hyperaldosteronism. Medical management with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like Spironolactone (Option A) is generally reserved for patients with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or those who are not fit for surgery. The ACTH stimulation test (Option C) is used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease), which presents with hypotension and hyperkalemia. The Dexamethasone suppression test (Option D) is the standard investigation for Cushing’s syndrome, which involves cortisol excess. Given the evidence of a unilateral functional tumor, surgical removal is the most appropriate management step

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 10-year- old child with a two-year history of recurrent fractures, blue sclera, dental abnormalities, and a positive family history?
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI), often called "brittle bone disease," is a genetic disorder of Type I collagen synthesis. The clinical presentation is classic: frequent fractures from minimal trauma, blue sclera (due to thinning of the scleral collagen allowing the underlying choroid to show through), and dentinogenesis imperfecta (dental abnormalities). The positive family history supports its autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Scurvy (Option A) involves Vitamin C deficiency and causes bleeding gums and subperiosteal hemorrhages. Rickets (Option B) is due to Vitamin D deficiency and presents with bony deformities like bowing of legs and "rachitic rosary". Osteomalacia (Option D) is the adult form of rickets, involving defective bone mineralization rather than a primary collagen defect. OI is diagnosed clinically and confirmed by genetic testing. There is no cure, so management focuses on preventing fractures and using bisphosphonates to increase bone density. Therefore, the ocular and dental findings confirm the diagnosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a study investigating insulin regulation, which of the following factors was found to inhibit insulin secretion?
questions.explanation: Insulin secretion from the pancreatic beta cells is tightly regulated by various neurological and hormonal signals. Epinephrine (and sympathetic stimulation) has a potent inhibitory effect on insulin secretion by binding to -adrenergic receptors on the beta cells. This mechanism is critical during stress or exercise (the "fight or flight" response) to prevent hypoglycemia and ensure that glucose is available for use by the brain and muscles. In contrast, Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide (Option B), now better known as Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide (GIP), is an incretin hormone that stimulates insulin release in response to food. Acetylcholine (Option C), representing parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation, also stimulates insulin secretion, particularly during the cephalic phase of digestion. None of the above (Option D) is incorrect as epinephrine is a well-established inhibitor. Understanding these regulatory pathways is fundamental for comprehending metabolic homeostasis and the pharmacological management of glucose disorders. The -mediated inhibition by epinephrine is a classic example of autonomic control over endocrine function

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with profuse vaginal discharge associated with a characteristic fishy odor. Microscopic examination of the vaginal smear reveals the cell shown in the image. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of profuse vaginal discharge, a characteristic fishy odor (especially noticeable after adding KOH—the "whiff test"), and the microscopic visualization of Clue cells is diagnostic for Bacterial vaginosis (BV). Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells so heavily coated with bacteria (Gardnerella vaginalis) that their borders appear blurred and stippled. Herpes (Option A) presents with painful vesicles. Candida albicans (Option B) causes a thick, "curd-like" discharge and shows pseudohyphae on microscopy. Trichomonas vaginalis (Option C) involves a green, frothy discharge and motile flagellated protozoa. BV results from a dysbiosis where normal lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobic bacteria. It is the most common cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age. Diagnosis is confirmed using Amsel's criteria. Management involves oral or topical metronidazole. While BV is not technically a sexually transmitted infection, it is associated with increased sexual activity and can increase the risk of acquiring other STIs, including HIV
questions.learning: The clinical triad of profuse vaginal discharge, a characteristic fishy odor (especially noticeable after adding KOH—the "whiff test"), and the microscopic visualization of Clue cells is diagnostic for Bacterial vaginosis (BV).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vertex positions is the least common during childbirth? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left Occipitoposterior (LOP)

The most common fetal vertex position during labor is occipitoanterior, especially Left Occipitoanterior (LOA), because the left oblique diameter of the maternal pelvis is slightly larger and better accommodates fetal descent.

Frequency of vertex positions:

• LOA → most common
• ROA → common
• Occipitoposterior positions → less common
• Left Occipitoposterior (LOP) → least common

Occipitoposterior positions are associated with:

• Prolonged labor
• Increased back pain (“back labor”)
• Higher risk of instrumental delivery or cesarean section

Thus, LOP is considered the least common vertex position during childbirth.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image shows methylene blue dye being injected in the peritumoral region. What is this procedure useful for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sentinel lymph node biopsy

The utility of injection of methylene blue in the region around the tumor is done for sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLN) in patients without clinically positive lymph nodes.

SLN biopsy rationale:

• Afferent lymphatics from a primary tumor first drain into the sentinel node before draining into the other nodes. So, if a sentinel lymph node is positive for metastsis, it is possible that the other axillary nodes are also involved. Hence, axillary dissection would be necessary.
• If the sentinel node is tumor-free, then regional nodal metastasis is unlikely.

The nodes can be identified using fluorescein dye, methylene blue, or radioactive sulfur colloid-labeled albumin. The dye can be injected into the peritumoral tissue, subareolar, periareolar, or intradermal plane.

Contraindicated in patients with inflammatory breast cancer, stage T4 disease, a history of previous breast cancer or chest wall surgery, breast scarring, and radiotherapy.
questions.learning: Sentinel lymph node biopsy — The utility of injection of methylene blue in the region around the tumor is done for sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLN) in patients without clinically positive lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient was suspected to have acute brucellosis. A serum sample was sent for a standard agglutination test. It came out to be negative initially but after serial dilutions of the serum sample, the test turned out to be positive. Which of the following is responsible for the initial negative test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prozone phenomenon

The initial negative test is explained by the prozone phenomenon. The standard agglutination test is a tube agglutination test that mainly identifies IgM antibodies. It is used in establishing a diagnosis of acute brucellosis.

Prozone phenomenon refers to the failure of a visible precipitation reaction due to inhibition of lattice formation by the presence of excessive antibodies. This gives rise to a false-negative test. This excess in antibodies can be overcome by diluting the serum sample, leading to an increase in the antigen-antibody interactions, eventually giving rise to a positive result.

Lattice hypothesis:

The lattice hypothesis explains precipitation reactions. The amount of precipitate formed is greatly influenced by the relative proportions of antigens and antibodies.

• Prozone phenomenon: Caused by excessive antibodies in the test system. (weak/absent precipitation- false-negative test)
• Zone of equivalence: Antigens and antibodies are in optimum proportions and maximum precipitation occurs.
• Post–zone phenomenon: (Option-D) Due to the presence of excessive antigen in the test system. (weaker/absent precipitation)

Standard agglutination test identifies mainly IgM antibodies, hence it is useful in acute brucellosis. Following 7-10 days of infection, both IgM and IgG antibodies appear. The IgM antibodies then gradually fall and only IgG antibodies persist in chronic brucellosis. The complement fixation test (Option-B) is more useful in chronic cases as it detects the IgG antibody also.

Brucellosis/ Undulant fever:

Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease caused by gram-negative, capnophilic coccobacilli. The most important species that are pathologic to humans are B.melitensis, B. suis, and B.abortus. It is transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products.

These bacteria proliferate within the reticuloendothelial system, which accounts for its resistance to simple antimicrobial therapy.

Patients with acute infection may present with undulant fever, arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.

Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis includes:

• Polymerase chain reaction
• Blood culture with Castaneda method
• Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
• Tests for animals and animal products: Milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests.

• Milk ring test- A sample of milk is mixed with stained brucella antigen and incubated. If the sample contains antibodies, agglutination occurs seen as a blue ring.

Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with IM streptomycin and oral doxycycline. Prevention of brucellosis can be achieved by pasteurization of milk and milk products.

The images below show the Casteneda's medium and the milk ring test respectively.
questions.learning: Prozone phenomenon — The initial negative test is explained by the prozone phenomenon. The standard agglutination test is a tube agglutination test that mainly identifies IgM antibodies.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Maternal infection that may lead to teratogenic effect is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

Several maternal viral infections can cross the placenta and cause teratogenic effects in the fetus. These infections are often grouped under the TORCH complex.

Rubella leads to congenital rubella syndrome, CMV causes microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss, and varicella (chicken pox) can result in congenital varicella syndrome.

Hence, all listed infections are associated with fetal malformations, especially when infection occurs in early pregnancy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A mother brought her 6 month old infant baby to an Anganwadi worker Lata for advice regarding the vaccination of her child. The last vaccines he had received were OPV3, PENTA 3, IPV2, and ROTA3 at 14 weeks of age. BCG and Hep B were given at birth. When is the next vaccination due?
options: MR vaccine at left arm intramuscularly and Vitamin A drops at the end of 9 months
MR vaccine at right arm subcutaneously and Vitamin A drops at the end of 8 months
MR vaccine at left arm intramuscularly and Vitamin A drops at the end of 8 months
MR vaccine at right arm subcutaneously and Vitamin A drops at the end of 9 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MR vaccine at right arm subcutaneously and Vitamin A drops at the end of 9 months

According to the National Immunization Schedule, the Measles/MR vaccine is given at 9 completed months (1st dose), and a second dose is given at 16-24 months. Measles vaccine can be given till 5 years of age. A dose of 0.5 mL is administered subcutaneously in the right upper arm.

Vitamin A schedule in the National Immunisation Schedule(NIS)

• 1 lakh IU at 9 completed months along with the Measles-Rubella vaccine
• 2 lakh IU is administered bi-annually for children between 1-5 years of age

Total number of doses administered- 9 doses,17 lakhs IU

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Major contributor for amniotic fluid post 20 weeks is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fetal urine

Fetal urine is the major contributor to amniotic fluid post 20 weeks.

Amniotic fluid is present in the amniotic cavity which is the space between the epiblast (ectoderm) and trophoblast. The volume of the amniotic fluid increases with pregnancy and reaches a maximum at term. It is contributed by:

• Early pregnancy - ultrafiltrate of maternal plasma (option D).
• Second trimester - the extracellular fluid that diffuses through the fetal skin (option B) and thus reflects the composition of fetal plasma.
• After 20 weeks - keratinization of fetal skin prevents diffusion across the skin. Hence, fetal urine forms amniotic fluid.

Note: Fetal kidneys start producing urine at 12 weeks (8–11 weeks), and by 18 weeks, they produce 7 to 14 mL per day.
